# Intent-Clustering Overlay Hardening - Plan

## Goal Capsule

- **Objective:** Close the gaps an adversarial review found in the shipped intent-clustering overlay (`sgt/intent/*`, U1-U8 of `docs/plans/2026-07-17-001-feat-intent-clustering-overlay-plan.md`) so it survives messy real-world history (non-add-only commits, rebases, non-conventional messages, large scope-less backlogs) without crashing, silently mis-reverting, or breaking its own stated invariants.
- **Authority hierarchy:** This plan's Key Technical Decisions govern implementation; where a unit's approach conflicts with the original U1-U8 plan's KTDs, this plan's decision supersedes it for the affected code path only (the original KTDs are not being re-litigated wholesale).
- **Stop conditions:** Stop and flag if fixing the `tier()` crash (U1) requires changing `order.py`'s public `upset_in`/`downset_in` contracts in a way that changes behavior for their existing callers (`group_requires`/`apply_subset`, U8's sync resolve, `restore`/`cherry-pick` verbs) — those must stay byte-identical.
- **Execution profile:** Standard code change across `sgt/core/order.py`, `sgt/intent/group.py`, `sgt/intent/theme.py`, `sgt/intent/resolve.py`, `sgt/cli/intent.py`, `sgt/api.py`, plus tests. No new dependencies, no schema migration (themes.json's shape is additive-only).
- **Tail ownership:** Whoever implements U1-U7 also updates the affected docstrings' claims (several currently assert invariants the review found unenforced) and runs the full existing test suite plus the new tests each unit adds.

## Product Contract

### Summary

An adversarial code review of the intent-clustering overlay (dispatched per explicit request, transcript-verified against the actual code) found six concrete defects ranging from a reproducible crash to unenforced docstring claims. The most severe two share one root cause: `sgt/core/order.py` has no primitive for "are these ops structurally connected" that works on an arbitrary op subset — only on a subset already known to be a valid, downward-closed ideal. `tier()` (rung-0/1 cross-feature grading) and `scope_bundles()` (rung-1 merging) both need exactly that arbitrary-subset connectivity question answered, and neither can safely reuse `upset_in`/`downset_in` as-is. This plan adds the missing primitive once and uses it to fix both call sites, then fixes four smaller, independent defects the same review surfaced.

### Problem Frame

The overlay's safety story rests on membership being a pure deterministic function of provenance and dependency data. Four of the six findings undermine that story in practice, not in theory:

- `tier()` (`sgt/intent/group.py:164`) passes a bare op-id set — "this commit's ops" or "this bundle's ops" — into `order.downset_in`, which internally calls `_ordered_chains` (`sgt/core/order.py:308-309`). `_ordered_chains` assumes every symbol touched by the input set has its chain head (`before=None` producer) inside that same set — true for a genuine ideal, false for an arbitrary commit/bundle op-set. Any commit that modifies a pre-existing symbol without also carrying that symbol's origin op raises `KeyError: None`. Because `sgt/api.py`'s `compose_view` builds its entire aggregate (`map`, `history`, `status`, `forks`, `plan`, `drift`, `sessions`, `trust`, `oracle_verdict`, `proposals`) as one unguarded dict literal that also calls `intent_view` (line 1066), this single crash takes down every one of those views, not just the intent overlay.
- `scope_bundles()` (`sgt/intent/group.py:107-126`) merges every atom sharing a conventional-commit scope string into one bundle with zero structural check — confirmed unconditional. `tier()`, the only signal that could flag a bad merge, is never consulted by `sgt intent revert` (`sgt/cli/intent.py:125-157` never references `tier`); it only renders as a list/show badge a user must separately notice before reverting.
- Persisted `themes.json` is keyed on commit shas that a rebase/amend/force-push can invalidate. `intent_view` (`sgt/api.py:1023`) and `resolve_group` (`sgt/intent/group.py:183`) both silently filter out vanished shas (`if sha in atoms_by_sha`, `if sha in by_sha`) with no staleness signal, so a revert can silently act on a diminished subset of what a theme claims, or report "no change" when the theme is actually orphaned.
- `group_scopeless` (`sgt/intent/theme.py:137-188`) has no cross-group dedup (an atom can appear in two persisted themes) and truncates scope-less atoms to `MAX_ATOMS=40` sorted by sha, silently dropping the rest from ever getting a theme — both falsify `build_themes`'s own docstring claim that "every atom lands in exactly one theme."

A fifth finding (`sgt/intent/resolve.py`'s independently-coded LLM-confinement check) is not unsafe today but is an architectural inconsistency worth closing while the rest of this code is being touched: it enforces "the LLM never invents a ref" by caller convention, while `theme.py` enforces the equivalent guard inside the module itself.

### Requirements

**Structural connectivity primitive**

- R1. `sgt/core/order.py` provides a connectivity primitive that answers "are two ops linked by a chain/reference/declared edge path" over an arbitrary op-id subset, without assuming the subset is downward-closed or grounded.
- R2. `tier()` uses that primitive instead of `downset_in`, so it never raises on a commit/bundle whose op-set omits a touched symbol's origin op, and correctly detects coupling that passes through an op outside the group (the review's finding #7 undercounting case).

**Rung-1 structural gating**

- R3. `scope_bundles()` splits same-scope atoms into separate bundles when they are not structurally connected (via the R1 primitive over the atoms' own op-ids), so two unrelated commits sharing a scope string no longer merge into one revertable unit.
- R4. `sgt intent revert`'s preview surfaces a bundle's tier so a `thematic`-only (no structural backing) group is visibly flagged before the user commits to reverting it as one unit.

**Staleness signaling**

- R5. `intent_view` reports which persisted theme shas no longer resolve against the current atom partition, instead of silently dropping them.
- R6. `sgt intent revert <theme>` refuses (with a clear message) to proceed on a theme with any unresolved member sha, rather than silently reverting a diminished subset or reporting a misleading "no change."

**Theme partition integrity**

- R7. `group_scopeless` never assigns the same atom sha to two different returned groups; on an LLM response that overlaps groups, the first group (in the LLM's returned order) keeps the atom and later groups drop it.
- R8. `group_scopeless` processes all scope-less atoms in bounded chronological batches (chunking, not truncating) so every atom ends up in exactly one theme regardless of how many scope-less atoms exist, and the cache key change from batching is accounted for in the existing content-hash cache.

**Shared LLM-confinement guard**

- R9. The "output refs/shas must be a subset of what was shown, or dropped" check that `theme.py` currently inlines is extracted into one shared function, and `sgt/intent/resolve.py` calls it too, so both modules enforce the invariant identically rather than independently.

### Scope Boundaries

- **In scope:** the six findings above, confined to `sgt/intent/group.py`, `sgt/intent/theme.py`, `sgt/intent/resolve.py`, `sgt/cli/intent.py`, `sgt/api.py`, and one new primitive in `sgt/core/order.py`.
- **Deferred:** `group_requires`/`apply_subset`'s own reliance on `_grounded` over a non-ideal `group_op_ids` (noted during review verification as a related but not-yet-confirmed risk — `_grounded` degrades to under-inclusion rather than crashing, so it is lower urgency than `tier()`'s crash). Flagged as a follow-up, not fixed here.
- **Outside this plan's identity:** rung-0 atom-identity stability under history rewrites at the `atoms()` level (the atom's `commit_sha` changing identity across a rebase is expected/by-design per the original plan's docstrings); this plan only fixes the *silent* consumption of that fact downstream (R5/R6), not the identity scheme itself.

## Planning Contract

### Key Technical Decisions

- **KTD1 — One connectivity primitive, not two crash-avoidance patches.** `tier()`'s crash and `scope_bundles()`'s fragility both reduce to the same missing capability: undirected structural connectivity over an arbitrary op-id subset. Rather than special-casing `downset_in` for `tier()` and inventing a separate walk for rung-1, `sgt/core/order.py` gets one new function, `components_in(op_ids, ops, declared)`, returning the connected components of `op_ids` under the union of `chain_edges | reference_edges | declared`, restricted to edges whose both endpoints are in `op_ids`. This is plain undirected BFS/union-find over a restricted edge set — it never calls `_ordered_chains`/`_grounded`, so it has no downward-closure precondition to violate. `tier()` and `scope_bundles()` both become callers of this one primitive.
- **KTD2 — Undirected connectivity, not directed reachability, for both call sites.** `tier()`'s question ("does this group's op-set touch more than one feature via a real dependency edge") and rung-1's question ("are these same-scope atoms actually one coherent change") are both connectivity questions, not "does A build on B" direction questions — `upset_in`/`downset_in`'s direction is the wrong shape here, not just their downward-closure precondition. `components_in` returns components; callers ask "are op X and op Y in the same component," never "does X precede Y."
- **KTD3 — Tier becomes a gate for revert confirmation, not just a list/show badge.** R4's fix keeps `tier()` computed the same way (descriptive), but `_revert` (`sgt/cli/intent.py`) now includes the tier in its preview output for every atom/bundle being reverted, so `thematic`-tier groups are visible at the point of action, not only in a separate `sgt intent list` call the user has to remember to run first. This does not block the revert (the original plan's "preview, never silent" discipline stays intact) — it surfaces the signal at the decision point instead of leaving it to be discovered elsewhere.
- **KTD4 — Staleness is a visible field, not a refusal, in `intent_view`; but `_revert` refuses.** `intent_view` (a read) reports staleness (R5) so `sgt intent list`/`show` can render it; `_revert` (a destructive action) refuses outright on any unresolved sha (R6) rather than silently reverting a subset. Read paths inform; the write path that can destroy data blocks until the user re-runs `sgt intent build` to reconcile.
- **KTD5 — Batch scope-less atoms instead of truncating.** R8 replaces the `[:MAX_ATOMS]` truncation with chunking: atoms are sorted chronologically (not by sha — sha-sort was itself part of the truncation's instability) and split into chunks of `MAX_ATOMS`, each chunk gets its own LLM call and its own cache key (content-hash over that chunk's members, same scheme as `_bundle_key`), and `build_themes` iterates all chunks. A store with 45 scope-less atoms costs two LLM calls instead of one, but every atom gets a theme and the cache still hits on an unchanged chunk.
- **KTD6 — Extract the hallucination guard as a pure function over (produced, shown) sets.** R9's shared guard takes "the items the LLM was shown" and "the items the LLM's output named" and returns "the output filtered to only items that were actually shown" — a pure set-intersection operation already implicit in `theme.py:183`'s `[g for g in groups if frozenset(g.atom_shas) <= valid_shas]`. Lifting this into `sgt/intent/_guard.py` (or a similarly-scoped shared module) and having `resolve.py` call it closes the divergence risk without changing either module's existing behavior for the common case.

### High-Level Technical Design

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph order.py
        CE[chain_edges] --> COMP[components_in - NEW]
        RE[reference_edges] --> COMP
        DE[declared edges] --> COMP
    end
    COMP --> TIER[group.tier - rewritten]
    COMP --> BUNDLE[group.scope_bundles - rewritten]
    TIER --> INTENTVIEW[api.intent_view]
    BUNDLE --> BUILDTHEMES[theme.build_themes]
    INTENTVIEW --> STALE[stale_shas field - NEW]
    STALE --> CLI_LIST[cli.intent._list / _show]
    STALE --> CLI_REVERT[cli.intent._revert - refuses on stale]
    BUILDTHEMES --> DEDUP[group_scopeless dedup - NEW]
    BUILDTHEMES --> CHUNK[group_scopeless chunking - NEW]
    GUARD[shared hallucination guard - NEW] --> DEDUP
    GUARD --> RESOLVE[resolve.py resolve_intent]
```

### Assumptions

- The existing test suite (`tests/intent/`, `tests/core/test_order.py`) is the correctness baseline; no unit in this plan changes `order.py`'s existing public function behavior for their current callers.
- `components_in`'s BFS over `chain_edges | reference_edges | declared` restricted to a given `op_ids` set is cheap enough for interactive CLI use at this repo's current scale (same assumption `tier()`'s original `downset_in` call already made — this plan does not need a new performance budget).
- No change to `themes.json`'s on-disk shape is required beyond adding fields (`stale_shas` is computed at read time in `intent_view`, never persisted); existing `themes.json` files remain readable.

## Implementation Units

### U1. `components_in`: undirected structural connectivity over an arbitrary op-id subset

- **Goal:** Add the one primitive KTD1/KTD2 call for — connected components of a given op-id set under `chain_edges | reference_edges | declared`, with no downward-closure precondition.
- **Requirements:** R1
- **Files:**
  - `sgt/core/order.py` — add `components_in(op_ids: frozenset[str], ops: list[Op], declared: Declared = frozenset()) -> list[frozenset[str]]`.
  - `tests/core/test_order.py` — new tests.
- **Approach:** Build the restricted undirected adjacency directly (mirror `_adjacency`'s edge-union logic but keep it undirected and restrict both endpoints to `op_ids`, not `ops`), then run the same `_reachable`-style BFS from each unvisited node to produce components. Do not route through `_grounded` or `_ordered_chains` — that is the exact precondition this primitive exists to avoid. Also add a convenience `connected(a: str, b: str, op_ids, ops, declared) -> bool` (are `a` and `b` in the same component) since both `tier()` and `scope_bundles()` ask that shape of question, not "list all components."
- **Test Scenarios:**
  - Two ops linked by a chain edge, both in `op_ids` → one component.
  - Two ops linked only through a third op *outside* `op_ids` → two separate components (confirms this does NOT silently walk through excluded ops — that would just reintroduce a different form of finding #7's miscount from the other direction; the fix is "answer connectivity correctly for the restricted set," not "pretend excluded ops don't exist as a boundary").
  - An op-id set where one op modifies a symbol whose origin op is *not* in the set → no crash, that op is simply its own singleton component (this is the direct regression test for the `KeyError: None` finding, run through the primitive in isolation before U2 wires it into `tier()`).
  - Empty `op_ids` → empty list, no crash.
  - A `declared` edge between two ops in `op_ids` → they're in the same component even with no chain/reference edge.
- **Verification:** `pytest tests/core/test_order.py -v`.

### U2. Rewrite `tier()` on `components_in`, fixing the crash and the undercounting

- **Goal:** `tier()` never raises on real, non-add-only commits, and correctly reports `coupled` when connectivity passes through an op outside the group.
- **Requirements:** R2
- **Files:**
  - `sgt/intent/group.py` — rewrite `tier()`'s body (lines ~145-168).
  - `tests/intent/test_group.py` — new tests; keep existing passing tests green.
- **Approach:** Replace the `order.downset_in(op_id, group_op_ids, all_ops, declared)` walk with `order.components_in(group_op_ids, all_ops, declared)` computed once per call, then for each component check whether it spans more than one feature via `feature_span` on that component's op-ids restricted to `op_leaf`. `coupled` fires when any single component (not the whole group) spans ≥2 features — this is what fixes finding #7: a component naturally includes any op needed to connect two group members, even one outside the group, because `components_in` computes components over the full `all_ops` edge set restricted to `group_op_ids`'s *membership test*, not restricted to walking only through `group_op_ids` internally. Re-verify this distinction against U1's second test scenario before wiring it in — the fix must connect *through* an external op's edges without ever admitting that external op's id into the reported component (since `tier()` only cares about the group's own ops' feature span).
- **Test Scenarios:**
  - The exact repro from the review: `feat(x): add foo` then `chore: tweak foo and add bar` (foo modified without its origin op in the same atom, bar in a different feature) → `tier()` returns a tier string, does not raise.
  - Two group ops in different features connected only through a third op outside the group → `coupled` (regression test for finding #7).
  - Existing `coupled`/`co-changed`/`thematic` fixtures from the current test file continue to pass unchanged.
- **Verification:** `pytest tests/intent/test_group.py -v`, `pytest tests/core/test_order.py -v`.

### U3. Structural gating in `scope_bundles()`

- **Goal:** Same-scope atoms only merge into one bundle when structurally connected; unconnected same-scope atoms become separate bundles.
- **Requirements:** R3
- **Files:**
  - `sgt/intent/group.py` — `scope_bundles()` (lines 107-126), signature gains `all_ops: list[Op]` and `declared` parameters.
  - `sgt/intent/theme.py` — `build_themes()` call site updated to load and pass `all_ops`/`declared` (mirroring the exact pattern `cli/intent.py::_revert` already uses at lines 132-133).
  - `sgt/cli/intent.py` — no signature change needed (calls `build_themes(repo)` only); confirm no other caller of `scope_bundles` needs updating.
  - `tests/intent/test_group.py` — new tests.
- **Approach:** Within each scope's candidate atom list, run `order.components_in(union of atom op_ids, all_ops, declared)`, then group atoms by which component their op-ids landed in — one `Bundle` per component, still keyed to the same `scope` string, sorted the same deterministic way `scope_bundles` already sorts. An atom whose ops touch no other same-scope atom's ops (a singleton component) becomes its own single-atom `Bundle` with that scope, same as today's scope-less singleton shape but now for a same-scope atom that failed to connect. This preserves the "every atom lands in exactly one bundle" total-partition property while removing the false-merge risk.
- **Test Scenarios:**
  - Two commits both `fix(auth): ...` whose ops share a chain edge → one bundle (current behavior preserved for the legitimate case).
  - Two commits both `fix(auth): ...` with no structural edge between their ops → two separate bundles, same scope string, each a small component (the review's exact repro: unrelated CVE patch and doc typo fix coincidentally both scoped `auth`).
  - Three same-scope atoms where two are connected and one is isolated → one two-atom bundle plus one singleton bundle.
  - Scope-less atoms are entirely unaffected (still singleton, still routed to rung 2).

- **Goal:** A user reverting a `thematic`-tier group sees that signal at the point of the revert, not only via a separate `list`/`show` call.
- **Requirements:** R4
- **Files:**
  - `sgt/cli/intent.py` — `_revert()` (lines 125-157): compute and print each chosen atom's/the group's tier before the existing "reverting N atom(s) as one group" print.

- **Approach:** `_revert` already has `all_ops`, `declared`, and the chosen atoms in scope (lines 132-142) — call the same `group.tier()` U2 rewrote, using `op_leaf` (load via the same tree-loading path `intent_view` uses) to compute one tier for the union of chosen atoms' op-ids, and print/emit it alongside the existing atom listing. Do not block the revert on tier — KTD3 keeps this informational, consistent with the "preview, never silent" discipline the rest of `sgt` follows.
- **Test Scenarios:**
  - Reverting a `thematic`-tier bundle prints the tier badge/word in the non-JSON path.
  - JSON revert preview includes a `tier` field.

### U5. Staleness signal in `intent_view`, refusal in `_revert`

- **Goal:** A theme whose persisted shas no longer resolve against the current atom partition is visibly flagged on read, and blocks revert on write.
- **Requirements:** R5, R6
- **Files:**
  - `sgt/api.py` — `intent_view()` (around lines 1019-1037): add a `stale_shas` list (persisted shas with no matching current atom) per theme.
  - `sgt/intent/group.py` — `resolve_group()` (lines 173-188): return enough information for the caller to detect a partial/total resolution failure, or add a companion check function.
  - `sgt/cli/intent.py` — `_list`/`_show` render `stale_shas` when non-empty; `_revert` (lines 125-157) checks for any unresolved sha in the target theme and fails with a clear message ("run `sgt intent build` to reconcile — N member commit(s) no longer resolve") instead of proceeding.
- **Approach:** In `intent_view`, compute `member_shas - {atoms present}` per theme (the set `atoms_by_sha` already filters against) and attach it as `stale_shas` rather than silently discarding it. In `_revert`, before calling `group.resolve_group`, compare the target theme's persisted `atom_shas` (if `target` resolves as a theme in `themes.json`) against `{a.commit_sha for a in all_atoms}` and refuse if any are missing — this is a stricter, earlier check than relying on `resolve_group`'s existing silent-filter behavior, which stays unchanged for other callers.
- **Test Scenarios:**
  - A theme with all member shas present → `stale_shas` is empty, `_revert` proceeds as today.
  - A theme with one member sha missing (simulating a rebase) → `intent_view` reports it in `stale_shas`; `_revert` on that theme fails with the reconcile message instead of reverting the remaining members.

### U6. Fix `group_scopeless`: no double-membership, no truncation-drop

- **Goal:** Every scope-less atom lands in exactly one theme, regardless of LLM response overlap or backlog size.
- **Requirements:** R7, R8
- **Files:**
  - `sgt/intent/theme.py` — `group_scopeless()` (lines 137-188) and `build_themes()` (lines 202-257).
  - `tests/intent/test_theme.py` — new tests.
- **Approach:** For R7, track a running `assigned: set[str]` while building `groups` from the LLM's `result.groups` in order; when resolving each group's `atom_shas`, drop any sha already in `assigned` before appending the group, then union the group's surviving shas into `assigned` — first group wins, matching the LLM's own returned order deterministically. For R8, replace the `[:MAX_ATOMS]` slice with chronological chunking (sort scope-less atoms by `_atom_sort_key`, split into `MAX_ATOMS`-sized chunks), call the existing per-chunk LLM/cache path once per chunk with a chunk-scoped cache key (extend `_scopeless_key` to hash the chunk's own members, which it already does per-list — just call it per chunk instead of once over a truncated list), and have `build_themes` merge results from all chunks into one `themes` dict as it already does per-bundle.

### U7. Shared LLM-confinement guard used by both `theme.py` and `resolve.py`

- **Goal:** One enforced implementation of "the LLM's output is filtered to what it was actually shown," not two independently-coded versions.
- **Requirements:** R9
- **Files:**

def tier(
    group_op_ids: frozenset[str], commit_shas: frozenset[str], all_ops: list[Op],
    declared, op_leaf: dict[str, str],
) -> str:
    """`coupled | co-changed | thematic` for one group (KTD3). `commit_shas` is the set of
    distinct commits the group's atoms came from -- a single-commit group can only ever be
    `co-changed` (same-commit, cross-feature, no edge) or below `coupled`; a multi-commit group
    with no dependency edge is `thematic`. Reuses `order.downset_in` exactly as
    `proposal_review_view` does, restricted to the group's own op-set -- never a new closure walk."""
    from sgt.core import order

    span = feature_span(group_op_ids, op_leaf)
    if len(span) < 2:
        return CO_CHANGED if len(commit_shas) <= 1 else THEMATIC

    for op_id in group_op_ids:
        leaf = op_leaf.get(op_id)
        if leaf is None:
            continue
        closure = order.downset_in(op_id, group_op_ids, all_ops, declared)
        if any(op_leaf.get(oid) not in (None, leaf) for oid in closure):
            return COUPLED

    return CO_CHANGED if len(commit_shas) <= 1 else THEMATIC

def tier(
    group_op_ids: frozenset[str], commit_shas: frozenset[str], all_ops: list[Op],
    declared, op_leaf: dict[str, str],
) -> str:
    """`coupled | co-changed | thematic` for one group (KTD3). `commit_shas` is the set of
    distinct commits the group's atoms came from -- a single-commit group can only ever be
    `co-changed` (same-commit, cross-feature, no edge) or below `coupled`; a multi-commit group
    with no dependency edge is `thematic`. Uses `order.components_in` -- undirected connectivity
    restricted to the group's own op-set -- rather than `downset_in`/`upset_in`: those assume
    `group_op_ids` is itself a valid, downward-closed ideal (they walk `_ordered_chains`, which
    raises `KeyError` on a modify op whose chain head is outside the set), and an arbitrary
    commit's or scope-bundle's op-set is not guaranteed to be one. `components_in` has no such
    precondition -- it answers "are these ops linked at all," which is exactly what a tier needs."""
    from sgt.core import order

    span = feature_span(group_op_ids, op_leaf)
    if len(span) < 2:
        return CO_CHANGED if len(commit_shas) <= 1 else THEMATIC

    for component in order.components_in(group_op_ids, all_ops, declared):
        leaves = {op_leaf[oid] for oid in component if oid in op_leaf}
        if len(leaves) >= 2:
            return COUPLED

    return CO_CHANGED if len(commit_shas) <= 1 else THEMATIC

def group_scopeless(self, atoms: list[IntentAtom]) -> list[ThemeGroup]:
        """Coalesce scope-less atoms into named themes. Unlike `label_bundle`, membership here
        *is* LLM-decided (this is the "coalescer" half of KTD4) -- so every returned `atom_shas`
        is validated as a subset of the shas actually shown, and any hallucinated sha is dropped
        before persistence, never trusted.

        Processes all atoms in bounded, chronologically-ordered chunks of `MAX_ATOMS` (R8/KTD5)
        rather than truncating to the first `MAX_ATOMS` -- every scope-less atom gets a theme
        regardless of backlog size, one LLM call + one content-hash cache entry per chunk (an
        unchanged chunk on rebuild hits the cache; a chunk with a new atom does not). Populates
        `scopeless_chunk_key_by_sha` so `build_themes` can look up which chunk's cache entry
        produced a given returned group, without re-deriving the chunking here."""
        if not atoms:
            return []
        ordered = sorted(atoms, key=_atom_sort_key)
        chunks = [ordered[i:i + MAX_ATOMS] for i in range(0, len(ordered), MAX_ATOMS)]
        groups: list[ThemeGroup] = []
        for chunk in chunks:
            chunk_key = _scopeless_key(chunk)
            for atom in chunk:
                self.scopeless_chunk_key_by_sha[atom.commit_sha] = chunk_key
            groups.extend(self._group_scopeless_chunk(chunk, chunk_key))
        return groups

    def _group_scopeless_chunk(self, chunk: list[IntentAtom], key: str) -> list[ThemeGroup]:
        """One `MAX_ATOMS`-bounded chunk's LLM/cache call. `assigned` (R7) tracks which atom
        shas an earlier group (in the LLM's own returned order) already claimed, so a later
        group naming an already-claimed sha -- an overlapping LLM response -- drops it instead of
        letting the atom land in two persisted themes; first group wins."""
        cached = self.cache.get(key)
        valid_shas = frozenset(a.commit_sha for a in chunk)
        if cached is not None and cached.get("source") == "llm":
            return [
                ThemeGroup(label=g["label"], rationale=g["rationale"], atom_shas=g["atom_shas"])
                for g in cached["groups"]
            ]

        lines = "\n".join(f"{a.commit_sha[:8]} | {a.subject}" for a in chunk)
        prompt = (
            "These commits in a semantic version-control tool declared no conventional-commit "
            "scope. Group any that plausibly share one underlying theme (e.g. fixing the same "
            "bug, building the same feature) into named groups; leave a commit out of every "
            "group if it doesn't plausibly share a theme with any other.\n"
            "For each group: label (2-5 words, Title Case), rationale (one line), and atom_shas "
            "-- the exact 8-char sha prefixes from the list below that belong to this group "
            "(>=1). Never invent a sha not shown.\n\n"
            f"Commits (sha | subject):\n{lines}\n"
        )
        try:
            result, source = self._request(prompt, ThemeGroups), "llm"
            groups: list[ThemeGroup] = []
            assigned: set[str] = set()
            for g in result.groups:
                kept = [sha for sha in g.atom_shas if any(sha == a.commit_sha[:8] for a in chunk)]
                resolved = [
                    a.commit_sha for a in chunk if a.commit_sha[:8] in kept and a.commit_sha not in assigned
                ]
                if resolved:
                    groups.append(ThemeGroup(label=g.label, rationale=g.rationale, atom_shas=resolved))
                    assigned.update(resolved)
            for atom in chunk:
                if atom.commit_sha not in assigned:
                    groups.append(ThemeGroup(
                        label=(atom.subject or atom.commit_sha[:8])[:60],
                        rationale="Ungrouped commit.", atom_shas=[atom.commit_sha],
                    ))
                    assigned.add(atom.commit_sha)
        except Exception:
            groups, source = _fallback_scopeless_groups(chunk), "fallback"

        groups = [g for g in groups if frozenset(g.atom_shas) <= valid_shas]
        self.cache[key] = {
            "source": source,
            "groups": [{"label": g.label, "rationale": g.rationale, "atom_shas": g.atom_shas} for g in groups],
        }
        return groups

def _scopeless_atoms(tmp_path, n: int) -> list:
    gb, _ = init_store(tmp_path)
    for i in range(n):
        (tmp_path / f"f{i}.py").write_text(f"def fn{i}():\n    return {i}\n", encoding="utf-8")

    get(tmp_path)
    return group.atoms(tmp_path)

    overlapping = theme.ThemeGroups(groups=[
        theme.ThemeGroup(label="Group A", rationale="first", atom_shas=[shas[0][:8], shas[1][:8]]),
        theme.ThemeGroup(label="Group B", rationale="second", atom_shas=[shas[1][:8], shas[2][:8]]),

"""Shared LLM-confinement guard (plan U7/KTD6, R9): the one enforced rule that an LLM's output
must never smuggle in an id it was never shown. Both `sgt.intent.theme` (scope-less coalescing)
and `sgt.intent.resolve` (NL target resolution) name candidates the LLM invented from a fixed

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Callable, Iterable

def filter_to_shown(items: list, shown_keys: frozenset[str], keys_of: Callable[[object], Iterable[str]]) -> list:
    """Keep only the items every one of whose `keys_of(item)` keys is in `shown_keys`. An item
    naming even one id it was never shown is dropped whole, never trusted -- this is a pure
    set-intersection check, no exceptions, no partial trust."""
    shown = frozenset(shown_keys)
    return [item for item in items if frozenset(keys_of(item)) <= shown]

# Performance rework of the clustering / labelling / map pipeline

## Context

`sgt`'s core kernel (mining, ideal reduction, the `opindex` footprint sidecar) is already
genuinely incremental — `mine(since=witness)` diffs only new commits and `opindex.apply_delta`
upserts only touched ops. **That layer is not the problem and is out of scope.**

The slowness the user reports ("startup, grouping/clustering/labelling all unoptimized;
incremental update claims to be incremental but everything updates anyway") comes entirely from
the **feature-tree / map overlay** (`sgt/lens/`) and its **LLM label fan-out**. This overlay was
designed as a pure from-scratch fold: every `sgt map` / TUI refresh / sync re-reads the whole op
store, re-derives the entire coupling graph, and re-clusters the entire symbol universe. Only the
*labels* (member-hash cache) and *feature ids* (Greene matching) survive between runs — the
clustering itself never does. A one-symbol edit pays the full-repo cost.

Intended outcome: the common case (`sgt map` after a small edit, or a no-op UI refresh) becomes
cheap and proportional to what actually changed, without degrading clustering quality (gated by
the existing BET-C / MoJoFM measurement) and without touching the kernel's correctness invariants.

Decisions locked with the user:
- Implement **all 4 phases**, but **Phase 2 (dirty-subtree reclustering) must pass a BET-C check
  before landing** — a speed win must not silently degrade feature grouping.
- LLM fan-out fix = **both** batching (fewer round-trips) **and** concurrency (parallel calls).

---

## Phase 0 — Mechanical waste removal (low risk, do first, establishes baseline)

Goal: kill compute that is paid for and thrown away, with near-zero behavior change. Measure
`sgt map` wall-clock before and after to get a real baseline for later phases.

1. **Stop decoding `images` on the clustering/label path.**
   `sgt/lens/map.py:24` calls `Store(repo).all_ops()`, which hex-decodes every op's `images` blob
   (~85% of on-disk bytes per `opindex.py:5`). Nothing under `sgt/lens/` reads `.images` (verified:
   `grep .images sgt/lens/*.py` is empty). Swap to `sgt.core.opindex.index_ops(repo)` (already
   self-healing, already used by `lens._sync`). Same for the two other full-store readers on the
   overlay path: `sgt/intent/theme.py` (`build_themes`) and `sgt/intent/group.py` (`atoms`,
   `scope_bundles`) — all read footprint/provenance only.
   - Guard: `index_ops` returns ops with `images={}`; `opindex.py:9-11` warns never to pass these
     to `fold.code`. Confirm none of these overlay paths materialize bytes (they don't — they
     cluster/group). Add an assertion-free comment at each swap site.

2. **Add an `edges_only` fast path to `build_entity_graph`** (`sgt/entities/graph.py:213`).
   It always computes `_transitive_reduction` (Tarjan SCC + per-edge reachability, `graph.py:182`)
   and `_components` (`graph.py:294`). Verified **nothing in production reads `.reduced_edges` or
   `.components`** — only `tests/entities/test_graph.py:14`. The clustering caller
   (`cluster.signals`, `cluster.py:189`) reads only `.edges`; the miner caller
   (`mine.py:337`) reads only `.edges` / `.entities`. Add a param (e.g.
   `build_entity_graph(codebase, *, edges_only=False)`) that skips the reduction + components when
   set, returning them as `[]`. Pass `edges_only=True` from both `cluster.signals` and `mine.py`.
   Keep the full path for the test. This removes an O(E·(V+E)) pass from every mine and every
   cluster build.

Verification for Phase 0: `pytest tests/` green; `sgt map` output byte-identical (diff
`tree.json` before/after); record wall-clock delta.

---

## Phase 1 — Incremental coupling-graph maintenance (the real "incremental" fix)

The fused coupling graph is `structural ⊕ co-change ⊕ scope` (`tree.fused_graph`, `tree.py:201`).
Co-change and scope edges are **sums over immutable, content-addressed ops** — ideal for
incremental accumulation instead of full re-scan. Structural edges depend only on HEAD's tree.

1. **Cache structural edges keyed by HEAD sha.** `cluster.signals` (`cluster.py:186-191`)
   re-parses the entire repo at HEAD every build via `build_entity_graph(gb.tree_at(head))`.
   Persist `{head_sha, edges}` to a new local artifact; if `gb.head()` is unchanged since the last
   build, skip the re-parse entirely. This alone makes the very common "re-ran `sgt map` / UI
   refresh with no commit" case nearly free on the structural side.

2. **Incrementally accumulate co-change + scope edges.** Persist the fused-edge accumulator plus
   the set of op-ids already folded in (mirror `opindex`'s staleness pattern: store
   `{op_ids_hash, cochange, scope, hub_freq}`). On rebuild, fold in only ops new since last build
   and remove edges from ops no longer present. Note the subtlety: **hubs** (`cluster.py:172-176`)
   and `hub_normalize` (`cluster.py:114`) are global-frequency-dependent, so recompute the hub set
   and the normalization from the (cheaply maintained) per-symbol frequency counter — don't try to
   incrementalize the normalization itself, just avoid the full op re-scan feeding it.

3. **New local artifact** in `sgt/state.py` `_ARTIFACTS` (follow the `op_index` entry pattern,
   `state.py:143`): `committed=False`, self-healing, never authoritative. Staleness = op-id-set
   mismatch or `MINER_VERSION` bump (reuse `opindex`'s dirent/mtime approach conceptually).

Verification for Phase 1: a new test asserting the incremental accumulator produces a
**byte-identical fused graph** to the from-scratch `fused_graph` on the same op set (this is the
correctness contract — incremental must equal full). `pytest tests/lens/` green. Wall-clock delta
on `sgt map` after a 1-commit edit vs. cold.

---

## Phase 2 — Dirty-subtree reclustering (highest value, gated on BET-C)

Currently `_subdivide` (`tree.py:129`) recurses the whole symbol universe and `_split_once`
(`tree.py:89`) binary-searches Leiden up to `MAX_SEARCH_ITER=20` times **per node**, each rebuilding
a fresh igraph (`_leiden`, `cluster.py:143`). Cost ≈ (tree nodes) × 20 × Leiden, every run.

Approach — reuse the previous `tree.json`:
1. Load `previous` tree (`tree.load`, already passed into `build`, `tree.py:253`). Build the
   `leaf_member_index` (`tree.py:180`) from it.
2. Diff the alive-symbol set + fused edges against the previous build (Phase 1's accumulator makes
   the changed-op set cheap to know). Mark a leaf **dirty** if: it gains/loses a member, or it
   gains/loses a cross-edge to another leaf above a threshold. Propagate dirtiness to the parent
   only when the child set changes.
3. Re-run `_split_once` **only on dirty subtrees**; splice unchanged subtrees through verbatim
   (keep their nodes, members, ids). Feed unchanged subtrees straight into `_register` /
   `assign_ops_to_leaves` (`tree.py:184`) as-is.
4. Greene `match_identities` (`tree.py:359`) still runs over the resulting leaf set for id
   stability — but most leaves now match trivially because they were spliced unchanged.
   Incidentally fix the O(|old|·|new|) double-`_jaccard` in `tree.py:386` (compute once, reuse).

**Semantics change (explicit):** results become path-dependent — a locally re-optimized tree, not
a fresh global optimum each run. This is the tradeoff the user accepted.

**BET-C gate (mandatory before landing):** `scripts/bet_c_mojofm.py` measures MoJoFM of the leaf
partition vs. a package gold. Procedure: (a) record baseline MoJoFM from the current full-rebuild
tree; (b) run N sequential incremental builds simulating real edit sequences; (c) assert the
incremental tree's MoJoFM stays within an agreed tolerance of a from-scratch rebuild at the same
HEAD. If it degrades beyond tolerance, Phase 2 does **not** land — fall back to Phases 0/1/3 (which
already give most of the speedup) and keep full-rebuild clustering. Add a "reclustered from scratch"
escape hatch (e.g. `sgt map --rebuild`) regardless, so a user can always force a global optimum.

Also apply to the sync path: `reconcile.reconcile_tree` (`reconcile.py:129`) currently rebuilds
full ("The tree is *rebuilt*, not merged", `reconcile.py:6`). It can reuse the same dirty-subtree
build with `previous` = the caller's last-known tree; correctness is identical since the tree is
derived, not authoritative.

Verification for Phase 2: BET-C tolerance check (above) is the gate. Plus `pytest tests/lens/`
green, and a determinism test (same op set + same `previous` → same tree).

---

## Phase 3 — LLM label fan-out: batch + concurrency

`tree.label_tree` (`tree.py:564-611`) walks bottom-up firing **one serial `responses.parse` call
per dirty node** (`labeler.label` / `label_super`), no batching, no concurrency. A 40-leaf cold
tree = 40 sequential network round-trips.

1. **Batch:** add a `label_many(items)` method to `Labeler` (`sgt/lens/label.py`) that names
   multiple clusters in one `responses.parse` call with a list-typed pydantic schema
   (`list[FeatureLabel]` with a stable index back to each cluster key). Keep the per-cluster cache
   keying (`_key(members)`, `label.py:36`) — only the cache **misses** go into a batch; hits are
   served locally as today. Group siblings/peers into batches of a bounded size.
2. **Concurrency:** run the batches concurrently. Simplest fit for the existing **sync** client is
   `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` (network-bound, releases the GIL on I/O) — avoids an
   `async` refactor of the whole call path. Bound the pool (e.g. 4–8) to respect rate limits.
   `Labeler`'s token counters (`tokens_in/out/calls`, `label.py:58`) must become thread-safe
   (a lock, or accumulate per-future and sum at join).
3. Keep the deterministic offline fallback (`_fallback_label`, `label.py:40`) per-item so a partial
   batch failure degrades gracefully rather than failing the whole tree.
4. `label_super` (`tree.py:599`) depends on child labels, so it must run after its children — keep
   the bottom-up dependency but parallelize **within** each tree level (all leaves concurrently,
   then all depth-d internal nodes concurrently, etc.).

Verification for Phase 3: existing label tests green; the persistence test
`test_build_map_persists_label_cache_so_reruns_dont_re_call_the_llm` (per memory
[[label-cache-and-rebuild-architecture]]) must still pass — a warm cache still makes zero calls.
Assert `label_many` on all-cached input fires zero network calls. Measure `sgt map` cold-cache
wall-clock (label phase) before/after.

---

## Cross-cutting notes

- **"Remove unnecessary attributes"**: concretely resolved by Phase 0.2 (`reduced_edges`/
  `components` no longer computed on hot paths) and Phase 0.1 (`images` no longer decoded on read
  paths). No struct field is *deleted* — they're kept for the one test / the materialization path
  that legitimately needs them; we just stop computing them where unused. If a later audit shows a
  field is truly dead everywhere, delete it then, separately.
- **Do not touch** the kernel: `mine.py`'s incremental mining, `order.py`'s ideal reduction,
  `store.py`'s op format, `opindex`'s sidecar. They're correct and already incremental.
- **Model config** is duplicated across 5 modules (`MODEL="gpt-5.4-mini"` in `label.py:25`,
  `theme.py`, `resolve.py`, `plan.py`, `api_backend.py`). Not a perf issue — leave it unless the
  user asks; centralizing it is a separate cleanup.

## Overall verification

1. `pytest tests/` fully green after each phase (14.6k lines of tests; `tests/lens/` = 1760).
2. Byte-identical `tree.json` after Phase 0; incremental-equals-full graph test after Phase 1;
   BET-C tolerance gate after Phase 2; zero-call warm-cache assertion after Phase 3.
3. End-to-end: on this repo (10,944 ops in `.sgt/ops/`, 114 MB `.sgt/`), time `sgt map` cold, then
   after a 1-file edit, then a no-op re-run — the last two should be dramatically faster than cold
   and than the current `main`.
4. Golden CLI-surface snapshot regenerated only if `sgt map` output shape legitimately changes
   (it shouldn't for 0/1/3; Phase 2 may reorder internal `N*` ids — those are non-identity-bearing
   per `tree.py:248`).

    gold = {sym: gold_package(sym) for sym in source}

Why semantic-git

a discussion of what a symbol-level version-control model learns from, and gives up against, git, jj, Darcs, Pijul, and lazy merging

Abstract Every version control system answers the same four questions differently: what is the smallest thing history remembers, how does it know two of those things are “the same thing” across edits, what happens when two edits disagree, and what has to be true for a merge to need no guessing at all. Git answers all four at the level of text lines inside file snapshots. Darcs, Pijul, jj, and a 2022 formalization called “lazy merging” each rebuild parts of that answer on more rigorous ground — patches as algebra, conflicts as graph structure, commits as an evolving identity, edits as CRDT lattice elements — while staying at the same grain: a line, a hunk, a tree. sgt (semantic-git) moves the grain itself, from line to symbol, and asks the same four questions again at that level. This is not a claim that symbol-level is a strictly better answer. It buys a specific thing — clean, undo-and-redo-safe removal and reattachment of a function's or feature's worth of history, which is the actual unit a coding agent or a reviewer thinks in — and it pays for that with weaknesses the line-level systems don't have. The rest of this piece works through where each system's soundness comes from, where it runs out, and what carries over, using one running scenario throughout so the differences show up as concrete, checkable facts rather than slogans.

§1The running scenario

One scenario, reused at every step. It is small enough to draw and specific enough that each system's answer to it is a fact, not an opinion.

A repository has one file, billing.py, with three top-level functions: charge, refund, and apply_discount. Call this state C0. Two lines of work start from C0 at the same time:

actor: the agent
An autonomous coding agent is told to harden billing.py for production. It runs for about an hour, unattended, and lands three things in one pass before handing control back: a caching layer wrapped around charge, a retry policy wrapped around refund, and — because it was already in the file — a broad “clean up billing.py” pass that also rewrites the internals of apply_discount, unrelated to the two features it was asked for.
actor: Alicia
Alicia, a human engineer, starts from the same C0 at the same time. She has noticed apply_discount mis-rounds fractional cents, and makes one small, surgical fix to it.

Neither knows about the other yet. Alicia's fix and the agent's cleanup pass both rewrite apply_discount — that is a real disagreement, not a tooling artifact, and no system in this piece makes it disappear. What differs, system to system, is how much of the rest of the hour's work gets dragged into that disagreement, how the disagreement is represented while it's unresolved, how it gets resolved, and whether the resolution has to be redone the next time either side changes. Later sections add two follow-up events to the same scenario: someone decides the caching layer was a mistake and wants it gone without touching the other two features, and someone wants Alicia's rounding fix carried onto a version of apply_discount that has since moved on. Every section below picks the scenario up where the last one left it.

§2The unit of history: snapshot, patch, or op

Before any system can talk about merging or reverting, it has to answer a much smaller question: when it remembers “something changed,” what is the smallest thing it remembers?

Git's answer is the one most readers already carry around without examining it: a commit is a complete snapshot of the whole file tree, plus a pointer to its parent commit(s). There is no patch object anywhere in a .git directory. A diff is not stored; it is computed, on demand, by comparing two snapshots' trees. This is why git is fast and simple to reason about — a commit is self-contained, checkout is just “read this tree” — and it is also the root of almost everything the rest of this piece is about, because a system that never stored the edit has nothing to consult when two edits need to be reconciled except the two end states. Git's three-way merge algorithm reconstructs a plausible edit by diffing each side against a common ancestor and hoping the two diffs land on disjoint regions of the file. When they don't, git has no record of why either side changed what it changed, only that they both changed something near each other.

Darcs was the first of the systems here to reject that. A darcs repository is not a sequence of snapshots but a set of patches — each patch a first-class value: insert these lines here, delete those lines, rename this file. The working tree is derived by applying the set; the patches are the primary data, and a snapshot is just one particular fold of them. This sounds like a small inversion, but it opens a real question snapshot systems can't even pose: do two patches commute — can you apply them in either order and land on the same file? Two patches that touch unrelated regions commute; two that touch the same region usually don't. Git cannot ask this question because it never has two patches to compare, only two snapshots.

Pijul pushes the same idea one level further: instead of a set of line-based patches applied to a flat file, the repository is a directed graph of byte ranges, where an edge means “change c says this span comes before that span,” and a patch is an operation that adds vertices and edges to that graph or relabels an edge dead. The unit of history is stored as graph surgery, not a textual insert/delete pair, which is what lets a Pijul conflict be a shape in the graph rather than a search problem — more on that in §4. jj keeps git's snapshot as the literal unit — a jj commit is still, on disk, a git tree — but layers a second identity, the change, on top of it (§5), so the unit of history a user thinks in (“this logical change”) is decoupled from the unit git actually stores (“this exact tree”). Lazy merging goes finer than any of these: its primitive is an editor transaction — a single causally-ordered edit to one cell of a document, recorded the instant it happens, not batched into a commit at all (§9).

sgt's answer sits at a different grain than any of the above: the unit is an op, one content-addressed record of a single symbol advancing from one version to another — billing.py::charge going from version h0 to h1, say. An op's identity is the hash of its own payload (which symbol, which before/after content, what it structurally requires), not the commit that happened to introduce it, so two independent mining runs that see the same edit always produce the same op id. Like Darcs and Pijul, the op is the primary data and files are derived (“folded”) from the live op set; like jj, this is built as a layer mined out of ordinary git commits rather than a replacement storage format, so an existing git history is the input, not a migration target.

scenario · C0 Git stores C0 as one tree object holding one blob for billing.py. There is no representation of “charge” anywhere in that object; the function is just some lines inside the blob. sgt mines the same commit into three ops — one per symbol — each independently addressable, independently removable, and independently a target for a future edit to build on:

where this costs something Mining ops out of commits after the fact is exactly the retrofit-friendliness Darcs and Pijul don't offer — you point sgt at an existing git history and it works, no migration. But it means the boundary of a symbol is only as good as the parser: sgt uses tree-sitter to find symbol spans, and a file it cannot parse into symbols — a config file, a binary asset, a language without a grammar — falls back to a single whole_file pseudo-symbol, which is exactly git's granularity again. The symbol-level story is real for code sgt can parse, and quietly degrades to line/byte granularity everywhere else. This isn't a rare edge case in a real repository; it's most non-code files in it.

§3Removing one thing cleanly

Pick up the scenario right after the agent lands its hour of work, before Alicia's fix enters the picture at all. Someone reviews the result and decides the caching layer is wrong — it has a stale-read bug — and wants it gone. The retry policy on refund is fine and should stay. This is the smallest possible test of what a system's unit of history actually buys you, because the answer depends entirely on whether the system can tell the three changes apart after the fact.

scenario · revert the caching layer The agent's hour of work is one git commit (call it C1) containing edits to all three functions plus a new helper, _charge_cache. Someone now wants billing.py back to: charge uncached, refund still retrying, apply_discount still cleaned up.

In plain git, C1 is one tree snapshot. There is no sub-object called “the caching layer” to point at. git revert C1 would invert the whole commit — undoing the retry policy and the cleanup pass along with the cache. The alternative is manual: open the diff, find every line that belongs to caching (the new function, the two call sites inside charge), and hand-edit them out, or run an interactive rebase to split C1 into three commits first and then revert just one. Either way, a human has to re-derive the boundary between the three features that the agent's single commit already erased. This is exactly the situation the sgt README opens with, and it is worth being precise about why it happens: git's snapshot model has nowhere to store “these edits belong together, and these other edits are unrelated,” so that information, which existed in the agent's head for the hour it was working, is thrown away the moment the work is committed.

jj's answer starts one level better and then hits the same wall. jj abandon removes a commit and automatically rebases every descendant onto its parent — a real improvement over git's reflog-only undo, and it works perfectly if the caching layer, the retry policy, and the cleanup pass are already three separate commits. But the scenario says the agent landed all three in one pass, which jj (like git) will most naturally represent as one commit, because jj's unit of storage is still a git tree snapshot (§2). To abandon just the caching part, a person first has to jj split the commit — manually partitioning the diff, hunk by hunk, into the piece that's caching and the piece that isn't. jj's own documentation frames this honestly: splitting means “thinking in terms of negation rather than addition,” and the tooling for it (an interactive diff editor) is explicitly less mature than either Git's own staging workflow or what jj offers for the cases it's built around (stacking, rebasing already-separate commits). The change-id/operation-log machinery that makes jj's undo so much more reliable than git's reflog (§7) is not doing any work here, because the problem isn't “undo an operation,” it's “the operation I want to undo was never recorded as its own operation.”

Darcs and Pijul are patch-based, so in principle a revert is just darcs unrecord / un-applying the caching patches — but only if the patches are already separated at that granularity, which requires whoever wrote the caching layer to have made it its own patch (or sequence of patches) rather than one big commit-sized changeset. Assume the agent had been disciplined about this and the caching work is its own patch, P_cache. Darcs can remove it cleanly only if P_cache commutes with everything recorded after it — if the retry-policy and cleanup patches didn't touch any line P_cache touched. If the cleanup pass happened to reformat a line adjacent to the cache call sites, darcs has to reconstruct the commutation, and in the worst case (§5) that reconstruction is where the exponential blowup historically lived. Pijul's version of the same operation is on much firmer ground: because Pijul's graph model guarantees that non-conflicting patches always commute by construction (§5), unrecording P_cache is a well-defined graph operation with no search involved, provided — same caveat as Darcs — the caching work was recorded as its own patch and not folded into a bigger one.

sgt's answer doesn't depend on discipline at commit time, because the separation happens at mining time, after the fact, from the symbols each edit touched — not from how the agent happened to batch its own commits. C1 is mined into ops on three independent chains (one for charge, one for refund, one for apply_discount) plus a fourth, brand-new chain for _charge_cache. sgt revert billing.py::_charge_cache removes that op and, because the ideal is downward-closed, also removes anything built on top of it — but nothing on the refund or apply_discount chains is built on top of a caching helper, so neither is touched. The command doesn't need the caching work to have been its own commit, patch, or even a deliberate unit at all; it only needs the caching edits to have landed on symbols that nothing else's *symbols* depend on.

where this costs something Downward-closure is a double-edged guarantee. If something legitimate had later been built on top of the caching layer — say a metrics function reading _charge_cache's hit rate — a plain sgt revert removes that too, because it is structurally in the caching op's up-set whether or not a human would call it “part of the caching feature.” The system has a second command, revert --keep-dependents, precisely because this happens: it drafts a continuation op for each direct dependent (something has to supply new bytes for the metrics function that no longer has cache stats to read) and carries everything else forward unchanged. That command exists as an escape hatch (§6) rather than the default because deciding what a dependent should become once its dependency is gone is exactly the kind of judgment call the ideal algebra can't make on its own — someone, or some agent, has to write the replacement logic.

§4What a conflict is, and where it lives

Now bring Alicia in. She started from C0 at the same time as the agent and fixed a rounding bug inside apply_discount — a small, one-line change to the same function the agent's cleanup pass rewrote wholesale. When the two lines of work meet, this is a real disagreement: two different, mutually unaware people (one human, one not) each think they know what apply_discount should look like right now. Every system downstream of this point has to answer three sub-questions: what does the system do with the rest of the work that isn't in dispute, what does a conflict look like while it's unresolved, and does resolving it once mean it's resolved for good.

Plain git answers all three the same way: a three-way merge diffs each side against the common ancestor C0, and if the two diffs to apply_discount overlap — which they will, since the cleanup pass rewrote the whole function and Alicia's fix is inside it — git gives up on computing an answer and writes conflict markers, <<<<<<< HEAD / ======= / >>>>>>> theirs, directly into billing.py. The file is now syntactically invalid Python until a human resolves it by hand. Nothing about this is persistent: once someone edits the markers away and commits, the record of “these two specific diffs disagreed here” exists only implicitly, inside that one merge commit's tree. If Alicia's branch or the agent's branch is later rebased or re-merged, git has no memory of the resolution at all — git rerere exists specifically to paper over this, by caching the literal conflict text and its resolution text so an identical conflict can be auto-resolved next time, which is a textual cache, not a structural fact recorded anywhere in the history graph.

Darcs keeps the record, but as a specific patch type: a conflictor, which stores the conflicting patches plus the transitive closure of what they conflict with, directly inside the repository's patch sequence — a real improvement, since un-pulling one side correctly un-conflicts the other. But the representation is brittle in a specific, documented way: because darcs' patch sequence is fundamentally linear, a conflict — which is naturally a graph (two things, mutually incompatible) — has to be flattened into that sequence, and Darcs' own team has an open issue describing exactly the failure mode this produces: a conflictor commuted past a duplicate or near-duplicate patch is “not reliably reversible.” The theory here was sound in spirit and informal in the place that mattered.

Pijul's answer is the most structurally elegant of the systems examined here, and it deserves to be stated plainly rather than hedged: a conflict is a shape in the graph, not a special patch type layered on top of one. Both Alicia's rewrite and the agent's rewrite of apply_discount add their own vertices to the line-graph; where they disagree, the graph simply ends up with two alive spans that have no path between them (or, if they both touch the same span, a cycle). Nothing is lost, no marker corrupts the file, and both sides' intentions are simultaneously present in the pristine — Pijul's own description of this is that “the presence or absence of conflicts are only computed afterward.” Resolving it is just another patch: someone adds ordering edges that linearize the two spans into one sequence, and because that resolution is a durable, content-identified change like any other, it does not have to be redone if the branches are touched again later — Pijul's own framing is that “conflicts never come back.” This is the conflict-as-CRDT idea in its purest form among the systems here: every operation Pijul performs (add a vertex, add an edge, relabel an edge dead) commutes with every other, so there is nothing for a conflict to do except sit in the graph until someone adds the missing order.

jj takes a related but distinct route, and is candid in its own docs about the tradeoff. A conflicted jj commit does not store markers; it stores an odd-length list of trees representing a small algebraic term — a base tree and alternating add/remove diffs, so a plain three-way conflict is A + (C−B). Markers are materialized only for display. The payoff is that rebasing a conflicted commit again does not nest: flatten() and simplify() reduce the accumulated term back down to a plain three-way form with no trace of the intermediate history, which is exactly what stops git's “resolve the same conflict three times across three rebases” problem. But the algebra is still over trees and line hunks; jj's own documentation states there is no notion of code syntax or semantics anywhere in it, and its “same-change rule” — auto-resolving when both sides made an identical edit — is explicitly lossy in terms of the underlying algebra, a deliberate convenience-over-purity call the docs name outright rather than hide.

Lazy merging, the most recent and most heavily formalized of the four, generalizes this into a proven lattice. Its unit is a document cell, and a cell that has received concurrent, unreconciled edits holds a variant potential — a small set of coexisting candidate values, each traceable to the causal edit that produced it, living inside a proven-commutative causality graph. Merge is not an algorithm the paper hopes is correct; it is defined as the lattice supremum of two causality graphs, and the paper proves (its Theorem apparatus, not an assertion) that this supremum exists, is unique, and that the practical per-cell projection used to answer “what's the current value” is a homomorphism of that lattice. This is real rigor Darcs never had and Pijul has only informally around its CRDT claim. The honest limits, which the paper itself states rather than the essay imposing them: resolution is a simple superseding assignment with no model of why one variant should win over another, there is no edit-context or semantic-implication detection, and the paper's own examples are structured documents — cells, tables — not source files with control flow and cross-references. It is also explicit that this is a real disagreement with the “CRDTs are sufficient for local-first collaboration” position associated with Kleppmann et al., precisely on the point that a plain state-based CRDT lattice, without the causal-graph apparatus this paper adds, loses information a real editing session needs.

sgt answers the first sub-question — what happens to the rest of the work — the same way Pijul would want to: sgt sync detects that Alicia's op and the agent's op share the same symbol and the same before_version (both are edits to apply_discount@h0) and calls this a fork. The caching and retry ops have no such collision, so the semilattice unions merge them immediately, with no human involved and no waiting on the fork's resolution. This is “divergence-as-state”: the fork is not an error, not a blocked merge, and not silently resolved by picking a side — it is committed, shared data, recorded in .sgt/forks.json, which every teammate's next sync sees. Where sgt parts ways with Pijul is the second and third sub-questions. The fork is represented at the granularity of a whole symbol: both of Alicia's and the agent's versions of apply_discount are parked, opaque, off the ideal, with no attempt to look inside either one and no line-graph to union automatically. Resolving it means a human or an agent runs sgt merge-op, which drafts a placeholder (“hollow”) op chain-extending the ideal's own tip and records the other tip's identity only as advisory intent — someone still has to read both versions and write the reconciled body by hand, the same work a git merge conflict demands. What is Pijul-like about it is durability: once sgt fulfill and sgt commit land that reconciliation, the fork record is closed and does not reappear on a later sync of the same history.

where this costs something Notice what Pijul's and jj's line/tree granularity would have caught that sgt, as described, does not: if Alicia's one-line rounding fix and the agent's rewrite happened to touch different statements inside apply_discount, a line-based three-way merge might well auto-resolve with no conflict at all, because the two diffs don't overlap. sgt's symbol grain is (in the current implementation) the whole function, so any two edits to the same function's body collide as a fork regardless of whether the specific lines overlap — a strictly coarser, more conservative notion of “disagreement” than any line-level system uses. This is not a bug so much as the other side of the bet symbol-identity makes; §8 comes back to it directly, because it is one of the two or three most important tradeoffs in this whole comparison.

§5Identity: what makes two edits “the same thing”

Every claim in §3 and §4 quietly depended on being able to say “this edit and that edit are about the same underlying thing.” That's a harder problem than it looks, and the five systems here split into two genuinely different strategies for solving it: carry an identity forward from the moment something is created, or detect it after the fact by comparing states. Neither is free.

Git carries nothing. A blob's identity is the hash of its bytes, full stop; there is no persistent handle for “this line” or “this function” that survives an edit. Every time git needs to know whether two things are related — git blame, a merge, a rename in git log --follow — it re-derives an answer on the spot with a content-similarity heuristic (the Myers diff algorithm, or a similarity threshold for rename detection), and a different invocation with a different threshold can give a different answer. Identity in git is not a fact stored anywhere; it's a guess made fresh every time someone asks.

jj's change-id is the opposite extreme: identity is minted once and carried, never re-derived. When a commit is created, jj generates a random 16-byte token and attaches it; every subsequent amend or rebase produces a new commit (new content hash) but copies the same change-id forward. This is why jj log can show you “this change,” stable, while its underlying commit hash churns underneath — and it is exactly what makes the automatic-descendant-rebase in §3 coherent: descendants are tracked by the change they're stacked on, not the commit hash that's about to be replaced. The cost is that carried identity is only as durable as whatever's doing the carrying: jj's own compatibility notes admit the change-id lives in a non-standard git commit header that git rebase, run directly, does not preserve, and that only some forges bother to round-trip. And a change-id identifies a commit's evolving lineage, not any object inside it — jj has no notion at all of “this function, as it moves through the file, is the same function,” because its unit of storage stopped at the tree, not the symbol.

Pijul carries identity one level further down, onto individual spans of text: a vertex in its line-graph is identified by (hash of the change that introduced it, byte position within that change) — decoupled from the current textual content, so a line keeps its identity even as the file around it changes. This is what lets Pijul's conflict detection stay precise (§4) and lets a deletion be recorded as a relabeled edge rather than a destroyed fact. Pijul extends the same carried-identity trick to whole-file renames with a dedicated name-vertex/inode-vertex pair, specifically so a rename commutes cleanly with concurrent edits to the file's content. But that is the ceiling: there is no analogous carried identity for an identifier renamed inside a file. Rename a function from apply_discount to apply_promo and Pijul sees new text at old byte positions, nothing more — the same gap sgt's own memory of its refactor limitations independently arrived at.

Darcs never solved this at all in a general way: a patch is tied to the exact input file it was recorded against (jneem's phrase is that darcs patches are “tied to a specific input context”), so identity across a rewrite is whatever commutation can reconstruct, with no separate identity layer underneath it. Lazy merging's cells are identified by their position in a fixed document schema (a table's row/column, a form's field) — carried in the sense that the schema defines it up front, but it presumes a structured document with a stable shape, which source code is not.

sgt takes the harder, opposite bet from jj: identity is detected, not carried. A symbol-id is minted once a symbol is first seen, but nothing forces the agent, or Alicia, or anyone else, to declare when they rename or move something — there is no “carry this id forward” step for a human to remember, unlike jj's change-id, which the tooling attaches automatically at the one moment (commit creation) it can. Instead, each mining pass runs a tiered matcher: an exact-content-hash tier first, then a fuzzy structural- similarity tier, to decide whether a symbol that disappeared in one commit and a symbol that appeared in the next are the same thing under a new name or location. This is why sgt can be pointed at history that was never instrumented for it at all (§2's retrofit story) — but it means identity is a claim the system infers and could get wrong, not a fact someone recorded. Two corrections exist for exactly that failure: sgt identity-split tells the matcher two ids it linked are unrelated, sgt identity-join tells it two ids it kept apart are actually the same thing, and both are permanent, team-shared constraints a later mining pass respects.

scenario · where detection could fail The agent's “cleanup pass” on apply_discount is the exact shape of edit that stresses this. If the cleanup is a light rewrite — renamed a variable, reordered two statements — the fuzzy tier almost certainly still links the before and after as one chain, and the fork in §4 is detected correctly. If the cleanup is aggressive — say it inlines apply_discount's body directly into charge and deletes the function — the matcher may see nothing left that resembles apply_discount at all. sgt would then mine this as a deletion, and Alicia's concurrent fix to the now-vanished symbol would sync in as a puzzling edit to a chain with no live tip, not as a same-symbol fork jj, Pijul, or even plain git would still notice (their line-diffs would still see her one changed line sitting inside the pre-inline version of the function). Symbol identity is a strictly more informative signal when it holds and a strictly worse one than a raw line diff when it silently doesn't.
