§6Merge as computation: search, pushout, lattice, fixpoint

Given two divergent histories, “merge them” can mean four structurally different things: search for a plausible reordering, evaluate a closed-form construction proven to have a unique answer, take the supremum of a lattice, or run a fixpoint computation to closure. Only one of those four is a search, and it's the one most engineers have actually used.

Git and svn compute a merge by heuristic three-way diff: take the two end states and the common ancestor, diff each side against the ancestor, and apply both diffs if they don't touch overlapping lines. This can be silently wrong in a specific, well-documented way, not just slow: if one side moved a line and the other side independently duplicated content near the old location, a three-way diff that only ever sees the two endpoint snapshots — never the intermediate patch that would have shown the line moving — can merge in a duplicate where the correct answer was a move. The algorithm isn't unsound because it's badly implemented; it's unsound because a snapshot diff structurally discards the information (the intermediate edit) that would have disambiguated the two cases. There is no proof of correctness to appeal to here, because there is no formal object the merge is supposed to satisfy — three-way merge is a good heuristic, not a specification.

Darcs tried to specify the good heuristic properly and the specification stopped short: merging meant finding a reordering of two patch sequences under which they commute, and when patches conflicted, darcs represented the failure as a nested merger patch (§4). Because darcs never formally proved a canonical answer existed for a conflicting pair, resolving an n-way conflict could require considering the pairwise merges of a growing recursive structure — the exponential blowup real users hit, in the worst documented case, several hours to merge a two-line change. The theory pointed at the right question (when do two patches commute) without ever proving the harder one (given that they don't, what is the merge) had a unique, computable answer.

Pijul's categorical reformulation answers exactly that harder question, and by construction, not search. A merge of two coinitial edits is defined as a pushout: the smallest object incorporating both edits, together with a universal property that makes it unique up to isomorphism — any other valid reconciliation factors uniquely through it. Where a pushout doesn't exist in the plain category of files (a genuine conflict), Pijul works in the free completion of that category, where conflicted states are legitimate objects (partial orders over lines, not flat sequences), so the pushout always exists there. The practical payoff is a closed-form construction — union the two sides, quotient by what they share, take the transitive closure — computed once, with nothing to search. Worth stating candidly: the categorical paper proves the algebra is well-defined and unique; it does not, on its own, prove a running-time bound. Pijul's claimed logarithmic merge cost is a separate engineering result that rests on Sanakirja, its purpose-built copy-on-write B-tree store, not on the category theory by itself. The theory buys correctness; the data structure buys speed.

jj computes the underlying auto-merge with the same kind of tree/hunk three-way diff git uses — there is no categorical proof underneath jj's merges, and no claim of one. Its rigor is one level up, in the algebra that represents the result (§4): flattening and simplifying a conflict term after a rebase is a proven-idempotent normalization, which is what stops repeated rebases from re-litigating the same conflict, but the initial merge computation itself is the same heuristic git has always used.

Lazy merging proves the strongest general statement of the five: merge is defined as the supremum in a lattice of causality graphs, and the paper proves that supremum exists, is unique, and that the practical “current value of a cell” projection (cartesian lifting) is a lattice homomorphism of the full causal-graph lattice. The one named limitation is itself formal, not a hand-wave: that projection is proven non-injective — it discards cross-cell causal correlation on purpose, in exchange for a tractable per-cell query, and the paper says so.

sgt's merge is a fixpoint computation over a union, in two layers, and it is worth separating what is deterministic-by-construction from what is deliberately refused rather than solved. The op layer takes the union of both sides' op-ids and runs grounding: a single ordered pass, structurally a topological closure (the same shape as Kahn's algorithm), that treats every symbol-version and every declared dependency as a requirement resolvable by any producer in the union, and keeps exactly the ops whose requirements are transitively satisfied. This has no search step and no heuristic branch — given the same two op-sets, it produces the same result every time, which is closer in spirit to Pijul's closed-form pushout than to git's heuristic diff. Layered on top, three small semilattices — an ACI union over build/test pins, a G-Set union over feature-id aliases, an OR-Set union over declared cross-symbol edges — guarantee the same order-independent convergence Pijul and lazy merging prove for their own lattices, but for sgt's metadata rather than for file content.

Where the analogy to Pijul's pushout stops is exactly at a fork. A pushout, when it exists, is a merged value — Pijul's graph-CRDT reconciles the conflicting content itself, automatically, into a single (possibly still-unresolved-looking, but structurally complete) graph. sgt's grounding pass does not attempt this at the symbol level at all: when two ops share a (symbol, before_version), both tips and everything built on either of them are excluded from the union wholesale — not reconciled, removed. The invariant that makes this safe is a simple, checkable fact about downward-closed sets (a downward-closed set minus an upward-closed set is still downward-closed), so the remainder is guaranteed to still be a valid ideal without needing to inspect either tip's content. This is deterministic and provably safe in exactly the sense Pijul's construction is deterministic and provably safe — but it is a narrower claim. Pijul's merge computation reaches through a conflict and keeps going. sgt's merge computation reaches around a conflict and stops, handing the excluded part to the explicit rewrite escape hatch in §7.

§7When the algebra can't express the edit

Every system in this discussion eventually hits an edit its merge algebra cannot express automatically — two changes to the same thing that mean genuinely incompatible things, where no formula produces “the” answer because there isn't one. That's not a defect in any of the formalisms above; it's their boundary, and it's supposed to exist. What actually distinguishes these systems is whether crossing that boundary is a marked, structured event or an unmarked one — whether the system remembers that a human (or agent) stepped outside the algebra and made a judgment call, or whether the judgment call just looks like an ordinary commit once it's done.

Git has no escape hatch as a distinct concept, because it has no algebra to escape from — the three-way merge fails, conflict markers appear in the file, a human edits the text, git add, git commit. The resulting merge commit is indistinguishable, in the object model, from any other commit. There is no record that this particular tree resulted from a human overriding an automatic merge rather than a clean apply; you'd have to notice two parents and go look. Darcs is only slightly more structured: an unresolved conflict is a real patch (“conflictor”) that persists until superseded, so at least the fact of the conflict is patch-shaped and inspectable — but resolving it is still an ordinary informal edit, recorded as an ordinary new patch.

Pijul's answer is the most elegant because, for a wide class of conflicts, there's no separate escape mechanism at all: a conflict is a graph shape (§4), and resolving it is a patch like any other, expressed in the same line-graph algebra that expresses everything else. When two threads insert different lines at the same point, the “resolution” can just be a patch that orders them relative to each other — still inside the formalism, no special case. Where Pijul's algebra genuinely can't decide (two edits that are semantically incompatible, not just graph-adjacent), a human still has to write replacement content, and at that point Pijul is no more structured than git about the content of the fix — only about everything surrounding it.

jj takes the algebraic conflict value (§4's odd-length list, A + (C−B)) and materializes it directly into the file as conflict markers, then re-parses whatever the human leaves behind back into a resolved Merge value. jj resolve, jj split, jj squash, and jj abandon all stay inside the same commit/operation algebra — nothing about jj's model needs a distinct “rewrite mode” — but the actual content of a resolution is, again, just a human editing text. Lazy merging names this boundary rather than gesturing past it: semantic conflict detection and resolution are explicit non-goals of the paper. Its contribution stops at producing the causally correct set of concurrent values; deciding what an application does when two edits disagree is left entirely outside the formalism, on purpose.

scenario Alicia's fork of apply_discount (§4) survives §6's grounding fixpoint untouched — both tips, and everything built on either, are excluded from the merged ideal, and .sgt/forks.json now carries a durable record of the two tip ids and a suggested remedy. Nobody has lost anything; nobody has to resolve it before they can keep working on unrelated code. Resolving it is a deliberate act, on someone's own schedule.

sgt gives that deliberate act its own machinery rather than leaving it as an unmarked edit: merge-op, split-op, transplant, and revert --keep-dependents are rewrite verbs that draft hollow ops — off-chain, provisional continuations that don't participate in fork detection until they're fulfilled and landed. An earlier design had these hollows reference-edge the other fork tip directly, and that design was rejected during implementation for a precise reason worth stating because it shows the fork invariant being taken seriously rather than special-cased away: referencing the other tip's requires would itself be grounded and re-detected as exactly the same kind of collision the hollow is supposed to resolve. The design that shipped instead chain-extends the ideal's own tip and records the other tip's identity only in advisory intent metadata — off the chain the merge algebra actually inspects, so the resolution can name what it's reconciling without the reconciliation itself becoming a second fork.

Running sgt merge-op on Alicia's and the agent's two tips drafts one such hollow, chain-extending (say) Alicia's tip, with the agent's tip id recorded in intent. Someone — Alicia, the agent, a reviewer — still has to write the actual reconciled body of apply_discount; that content decision is exactly as off-algebra here as it is in git, Pijul, or jj. What differs is everything downstream of writing it: build_candidate and stage compute and validate the resulting ideal without committing anything, and land — the only step in the whole rewrite path that writes — refuses to commit on a stale stage or a failing build/test verdict unless an explicit override is supplied. The judgment call is still human (or agent) judgment; it just can't become durable history without being checked, and the fact that it was a rewrite — not an ordinary edit — is structurally recorded rather than inferred from having two parents.

candid The verified-gate story is real for direct edits, but revert --keep-dependents quietly trades completeness for cost on everything past the first hop. Only the target's direct reference-edge dependents get a real hollow (and, implicitly, a chance for someone to reconsider whether they still make sense once the target is gone); everything further out in the up-set is carried forward mechanically, with no hollow and no LLM call at all. The module's own justification is candid about why: minting a drafted continuation for every transitive dependent would mean “spend a backend call on every intermediate symbol,” which doesn't scale on a long dependency chain. That's a defensible engineering tradeoff, not a soundness result — it means a revert can leave a distant dependent technically well-formed (it still type-checks against something) while silently resting on an assumption that's no longer true three hops back, and nothing in the rewrite path is designed to catch that.

§8Concurrency: what happens when three people sync at once

Everything in §6 and §7 was framed as two histories meeting. Real teams are rarely that tidy — Alicia, the coding agent, and now a CI bot publishing an auto-formatted commit can all be pushing at once, and the question of what “merge” even means starts to depend on who's coordinating with whom, and how.

Git's answer is the one everyone already knows and mostly tolerates: a remote ref is a single mutable pointer, updated by whoever's push wins the compare-and-swap on the server, and every other actor's next fetch does its own pairwise three-way merge against the new tip. There is no built-in notion of a repository-wide operation that spans multiple refs atomically — a script that updates main and a tag together can succeed on one and fail on the other, and git's reflog, being per-ref, won't show you the two as a single undoable unit. Darcs and Pijul inherit the same pairwise push/pull topology at the network level; what they change is what happens once two histories meet, not how many can meet at once or whether that meeting is atomic across more than one branch.

jj is the one system here that treats the whole repository state, not a ref, as the unit of atomicity. Every jj command that changes anything appends a new snapshot — a whole-repo view: every branch pointer, every working-copy commit, together — to an operation log, itself a DAG. Undo isn't “revert this one ref's last move,” it's “go back to the view the operation log recorded before this operation,” which is why jj can cleanly undo a rebase that touched a dozen branches: the whole multi-branch state was one node in the op log, not a dozen independent ref updates. When two processes race — two jj invocations against the same repo, or two machines whose op logs diverged — jj snapshot-isolates each operation and, if their op-log heads have diverged, runs a three-way merge on the operation log itself: the resulting view unions non-conflicting ref moves and, where two operations moved the same ref differently, keeps both and surfaces the disagreement rather than silently picking a winner. Concurrency safety here is closer to an MVCC database than to a file lock: nothing blocks, nothing is silently lost, and the reconciliation itself is content-addressed and atomic.

Lazy merging is the only system in this set actually designed for the “three people are typing into the same document right now” case rather than the “three people push independently and occasionally overlap” case. Its whole apparatus — cell segmentation, per-cell variant potentials, the causality-graph lattice — exists so that any number of sites can apply local edits without any coordination at all and still be guaranteed to converge to the lattice supremum once they've all seen each other's operations, with no server, no lock, no retry loop. That guarantee is real and it is stronger, in this specific dimension, than anything git-shaped tooling offers: convergence is proven for arbitrarily many concurrent sites, not just demonstrated for two.

scenario Say a third actor joins: a CI bot that auto-formats billing.py and pushes its own commit, at roughly the same moment Alicia and the agent are syncing their apply_discount fork from §7. Three op-sets now exist that no single pairwise fetch has ever seen all at once.

sgt does not invent a new topology for this. Sync is still pairwise — fetch, ingest, resolve, materialize — against whatever the remote's main currently points at, exactly like git, and a genuinely three-way-simultaneous push still resolves as two sequential pairwise merges, in whatever order the remote's ref updates happen to land. What sgt changes is what's cheap and safe to redo at each of those pairwise steps: the CI bot's formatting ops union into the ideal via the same fixpoint grounding pass as anything else, the three metadata semilattices (pins, aliases, declared edges) absorb a third contributor's writes with no extra case — a G-Set union and an OR-Set union don't care how many sites contributed, only that each write is idempotent to re-apply — and the fork between Alicia and the agent survives a third party's unrelated push completely undisturbed, because grounding excludes exactly the two colliding tips and nothing else, regardless of what else is in the union.

candid That resilience is real, but it would be overselling it to call sgt's concurrency model an answer to the same question jj's operation log or lazy merging's lattice answer. sgt's locked_section and Store.add's own lock are local safety devices — they stop one machine's concurrent processes from observing a half-written union, nothing more. Across machines, the actual coordination mechanism is still git's: a mutable ref, a compare-and-swap on push, and a pairwise merge on the losing side's next fetch. jj's operation log gives you atomic undo across every ref at once and a principled three-way merge when op-log heads themselves diverge; lazy merging gives you a proof that convergence holds for any number of uncoordinated concurrent sites. sgt gives you a merge step, at each pairwise meeting, that is safer and more structured about symbol-level content than git's — but the meetings themselves are arranged exactly the way git arranges them, with exactly git's race on the ref pointer. Grafting jj's whole-repository operation log under sgt's op-DAG is a real, unclaimed opportunity, not a solved problem.

§9Granularity: the smallest thing two edits can disagree about

§4 flagged this and deferred it: sgt detects a conflict at the grain of a whole symbol — a function, a class body — while git, jj, Darcs, and Pijul all detect conflicts at the grain of a line or a byte range. That one sentence hides a real tradeoff, and it's worth making the tradeoff concrete rather than just naming it, because it cuts both ways.

variant Change the scenario slightly from §4: instead of both edits touching the discount percentage, suppose the agent's commit C1 only renamed a local variable inside apply_discount for clarity, on a line Alicia's concurrent fix never touches. Alicia's one-line off-by-one fix is two lines away, inside the same function, same file.

Under git, jj, Darcs, or Pijul, this variant auto-merges cleanly, and correctly so: the two edits touch disjoint lines (git/jj's three-way diff), disjoint byte ranges with no shared context (Pijul's line-graph), disjoint token windows the patches commute across (Darcs). Nobody has to look at anything. Under sgt, this variant is still a fork. A footprint entry is keyed by symbol, and its identity is the whole symbol's before-image — there is no sub-symbol address two ops can occupy without colliding at the (symbol, before_version) level, so a rename two lines away from an off-by-one fix forks apply_discount exactly as hard as the real semantic conflict in §4 did. This is a strictly coarser conflict detector than any of the other four systems, full stop, and the running example makes that cost visible rather than asserting it away.

What the coarser grain buys back is a different property, and it's worth being precise about which one. Consider the opposite variant: two edits to different lines of apply_discount that are individually harmless but jointly wrong — one changes the discount rate constant, the other changes the rounding direction two lines later, and the combination silently produces a discount that rounds the wrong way for exactly the boundary case the constant change was supposed to protect. Line-based systems have no way to notice this: neither edit touches the other's lines, three-way diff (or its Pijul/Darcs equivalents) applies both without a flag, and the bug ships in a merge commit that looks, structurally, like the cleanest possible merge. sgt's whole-symbol grain would fork this case — both edits share the same (symbol, before_version) regardless of which lines they touch — and a fork can never silently resolve. Someone has to run merge-op and write a reconciled body, which is at minimum a chance to notice the two changes interact, even though nothing about the mechanism proves the reconciled body gets the interaction right; that check still only happens at whatever the oracle (§7) actually tests.

This is fundamentally a consequence of what §2 already established about the unit of history: the finer-grained systems can be finer-grained about conflicts because their patches already address sub-symbol regions. sgt's ops are minted from tree-sitter symbol boundaries (§2's own candid admission — unparseable regions fall back to whole-file grain, which is this same tradeoff again, one level coarser still), so its conflict detector inherits that grain whether or not the particular edit pair would have been harmless at a finer one. The honest framing is not that one grain is better than the other in general; it's that the finer grain optimizes for not bothering anyone when edits are truly disjoint, and the coarser grain optimizes for never letting a same-symbol interaction resolve itself without anyone looking — and which of those failure modes is more expensive depends entirely on how often real teams hit each one, which is an empirical question this document doesn't answer.

§10Three different questions have been hiding inside “the unit”

§2 asked what gets content-addressed. §9 asked what has to overlap for two edits to conflict. There's a third question, quietly different from both, that this discussion hasn't separated out yet: what is the smallest thing that gets recorded and undone atomically — the transaction boundary. In git these three questions have one answer (the commit). In every other system reviewed here, they have at least two, and the gap between them is where some of the more interesting design decisions live.

A git commit is simultaneously the content-addressing unit, the (implicit) conflict-detection scope, and the atomic undo boundary — and it's a boundary a human draws by hand, at whatever grain they felt like drawing it that day. That's exactly why C1 in §1 could bundle a caching layer, a refund fix, and a discount-logic edit into one indivisible transaction: nothing in git's model asks whether those three things belong together, because git only has the one grain to work with, and it's the author's call every time.

Darcs and Pijul separate content-addressing from the transaction boundary a little: what's recorded (a patch, chosen via darcs record's or Pijul's interactive hunk selection) can be finer than a git commit, but it's still a human choosing hunks by hand at record time — the grain is still authored, just with a finer-toothed comb. Underneath, Pijul's real atoms are line-graph vertex operations, finer still than the patch a human actually recorded; the patch boundary is a convenience layer over a finer substrate, which is part of why unrecording and reordering patches composes as cleanly as it does.

jj keeps the commit as its content unit but gives the transaction boundary an entirely different, and stronger, meaning: the operation log (§8) makes an atomic transaction span the whole repository view — every ref, every working-copy commit — not one commit's tree. A single jj rebase that moves a dozen branches is one entry in the operation log and one undoable step, regardless of how many individual commits it touched. That's a transaction grain coarser than a commit, chosen automatically by the system rather than authored by a human, and it exists specifically to make multi-branch operations safe to attempt and cheap to reverse.

Lazy merging names this axis explicitly and puts the decision at the opposite end of the pipeline from git's: an editor transaction is whatever the source editor itself groups as one edit gesture — a paste, an autocomplete replacement, a multi-cursor edit — recorded as a single CRDT operation before it ever reaches anything resembling a commit. Nobody chooses this grain at record time the way a darcs user chooses hunks; the editor decides it automatically, at the moment of typing, and the whole causality-graph machinery is built to take editor transactions as its atoms rather than characters or lines.

back to the scenario C1's three unrelated changes were one git transaction because a human chose them to be. The sgt miner decomposed that same diff into three ops automatically, at commit-ingest time, from tree-sitter symbol boundaries — nobody selected hunks, the way §3's independent revert of just the caching op already depended on. That's the content-addressing grain, decided the way lazy merging decides its editor transactions: by structural analysis at write time, not by human selection.

What sgt does that none of the four comparison systems do is decouple that write-time content grain from the transaction that's actually allowed to become checked history. The atomic unit gated by land (§7) isn't one op; it's the whole candidate ideal — however many ops happen to be staged — evaluated by the oracle and committed or refused as a single all-or-nothing step. An op can be as small as one symbol edit; a landing transaction can bundle dozens of ops from several people's work, exactly the way C1 bundled three unrelated changes, except now that bundling is a choice made at land time over already-atomic, already-addressable, already-independently-revertible pieces, not a choice baked irreversibly into the recording grain itself.

Six axes, six systems, no cell in this table designed to make one column look better than the others — the point of laying it out flat is that the actual pattern is a set of genuine tradeoffs, not a ranking. Read across any single row and one system looks best on that axis — Pijul on merge computation, jj on concurrency, lazy merging on coordination-freedom, Darcs and Pijul on sub-symbol conflict grain. Read down any single column and sgt looks reasonable but not remarkable. That's the honest picture: sgt isn't the strongest entry on any one of these six axes measured in isolation. What the running example was for — and the reason it kept coming back across ten sections instead of resetting per topic — is that these axes aren't independent for a real codebase with an LLM agent as one of its regular contributors. A system that mints an addressable unit automatically at write time (§10, like lazy merging, not like git or Darcs), that turns a bundled commit into independently revertible pieces (§3), that refuses to silently resolve a same-symbol collision (§4, §6) while still handing that collision a structured, gated way back into history (§7) — that's a specific bet about where an agent-heavy workflow's actual failure mode lives, not a claim to have out-designed Pijul's category theory or jj's operation log on their own terms.

§12What this actually is

Alicia never got mentioned as evidence that anything is broken elsewhere. That was deliberate. The question this whole discussion has actually been circling isn't “which of these six systems is correct” — Pijul's pushout is correct, in the strict sense of having a proof; lazy merging's lattice supremum is correct in the same sense; jj's flatten/simplify normalization is correct; git's heuristic diff is not, and never claimed to be. The question is which grain a system answers those correct (or heuristic) constructions at, and what that grain buys and costs once an LLM agent is producing a meaningful share of the edits landing in a repository as often as a human is.

Every comparison system reviewed here answers at the line, the hunk, or the byte range, because that's the grain a text editor actually produces and a human actually reviews. That grain is not a historical accident anyone should feel bad about — it's the correct grain for what version control has mostly been for: humans, typing, reviewing each other's typing. An agent doesn't produce edits at that grain by default. It produces a diff shaped like a whole rewritten function, frequently touching a dozen lines to change one behavior, and a text-line VCS has no way to tell “this touched twelve lines because it's a genuine twelve-line change” apart from “this touched twelve lines because the model regenerated a function it only needed to patch.” Moving the unit of history to the symbol (§2), the unit of identity to something carried and correctable rather than only ever re-derived (§5), and the unit of an atomic, checked transaction to the candidate ideal rather than the hand-drawn commit (§10) is a bet that this particular failure mode — agent-shaped diffs colliding with human-shaped review tools — is common enough now to be worth the costs this document has tried not to hide: a coarser conflict detector than Pijul's or jj's (§9), a merge computation that's a deterministic fixpoint rather than a proven-unique pushout (§6), a concurrency story still borrowed wholesale from git's pairwise ref model rather than jj's whole-repository operation log (§8), and an identity mechanism that has to be detected and occasionally corrected by hand rather than carried for free the way jj's change-id is (§5).

None of the other four systems were built for that failure mode, so none of them are wrong for not addressing it — Pijul's categorical rigor and Darcs's original patch-commutation idea were answering “how do we make merge mathematically well-defined,” jj's operation log was answering “how do we make history-rewriting safe enough to attempt casually,” and lazy merging was answering “how do collaborative editors converge with zero coordination.” Those are all real, valuable, mostly still-open questions independent of who or what is producing the edits, and this document's own §8 and §9 callouts named specific places where sgt's answers are strictly weaker than theirs and gestured at, rather than closed, the gap. Whether the tradeoff in the other direction — symbol-level addressing, detected identity, a fixpoint merge, an oracle-gated escape hatch — is worth those costs for a given team isn't a claim this document is trying to settle by assertion. It's the thing the running example was for: by the time Alicia's fork survives a sync untouched in §6, gets a durable record in §7, and coexists with a CI bot's unrelated push in §8 without any of the three losing anything, the reader has everything needed to weigh that tradeoff against their own repository's actual mix of human and agent authorship — which is exactly where this discussion should stop making the case for them.

§1What sgt is

sgt sits on top of a normal git repository. It watches commits and mines each diff into a set of operations, one per changed function, method, or class. Each operation records which symbol changed, the code before and after the change, and which other symbol-versions it depends on. History in sgt is this set of operations, not the sequence of commits that produced them.

Git already gives you commits and trees. sgt adds a second, finer index underneath that: symbols instead of files, dependencies instead of parent pointers. The commits still exist and still work with any other git tool. sgt's operations are derived from them and can be recomputed from them at any time.

This document goes through the design choices behind that operation layer. What the unit of history is. How sgt recognizes that two edits touch the same thing. What happens when two edits collide. How a merge actually gets computed. What happens when the automatic parts can't decide something on their own. Git, Darcs, Pijul, jj, and a formal model called lazy merging come up throughout, wherever their design answers the same question sgt is answering. Most of them got there first, and sgt's choices are often a direct reaction to trade-offs they already made explicit.

§2The unit of history is a symbol edit

A git commit stores a whole tree. If ten files changed and only one line in one of them actually mattered, the commit still carries the full state of all ten. sgt's miner reads that same commit, parses the files with tree-sitter, and cuts the diff along symbol boundaries. Each function or method or class that changed becomes its own operation, with its own before and after content and its own list of dependencies on other symbol-versions. A commit that touched three unrelated functions becomes three operations.

Darcs and Pijul made a related move earlier: both treat a patch, not a snapshot, as the thing that gets stored and reasoned about. The difference is where the boundary of that unit comes from. A darcs or Pijul patch is whatever hunks a person selected at record time. sgt's operation boundary comes from parsing, not selection, so nobody has to decide where one operation ends and the next begins.

jj keeps the commit as its stored unit, but gives each commit a change-id that survives rebases and edits. That's the same instinct, attaching a stable identity to something below the raw content, applied one level up: a whole commit instead of a symbol. Lazy merging's editor transactions are closer to sgt's grain in spirit. Both are drawn automatically rather than by hand. The difference is where the automatic boundary comes from: an editor transaction is grouped at the moment of typing, from paste and autocomplete events; sgt's operation boundary is drawn later, by parsing a diff after the fact.

cost Symbol-level parsing needs a grammar for the language and a file that actually parses. When a file doesn't parse cleanly, sgt falls back to treating the whole file as one symbol, which is exactly git's grain. This happens for generated files, badly formatted files, and languages without a tree-sitter grammar. The fallback is safe, but in that case sgt is not buying anything over a plain commit.

§3A running example

Here is a small case to make the rest of this concrete. A file billing.py has three functions: charge, refund, apply_discount. A commit C0 introduces all three. sgt mines C0 into three operations, one per function, each with no dependency because each is a first version.

From there, two things happen at the same time. A coding agent opens one commit, C1, that does three unrelated things: adds a caching helper used by charge, tweaks rounding in refund, and changes the discount tiers in apply_discount. Separately, before pulling C1, Alicia fixes a one-line off-by-one bug directly in apply_discount, working from the same C0 version of that function.

Nothing about this setup is unusual. It's the same thing that happens whenever two people, or a person and an agent, work from the same base and haven't synced yet. The next few sections use these seven operations to walk through what sgt actually does with them.

§4Removing one change

Say the caching helper turns out to be a bad idea and has to go, while the refund and discount changes from the same commit should stay. In git, C1 is one commit, so pulling the caching helper back out means editing the file by hand or splitting the commit after the fact. In sgt, d2a5 is its own operation and nothing depends on it, so sgt drops it directly. e88c and f009, the other two operations mined from the same commit, are untouched.

jj makes this easier than plain git with jj split, which pulls a commit apart into pieces you can abandon separately, but that split is still done by hand, choosing which lines go in which piece. Darcs and Pijul can unrecord a single patch directly, the same way sgt drops d2a5, as long as no later patch commutes past it. If a later patch touches the same lines, that patch has to be unrecorded first. sgt doesn't hit that requirement here because d2a5 has no dependents.

If something did depend on the caching helper, dropping it stops being free. sgt keeps its set of operations downward-closed, so removing one operation also removes everything built on top of it, unless you explicitly ask sgt to keep the dependents and give them something new to build on instead. §8 covers that case.

§5Identity: carried or detected

Two edits can only be recognized as touching the same thing if something ties them together across the edit. Systems solve this two ways. Some carry an identity forward from the moment something is created, so it never has to be re-derived later. Others detect identity after the fact, by comparing content or position.

jj carries identity directly. A change-id is minted once when a commit is created and stays attached to that commit through every rebase and rewrite, even after the commit hash itself changes. Pijul carries identity at a finer grain: each line gets a vertex identified by the hash of the change that introduced it plus its position, and that vertex identity survives edits happening around it. Lazy merging carries identity through the document's schema, since a cell's position in the schema is fixed and edits to it are tracked against that fixed position.

git detects identity instead of carrying it. A blob's hash is its content, so a renamed file with unchanged content is recognized as a rename only because a heuristic spots the match afterward. Change the content even slightly during the rename and git usually stops connecting the two. Darcs is close to git here: a patch is tied to the exact file context it was recorded against, so a later restructuring can break the commutation check that identity depends on.

sgt also detects identity rather than carrying it. A symbol gets a canonical id the first time it's seen, and later commits are matched against it by a tiered check, an exact hash match first, then a fuzzy match on the body and surrounding context if the hash moved. Renaming apply_discount or moving it to another file still resolves to the same id as long as enough of the body matches. A large rewrite bundled into the same commit as the rename can break that match, and sgt then treats it as a brand new symbol with no history. That's a real gap next to jj's change-id, which survives a rewrite with no matching step at all, because it was never re-derived in the first place.

§6What a conflict is

f009 and g5c2 both list c91d as their required version of apply_discount. That's a fork: two different next versions built from the same starting point. sgt detects this by checking for exactly that pattern, two operations claiming the same symbol and the same before-version, and once it finds one, it excludes both operations, and anything built on either of them, from the set it treats as valid history. Neither one wins. Both stay on record as an open fork, and everything else in the repository keeps working normally.

Other systems locate a conflict differently. git's three-way merge finds a conflict only when the same lines are touched on both sides, so if Alicia and the agent had touched different lines of the same function, git would merge them automatically with no conflict at all, whether or not that result was actually correct. Pijul finds a conflict as a shape in its line graph, two insertions with no ordering between them, which can be as fine as a single overlapping line. jj represents an unresolved conflict as a value stored in the commit itself, an algebraic list of the pieces that disagree, and materializes it into the file as ordinary-looking conflict markers so a person can resolve it by editing text. Darcs represents a conflict as its own kind of patch, called a conflictor, that stays in the history until something later supersedes it.

sgt's fork is coarser than all of these because it compares whole symbols instead of lines or byte ranges. Two edits to different lines of the same function still fork in sgt, even in cases where they would merge cleanly under any line-based system. §9 covers that cost directly.

§7How a merge is computed

Once a fork is on record, sgt still has to decide what "current" means for everything that isn't part of the fork. It does this by grounding, which means starting from the set of all known operations and removing anything whose required version never landed. What's left after that pass is the valid set. This is a fixpoint computation, not a three-way diff, and it runs over the whole op graph, not just the two branches that happen to be in front of you.

Run it over the seven ops from §3. a3f1, b7e0, and c91d have no requirements, so they ground immediately. d2a5 requires nothing either and grounds on its own. e88c requires b7e0, which is already grounded, so it grounds too. f009 and g5c2 both require c91d, and c91d is grounded, but sgt already flagged this pair as a fork in §6, so neither one is added to the valid set. The result is five grounded ops and two excluded ones, sitting off to the side until someone resolves the fork.

Pijul computes the analogous result with a pushout in its category of patches, which produces a new graph state directly from the two branches without ever naming intermediate steps, and proves the result is the smallest state consistent with both. That proof is stronger than anything sgt offers. sgt's grounding pass gives you a valid set and an excluded set, not a proof that the result is minimal or unique, because it is working over dependency edges between whole symbols rather than a line-level graph with an established algebra behind it. Darcs computes a similar result by commuting patches past each other one pair at a time, which is exactly why it can blow up combinatorially on repositories with a lot of concurrent history. jj takes a different approach again and does not try to resolve most conflicts automatically at all, it packages the disagreement as a value and lets the working copy carry it forward until a person edits it away. Lazy merging's lattice join is the closest formal cousin to sgt's grounding pass, both compute a result from partial, possibly conflicting inputs without requiring a total order first, though lazy merging's join is defined and proven over abstract cells and never claimed as a fit for real source files.

§8When you have to step outside the algebra

Grounding tells you f009 and g5c2 are excluded. It does not pick one, and it does not write a third version that combines them. Someone has to look at both edits to apply_discount and decide what the function should actually say. sgt's answer for this step is a small set of rewrite verbs: merge-op to fold two operations into one, split-op to break one operation into smaller pieces, transplant to move an operation onto a different base, and revert --keep-dependents to undo an operation while leaving whatever was built on top of it alone. Running merge-op on f009 and g5c2 produces a new operation, hollow rather than mined from a diff, that chains onto one tip's own history instead of pointing at both parents. It never re-triggers the fork check, because the fork check only fires on two operations claiming the same before-version, and a hollow op has no before-version of its own to collide on.

git leaves this same step almost entirely to you. A conflicted merge drops both versions into the file with conflict markers, commits nothing until you edit them out by hand, and records no structured trace of what the two sides actually were once you're done. Pijul stays inside its own algebra here instead of stepping outside it, resolving a conflict by inserting a new patch that supplies an explicit order for the colliding lines, so the resolution is itself a first-class patch subject to the same laws as everything else. jj also stays inside its model, since the conflict is already a value living in the commit, and resolving it is just editing the file until the algebraic representation collapses back to a single value with no listed alternatives. Lazy merging does not attempt this step at all. The paper is explicit that producing a semantically correct merged result is outside its scope, and leaves conflict resolution to whatever system sits on top of the lattice.

sgt's rewrite verbs are the one place in the whole design where a person, or an agent, makes a judgment call that the op graph itself cannot make. Everywhere else in this document, the answer comes out of dependency data alone.

§9Syncing over git

sgt does not run its own server or its own network protocol. Operations, forks, and the metadata around them get pushed and pulled through ordinary git refs, the same transport everyone already has configured. Locking is local only, so two people syncing at the same moment don't coordinate through anything shared, they just each pull, merge what they see, and push. If both push at once, git's own ref update rejects the second one, and that person pulls again and retries.

This is a real gap next to jj, which keeps an operation log for the whole repository, a single ordered history of every change anyone made to the view of the repo itself, not just to the files in it. That gives jj a consistent point to reason from when several people are editing at once. sgt has no equivalent. Its sync model is pairwise and eventually consistent, closer to how git itself behaves than to jj's more centralized log. For a small team pushing every few minutes this rarely matters in practice, since forks get recorded rather than silently dropped either way, but it means sgt inherits git's race conditions on the sync path itself, even though it does better than git once the data has landed.

§10The cost of symbol-level grain

Look again at what f009 and g5c2 actually changed inside apply_discount. The agent's edit touched the tier lookup near the top of the function. Alicia's one-line fix touched a boundary check near the bottom. The two edits don't overlap by a single line. A line-based system would merge them without any trouble, since nothing about the diffs themselves collides. sgt forks them anyway, because both operations declare the same before-version of the same symbol, and the symbol is the whole function, not the lines inside it.

example 
def apply_discount(cart, tier):
    rate = TIERS[tier]          ← agent's edit is here
    ...
    if idx >= len(items):        ← alicia's edit is here
        idx = len(items) - 1
    return cart.total * (1 - rate)

This is the real price of choosing a symbol as the unit of history instead of a line or a hunk. Pijul and Darcs both work at line granularity, so this exact pair of edits would merge cleanly for either of them, no fork, no rewrite step, nothing for a person to look at. sgt trades that precision for a simpler identity story. A symbol has one name and one AST node to hang an identity on, where a line has neither, it's just a position that shifts every time something above it grows or shrinks. Coarser grain buys sgt a cheap, robust way to say "this is the same thing across two edits," at the cost of forking pairs of changes that a finer-grained system would have let through.

In practice this shows up most on long functions with several unrelated concerns living inside them. Splitting a large function into smaller ones lowers the odds of a spurious fork, for the same reason smaller commits lower the odds of a merge conflict in git. That's a real workaround, not a fix, and it's worth knowing about before you hit it the first time on a file you didn't write.

Reading down the identity column and the formal-guarantee column together is the fastest way to see where each system spent its effort. §12Closing

sgt tracks history at the level of a function or a class instead of a file or a line. That choice gives it a cheap, stable identity for the things it tracks, a straightforward way to notice when two edits collide, and a fixpoint pass that keeps the rest of the repository working while a collision sits unresolved. It gives up the proofs that Pijul and lazy merging built their systems around, and it forks pairs of edits that a line-based system would have merged without complaint.

None of the other systems in this document are wrong. Darcs found the combinatorial edge of patch commutation and documented it honestly. Pijul built the category theory to fix that edge properly. jj showed that a working copy can be a commit like any other, and that a conflict can be a value instead of a crisis. Lazy merging proved a lattice join can work on partial, disordered input without a total order, and said plainly that turning that join into correct source code was somebody else's problem. sgt is that somebody else's attempt, built on a coarser unit than any of them, betting that symbol-level identity is precise enough to be useful for real code and simple enough that a team can actually run it.

Sources: Mimram & Di Giusto, "A Categorical Theory of Patches" (arXiv:1311.3903). Jujutsu (jj) documentation and design docs, github.com/jj-vcs/jj. Darcs manual and wiki, darcs.net. Pijul manual, pijul.org/manual. sgt's own source, this repository.

# refactor: architectural options inspired by jj, Darcs, Pijul, and lazy merging

## Summary

Writing `why-semantic-git.html` forced a close, honest comparison between sgt's kernel and four
other systems that solved adjacent problems: jj (change-id, operation log), Darcs (patch
commutation, conflictors), Pijul (categorical pushout over a line graph), and the lazy-merging
paper (proven lattice join over abstract cells). Three of those systems back their conflict
handling with either a formal proof or a persisted log sgt does not have. This doc turns that
comparison into six concrete architectural options for sgt's own kernel, each grounded in the
current code (file and line cited) and in the specific mechanism it's borrowed from. None of these
are decided. Each section ends with the tradeoff stated in plain language and the pitfall that
would bite if we did it carelessly. You pick which ones, if any, are worth the churn.

This is not a patch list. Two of the options (D1, D2) touch a core data structure — the sync base
model and the identity model, respectively — and would need their own migration the way the
`MINER_VERSION` 2→3 bump did.

| conflict detection | fork = two ops claiming the same `(symbol, before_version)` | `order.py:149-183` | correct but coarse — whole-symbol grain, not line grain |
| conflict resolution | `_grounded` fixpoint excludes both fork tips + their upset; a human runs a rewrite verb to fix it | `order.py:267-338`, `rewrite.py:177-220` | no proof of minimality, unlike Pijul's pushout |
| identity | tiered detection: exact hash → structural hash → fuzzy Jaccard ≥0.80 | `identity.py:16-19,99-211` | per-call union-find, "not persisted across separate calls" (`mine.py:17-20`, flagged in the code itself as future work) |
| resolution provenance | recorded as a free-text `intent` string on the hollow op | `rewrite.py:204-205,27-30` | not queryable or structured |
| sync base recovery | trailers → committed ideal record → full remine → naive union | `ingest.py:242-271` | "resolve just keeps union semantics" when no base is found (`ingest.py:249-251`) — a silent degrade, not a refusal |
| sync topology | pairwise, one remote ref at a time, no shared log | `ingest.py:1-13,78` | no equivalent of jj's whole-repo operation log |
| locking | local, per-mutation `flock` on `.sgt/local/lock` | `store.py:38,126-184` | fine for one machine, says nothing about two people syncing at once |

---

## D1. Sync base recovery: heuristic ladder with a silent union fallback, vs. an append-only operation log

**What sgt does now.** When sgt needs a three-way base for a sync, it tries commit trailers, then
a committed `.sgt/ideal.json` record, then a full remine of the base commit. If none of those
produce a verified base, `resolve.py` does not refuse. It falls back to a plain union of both
sides' op-ids and runs grounding on that (`ingest.py:249-251`). This is documented in the code as
intentional degrade-gracefully behavior, not a bug, but it means the "no verified base" case is
silent. Nothing in the CLI output distinguishes a real three-way merge from an unverified union
unless you go looking.

**What jj does instead.** jj keeps an append-only operation log, one ordered history of every
change to the repo's own view, not just to file content. Any clone can walk that log to reconstruct
an exact prior state without needing trailers or heuristics.

**The option.** Add an append-only sgt-native log (most likely a dedicated git ref, notes-style,
so it rides the same transport §9 of the essay already relies on) recording every land/sync event
and the ideal it produced. Base recovery becomes a log lookup instead of a three-tier guess, and
the "no verified base" case becomes something the log can name explicitly rather than something
resolve.py quietly papers over.

**Tradeoff, plainly put.** This fixes a real, already-documented gap, and it removes a silent
failure mode. It also adds a second thing that has to sync and, in principle, a second thing that
can itself get out of order across clones — the log needs its own append-only merge rule, though
that's the same CRDT pattern sgt already uses for declared edges and feature aliases, so the
pattern isn't new to the codebase. The honest cost is engineering effort and a migration, not new
research risk.

**Lower-risk half-step.** If a full log feels like too much change right now, the full-remine
tier of the existing ladder can be cached by commit SHA, since a commit's tree is immutable and
the remine result is therefore stable forever. That doesn't fix the silent-union case, but it
removes the repeated cost of the current fallback and ships as a pure cache, no schema change.

---

## D2. Identity: per-call fuzzy detection, vs. a persisted carried id

**What sgt does now.** A symbol's identity is detected, not carried. Mining runs a tiered matcher
per call — exact hash, then structural (AST-modulo-formatting) hash, then fuzzy token-Jaccard
above 0.80 with a size guard — through a union-find that is explicitly scoped to one `mine()` call
and not persisted across calls (`mine.py:17-20` says so directly, and flags a persistent registry
as future work).

**What jj does instead.** jj mints a change-id once, at commit creation, and that id survives
every rebase and rewrite because it was never re-derived. It's carried, not detected, so there is
no matching step at all, and therefore no threshold that can misfire.

**The option.** Build the persistent identity registry mine.py already gestures at: a store-level
table mapping canonical symbol-id to its detection history, populated the first time a symbol is
seen and consulted (not re-derived) on every later commit. This is close to the "symbol identity
scheme" already sketched in an earlier design note in this repo, so this option is less "new idea"
than "the natural next step of something already scoped."

**Tradeoff, plainly put.** A registry removes the token-Jaccard threshold as a live failure mode
for anything sgt has already seen once, which is the majority case in a repo it's tracked for a
while. It does not remove fuzzy matching entirely — every symbol sgt has never seen before (a fresh
clone's first mine, a symbol copy-pasted in from outside, history mined before the registry
existed) still needs a first-contact detection step, so this is additive, not a replacement. The
real cost is that the registry becomes another piece of `.sgt/` state that has to be synced and
merged across clones, and getting that merge rule wrong is exactly the kind of cross-replica bug
that's hard to notice until two people's registries disagree about the same symbol.

**Pitfall.** jj's change-id has no matching problem because it's never re-derived by content at
all — it's opaque metadata stamped once. If sgt's registry is instead a cache of detection
*results* that still falls back to fuzzy matching whenever the cache misses or two clones disagree,
it inherits all of fuzzy matching's edge cases plus a new cache-invalidation problem on top. The
registry is worth building only if it's the authority, not a memo.

---

## D3. Fork granularity: whole-symbol collision, vs. a Darcs-style commutation pre-check

**What sgt does now.** Two ops fork the instant they claim the same `(symbol, before_version)`,
regardless of whether the actual edited regions inside that symbol overlap. §10 of the essay walks
exactly this case: an edit to the top of a function and an edit to the bottom fork in sgt even
though no line-based system would blink.

**What Darcs does instead.** Darcs checks whether two patches commute, meaning whether applying
them in either order produces the same result. If they commute, there's no conflict. Commutation
is decided by comparing what each patch actually touches, not by comparing identities.

**The option.** Before declaring a fork, run a lightweight region-overlap check on the two
candidate ops' actual diffs against the shared before-version. If the changed regions don't
overlap, auto-produce a merged op instead of forking.

**Tradeoff, plainly put.** This would measurably cut the granularity cost from §10, which is real
and already documented as a known cost of sgt's design. It's also the one option on this list that
reopens a door sgt deliberately closed. The whole point of choosing a symbol as the unit of
identity, laid out in §2 and §5 of the essay, was to get a cheap, robust "is this the same thing"
answer without doing line-level bookkeeping. A region-overlap pre-check puts line-level reasoning
back in, just scoped to conflict avoidance instead of identity. Darcs and Pijul can do this safely
because their whole formal apparatus, patch commutation and the categorical pushout, was built
around exactly this question and has been stress-tested for over a decade between the two of them.
An ad hoc overlap heuristic bolted onto sgt would not carry that backing. Two edits can touch
disjoint line ranges and still be semantically related, one changing a constant the other's new
branch depends on, and a heuristic auto-merge would produce a function that looks coherent and
runs fine at merge time while being wrong in a way no fork would have caught.

**Recommendation if you want a smaller bite.** D4 below is a narrower, safer version of this same
idea, worth reading before deciding on this one.

---

## D4. A bounded "safe join" tier for provably commutative op kinds, inspired by lazy merging's lattice

**What sgt does now.** Every op is metadata for sgt's own CRDT layer (attribution, declared edges,
feature aliases), which already lattice-joins cleanly. But op *content* itself has no join. Two
ops on the same before-version either both make it into the valid set or both get excluded. There
is no middle tier.

**What lazy merging does instead.** The paper defines a join over abstract cells that produces a
correct combined result from partial, possibly conflicting inputs, without needing a total order
first, and without claiming that join is a general solution to merging real source code. It's
explicit that its guarantee only covers the abstract cell model, not arbitrary semantic content.

**The option.** Rather than D3's general overlap check, define a join only for `kind` pairings
that can be shown never to conflict by construction, for example a pure rename (`kind="move"`)
against an unrelated pure `rework` of the same symbol's body, where the rename touches only the
symbol's identity metadata and the rework touches only content. Auto-join those specific pairings.
Leave every other kind pairing, including two `rework`s on the same before-version, forking exactly
as today.

**Tradeoff, plainly put.** This is D3's idea with the scope cut down to cases the `kind` field
already tags, which makes it much cheaper to reason about and much smaller in surface area. It's
also only as good as the proof behind each declared-safe pairing. Doing this for one or two kind
pairs where the argument is genuinely airtight is a reasonable, bounded addition. Doing it for many
pairs on the strength of "seems fine in practice" is the worst version of D3's pitfall wearing a
smaller costume, a set of ad hoc safety claims with none of Pijul's or lazy merging's proof behind
any of them.

---

## D5. Resolution provenance: free-text intent string, vs. a structured field

**What sgt does now.** When `merge-op` resolves a fork, the identity of the tip it's resolving
*against* is recorded only in the hollow op's `intent` string, a free-text advisory field
(`rewrite.py:204-205`). It's already excluded from the content hash the same way `attribution` and
`derived` are, so recording more there costs nothing in the id computation.

**What Darcs does instead.** A conflict's resolution is itself a first-class patch, a conflictor,
that stays in history as structured data. Later tooling, or a person, can query what resolved what.

**The option.** Add a small structured field, something like `resolves: frozenset[op_id]`, to the
hollow op, alongside the existing `intent` string rather than replacing it. This turns "which
resolution touched which fork" from a grep-the-intent-string question into a query, which matters
for anything downstream that wants to reason about resolution history, an audit tool, a `sgt log`
view, a metric on how often forks recur on the same symbol.

**Tradeoff, plainly put.** This is the lowest-risk item on this list. It's an additive schema
field on a type (`Op`) that already excludes several fields from its content hash by design, so it
doesn't touch fork detection, grounding, or sync semantics at all. The cost is a `MINER_VERSION`
bump and the migration that comes with it, the same mechanical cost as any other schema addition,
not a new kind of risk.

---

## D6. Locking scope: local per-mutation flock, vs. jj's whole-repo operation log as a coordination point

**What sgt does now.** `Store._locked()` takes a local `flock` scoped to one mutation
(`store.py:126-184`), explicitly not a verb-wide lock. Two people syncing at the same moment don't
coordinate through anything shared. §9 of the essay names this directly as a real gap next to jj.

**What jj does instead.** jj's operation log gives every clone a single ordered view of repo-level
changes to reason from, which is what makes its handling of concurrent operations more consistent
than sgt's pairwise git-ref sync.

**The option.** This is the same log from D1, looked at from the coordination angle instead of the
base-recovery angle. If D1's log gets built, it becomes a natural place to also detect "someone
else landed since I last synced" before a `land` attempt, rather than relying purely on git's
ref-update CAS to reject the loser after the fact.

**Tradeoff, plainly put.** This isn't a separate build, it's a second reason to do D1. Worth noting
as a factor in that decision rather than deciding on its own.

---

## If you want an order to think about these in

Roughly cheapest-and-safest to most-invasive:

1. **D5** — additive field, no semantics change, ships behind the next version bump regardless.
2. **D1's cache half-step** — pure performance, no schema change, no new failure mode.
3. **D2** — the registry mine.py already flags as planned work; mostly a matter of building what's
   already scoped.
4. **D1's full log** — real gap, real fix, real migration; also strengthens D6 for free.
5. **D4** — a narrow, provable safe-join tier, worth it only if you're comfortable with the proof
   burden on each kind pairing you add.
6. **D3** — the biggest idea and the one that walks back a deliberate earlier choice (§2, §5, §10
   of the essay). Worth doing only if the granularity cost in practice turns out to be bigger than
   the essay's example suggests.

None of these are required to keep sgt working the way it does today. They're what the comparison
against jj, Darcs, Pijul, and lazy merging surfaced as the places where another system's answer is
more rigorous than sgt's, and what it would concretely cost to borrow that rigor.

---

## Sources

`why-semantic-git.html` (this repository), particularly §5 (identity), §6-7 (fork and grounding),
§9 (sync), §10 (granularity cost). Mimram & Di Giusto, "A Categorical Theory of Patches"

`sgt/core/sync/resolve.py`, `sgt/core/store.py`.

# Plan: D5 (resolution provenance) + D1 (append-only sync log) + D6 (land pre-flight staleness)

## Context

`docs/plans/2026-07-18-001-refactor-vcs-inspired-architecture-options-plan.md` lists six
architectural options borrowed from jj/Darcs/Pijul/lazy-merging. The user chose to implement
**D5, then D1 + D6**, in that order:

- **D5** — resolution provenance is currently recorded only in a free-text `intent` string on the
  merge hollow (`rewrite.py:204-205`). Make it a structured, queryable field.
- **D1** — sync base recovery falls back to a *silent* plain union when no witnessed base is found
  (`ingest.py:249-251`, `resolve.py:71-78`). Add an append-only sgt-native log (a dedicated git
  ref) recording every shared-branch `land`, so base recovery becomes an authoritative log lookup
  and the "no verified base" case can be named instead of papered over.
- **D6** — the same log, viewed from the coordination angle: detect "someone landed since I synced"
  *before* a land attempt, rather than relying purely on git's ref CAS to reject the loser after
  the fact. The doc is explicit that D6 "isn't a separate build, it's a second reason to do D1."

Another line of work on `main` is live-editing `mine.py`, `order.py`, `state.py`, `lens/*`,
`entities/graph.py`, `cli/inspect.py` (all uncommitted). **None** overlap D5/D1/D6's target files,
so this work will be done in a **git worktree** for isolation (per the user's instruction).

### Correction to the plan doc (D5 cost)

The doc claims D5 "costs a `MINER_VERSION` bump and the migration that comes with it." **This is
wrong**, and the doc contradicts itself — its own D5 section says the field "is already excluded
from the content hash the same way `attribution` and `derived` are." `compute_id`
(`op.py:140-161`) hashes only `(footprint, images, requires, kind, miner_version)`; excluded
fields are excluded simply by *not being passed*. Adding `resolves` changes **no op id**, opens no
new identity space, and needs no migration — old on-disk payloads round-trip via `.get()` defaults
exactly like `intent`/`off_chain`/`derived` already do (`store.py:_op_from_payload`, lines
102-114). **No `MINER_VERSION` bump.**

---

## D5 — structured `resolves` field on `Op`

Additive, advisory, excluded-from-id field. Five small edits:

1. **`sgt/core/op.py`** — add `resolves: frozenset[str] = frozenset()` to the `Op` dataclass
   (alongside the other advisory fields, after `derived`, lines 135-137), with a comment that it is
   excluded from the id like `intent`/`attribution`/`derived`. Add a `resolves: Requires`-style
   kwarg (`frozenset[str]`) to `make_op` (lines 164-193) and pass it into the `Op(...)`
   construction — **not** into the `compute_id(...)` call.

2. **`sgt/core/store.py`** — in `_payload` (lines 48-76) serialize `"resolves":
   sorted(op.resolves)`; in `_op_from_payload` (lines 83-114) read `resolves=frozenset(
   payload.get("resolves", []))`. This mirrors the existing `off_chain`/`derived` `.get(...,
   default)` pattern exactly, so committed v0/v1 op files keep round-tripping unchanged.

3. **`sgt/core/rewrite.py` `merge_op`** (lines 200-206) — the drafting call site. Add
   `resolves=frozenset({a_id, b_id})` to the `make_op(...)` that builds each hollow, so the hollow
   carries the two fork tips it reconciles as structured data (the `intent` string stays as the
   human-readable label).

4. **`sgt/core/rewrite.py` `build_candidate`** (lines 432-435) — the fulfillment site. When
   fulfilling a hollow into its real committed op, carry the field forward:
   `resolves=hollow.resolves`. (Id is unaffected since `resolves` is excluded from `compute_id`;
   this just moves the provenance onto the durable op the hollow becomes.)

No other consumer needs to change — `_close_resolved_forks` (rewrite.py:559-585) already keys off
footprint chaining, not intent, and stays as-is.

---

## D1 — append-only shared-branch land log

A dedicated git ref `refs/sgt/log/<branch>`: a parent-chained series of empty-tree commits, one per
successful `land`, each carrying the landed commit sha and the ideal it produced as trailers.
Reuses existing gitbind primitives (`EMPTY_TREE`, `commit_tree`, `update_ref_cas`, `commit_shas`,
`OP_TRAILER_KEY`/`format_op_trailers`/`parse_op_ids`) — no new serialization or CRDT machinery.

### New module `sgt/core/sync/log.py`

- `LOG_REF_PREFIX = "refs/sgt/log/"`; `log_ref(branch) -> str`.
- New trailer key `LANDED_SHA_KEY = "Sgt-Landed-Sha"` (defined in `gitbind.py` next to `OP_TRAILER_KEY`,
  with `format_landed_sha`/`parse_landed_sha` helpers mirroring the op-trailer helpers).
- `append(gb, branch, landed_sha, ideal_ids) -> bool` — read the current log tip
  (`gb.rev_parse(log_ref)`), build an empty-tree commit parented on it (`commit_tree(EMPTY_TREE,
  [tip] if tip else [], message, trailers)`) with trailers = `Sgt-Landed-Sha: <sha>` +
  `Sgt-Op:` lines for the ideal, then `update_ref_cas(log_ref, new, tip)`. Small bounded retry
  (re-read tip on CAS loss). Returns success; **best-effort — never raises into the caller** (the
  land already succeeded and the log is advisory; on exhaustion base recovery simply falls through
  to the existing ladder).
- `read(gb, branch) -> list[LogEntry]` — walk `commit_shas(log_ref)` newest-first, parse each
  commit's trailers into `LogEntry(landed_sha, ideal_ids)`.
- `ideal_for_sha(gb, branch, sha) -> frozenset[str] | None` — the base-recovery join: return the
  recorded ideal for a landed `sha`, or `None` if not in the log.

### Wire the append into `land()` (`sgt/core/sync/land.py`)

Inside the CAS-win branch (after `lens.record_ideal(...)`, line 191), call
`log.append(gb, branch, new, res.merged_ideal.op_ids)` best-effort. This is the only writer.

### New recovery rung in `ingest.py`

Add the log lookup as **rung-0** (cheapest, most authoritative) in both ladders:
- `recover_base(repo, gb, base_sha)` (lines 242-271): before the trailers check, try
  `log.ideal_for_sha(gb, branch, base_sha)`; if present **and** still witnessed
  (`_witnessed(gb, base_sha, ids)` — same "full-and-witnessed or unusable" discipline the trailers
  path enforces), return `(ids, "log")`.
- `_theirs_ideal(...)` (lines 194-239): same rung-0 log lookup for `theirs_sha` before the trailers
  check.
- `recover_base`/`_theirs_ideal` need the branch name to build the log ref — thread it through from
  `ingest()`'s callers (`sync()` has `fetched.branch`; `land()` has `branch`). Add `branch` param to
  `ingest()`.
- Extend the recovery vocabulary comments (`ingest.py:56-65`, `SyncReport`/`LandReport` docs) with
  the new `"log"` method value.

### Cross-clone transport (so the log actually helps a team)

The log only aids base recovery across clones if the ref syncs. Add **best-effort, non-fatal**
secondary fetch/push of the log ref:
- **`gitbind.py`** — new `fetch_ref(remote, refspec)` and `push_ref(remote, refspec)` helpers
  (existing `fetch`/`push` only take a plain branch name). Both `check=False`, swallow failure
  (an old remote without the ref is not an error).
- **`sync/fetch.py`** — after the branch fetch (line 44), a best-effort
  `gb.fetch_ref(remote, f"{log_ref}:{log_ref}")` in a try/except that never fails the sync.
- **`cli/sync.py` `_push`** (lines 86-99) — after the branch push succeeds, a best-effort
  `gb.push_ref(remote, f"{log_ref}:{log_ref}")` that never fails the push.

**Scope note (deliberate):** the log records `land` events only — the authoritative *shared-branch*
advances. Local `sync` merges already carry `Sgt-Op:` trailers and advance only the local branch,
so they don't need a log entry; a merge-base on a shared branch was a landed commit and is therefore
in the log. A pair of clones that only ever `sync` (never `land`) sees no log and falls through to
today's ladder — no regression.

---

## D6 — land pre-flight staleness advisory

Purely additive, non-blocking, does **not** touch the CAS/retry correctness logic.

- **`sgt/core/sync/land.py`** — add `advisory: str | None = None` to `LandReport`. Just before the
  retry loop (line 152), read the log tip's latest landed sha; if it is **not** an ancestor of our
  HEAD (`not gb.is_ancestor(latest_landed, ours)`), someone landed since our sync point — set an
  advisory string. Carry it into the returned `LandReport` on both the success and blocked paths.
  (The land still proceeds and re-unions on CAS loss exactly as today; this only surfaces the
  situation proactively.)
- **`sgt/cli/sync.py` `_land_branch`** (lines 126-135) — print `report.advisory` when set, mirroring
  the existing advisory-warning style used for `report.base_recovery == "none"` in `_sync`
  (lines 169-171).

---

## Order of implementation

1. Create a git worktree off `main` (isolation from the concurrent `main` work).
2. **D5** — the five edits above; targeted test.
3. **D1** — `log.py` module + gitbind trailer/ref helpers + `land.py` append + `ingest.py` rung +
   fetch/push wiring; targeted tests.
4. **D6** — `LandReport.advisory` + pre-flight check + CLI print; targeted test.

"""D1: an append-only, sgt-native record of every shared-branch `land`.

A dedicated git ref per branch (`refs/sgt/log/<branch>`) holds a parent-chained series of
empty-tree commits, one per successful `land`, each carrying the landed commit's sha and the
ideal it produced as trailers. It gives base recovery (`ingest.recover_base`/`_theirs_ideal`) an
authoritative rung-0 lookup for "what ideal did commit X land with" -- no trailers to lose in a
squash, no `.sgt/ideal.json` to go stale -- and gives `land` a pre-flight signal for D6 (someone
landed since our last sync point).

The log only records `land` -- the authoritative shared-branch advance. A local `sync` merge
advances only the local branch and carries its own `Sgt-Op:` trailers, so it needs no entry; any
merge-base on a shared branch was itself a landed commit and is therefore already in the log. This
module is best-effort throughout: a failure to append or read never blocks `land` or `sync`, it
just means base recovery falls through to the existing trailers/ideal-record/mine ladder.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

from sgt.store.gitbind import (
    EMPTY_TREE,
    GitBinding,
    format_landed_sha,
    format_op_trailers,
    parse_landed_sha,
    parse_op_ids,
)

LOG_REF_PREFIX = "refs/sgt/log/"

_APPEND_RETRIES = 5


def log_ref(branch: str) -> str:
    return f"{LOG_REF_PREFIX}{branch}"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LogEntry:
    landed_sha: str
    ideal_ids: frozenset[str]


def append(gb: GitBinding, branch: str, landed_sha: str, ideal_ids: frozenset[str]) -> bool:
    """Record that `landed_sha` just advanced `branch` with `ideal_ids`. Best-effort: `land`
    already succeeded by the time this is called, so a failure here (a CAS race with another
    lander's log append, or any git error) is swallowed rather than raised -- it only costs the
    next reader a fallback to the older recovery ladder, not correctness."""
    ref = log_ref(branch)
    trailers = "\n".join([format_landed_sha(landed_sha), format_op_trailers(sorted(ideal_ids))])
    try:
        for _ in range(_APPEND_RETRIES):
            tip = gb.rev_parse(ref)
            parents = [tip] if tip else []
            new = gb.commit_tree(EMPTY_TREE, parents, f"sgt land-log: {branch}", trailers=trailers)
            if gb.update_ref_cas(ref, new, tip):
                return True
        return False
    except Exception:
        return False


def read(gb: GitBinding, branch: str) -> list[LogEntry]:
    """Every entry for `branch`, newest first. Empty if the log ref doesn't exist or a read fails
    -- the same best-effort discipline as `append`, since a missing/corrupt log is just an absent
    rung-0, not an error."""
    try:
        entries = []
        for sha in gb.commit_shas(log_ref(branch)):
            message = gb.commit_message(sha)
            landed_sha = parse_landed_sha(message)
            if landed_sha is None:
                continue  # not one of ours (shouldn't happen on our own ref, but don't trust blindly)
            entries.append(LogEntry(landed_sha=landed_sha, ideal_ids=frozenset(parse_op_ids(message))))
        return entries
    except Exception:
        return []


def ideal_for_sha(gb: GitBinding, branch: str, sha: str) -> frozenset[str] | None:
    """The ideal the log records `sha` having landed with, or None if `sha` isn't in the log."""
    for entry in read(gb, branch):
        if entry.landed_sha == sha:
            return entry.ideal_ids
    return None
