def render_verb_preview_lines(
    map_view: dict,
    grid_view: dict,
    segments: list[dict] | None,
    preview_view: dict,
    *,
    focus_fid: str | None,
    color: bool = True,
) -> list[str]:
    """The **feedforward** graph for a revert/restore: instead of applying blind, draw *where it
    lands*. The target feature's checkpoints are shown vertically (like `--focus`) with the affected
    slice marked -- `▸`/`✗` a checkpoint the edit removes, `◐` one partly touched, else `kept`; a
    restore marks the re-added slice instead. Below it, the OTHER features the dependency blast hits,
    each badged `blast` (loses ops -> must re-draft) or `foundation` (a locked prerequisite). Ends
    with a one-line summary. Pure over the `_project_verb_preview` dict + the same
    map/grid/segments the log reads, so it's testable and shares `_render_car`/`color_for` with the
    overview. The `[y/N]` prompt and any capped diff stay in the CLI caller."""
    from sgt.intent.segment import checkpoint_slug

    segments = segments or []
    verb = preview_view.get("verb", "revert")
    target = preview_view.get("target", "")
    removed = set(preview_view.get("removed", []))
    added = set(preview_view.get("added", []))
    touched = removed if verb == "revert" else added
    affected = preview_view.get("affected", []) or []
    files = preview_view.get("files", {}) or {}

    layout = segment_layout(map_view, grid_view, segments)
    labels = {n["id"]: n.get("label", n["id"]) for n in map_view.get("nodes", [])}
    prefix_len = _min_unique_prefixes(list(layout["node_by_id"]))

    def bp(fid: str, hexc: str, disp: str | None = None) -> str:
        disp = fid[:10] if disp is None else disp
        k = min(prefix_len.get(fid, 5), len(disp))
        head = _bold(_paint(hexc, disp[:k], color=color), color=color) if color else disp[:k]
        return head + _dim(disp[k:], color=color)

    # Per-checkpoint status for the target feature: is the whole segment in the edit's op-set, some
    # of it, or none? (segments carry their `op_ids`; the car dict drops them, so join on segments.)
    seg_status: dict = {}
    for seg in segments:
        if seg.get("feature_id") != focus_fid:
            continue
        ops = set(seg.get("op_ids", []))
        hit = ops & touched
        seg_status[seg["seg_index"]] = "gone" if (ops and hit == ops) else ("partial" if hit else "kept")

    lines: list[str] = []
    hexc = color_for(focus_fid) if focus_fid else "#888888"
    flabel = labels.get(focus_fid, focus_fid or "?")
    action = "rewind" if verb == "revert" else "restore"
    lines.append(f" {_paint(hexc, '▸', color=color)} {_bold(action, color=color)}  "
                 f"{_bold(flabel, color=color)}  {bp(focus_fid, hexc) if focus_fid else ''}")
    lines.append(_dim(f"      {verb}  {target}", color=color))
    lines.append("")

    lane = layout["node_by_id"].get(focus_fid) if focus_fid else None
    if lane is None or not lane.get("cars"):
        lines.append(_dim("   (no checkpoints cached for this feature -- run `sgt log --refresh`)", color=color))
    else:
        gone_word = "removed" if verb == "revert" else "restored"
        first_gone = True
        for car in lane["cars"]:
            status = seg_status.get(car["seg_index"], "kept")
            head = _render_car(car, 6, hexc, color=color)
            slug = checkpoint_slug(car["label"])
            tail = f"@{car['seg_index']} :{slug}  {car['label']}"
            if status == "gone":
                mark = _paint(hexc, "▸", color=color) if (verb == "revert" and first_gone) else _dim("✗", color=color)
                first_gone = False
                note = _dim(f"· {car['op_count']} op {gone_word}", color=color)
                lines.append(f"   {mark} {head}  {_dim(tail, color=color)}  {note}")
            elif status == "partial":
                lines.append(f"   {_dim('◐', color=color)} {head}  {tail}  {_dim('· partly affected', color=color)}")
            else:
                lines.append(f"     {head}  {_dim(tail, color=color)}  {_dim('· kept', color=color)}")
    lines.append("")

    others = [a for a in affected if a.get("feature_id") != focus_fid]
    if others:
        lines.append(_dim(" also affected (dependency blast):", color=color))
        for a in others[:8]:
            afid = a["feature_id"]
            ahex = color_for(afid)
            albl = labels.get(afid, afid)
            if a.get("direction") == "blast":
                glyph, badge = _paint(ahex, "●", color=color), f"{a.get('op_count', 0)} op · must re-draft"
            else:
                glyph, badge = _paint(ahex, "◈", color=color), "locked prerequisite"
            lines.append(f"   {glyph} {bp(afid, ahex)} {albl}  {_dim('[' + badge + ']', color=color)}")
        if len(others) > 8:
            lines.append(_dim(f"   +{len(others) - 8} more feature(s)", color=color))
        lines.append("")

    n_op = len(removed) if verb == "revert" else len(added)
    verbword = "removes" if verb == "revert" else "restores"
    lines.append(_dim(f" {verbword} {n_op} op · {len(files)} file(s) changed · "
                      f"{len(others)} other feature(s) affected", color=color))
    return lines

def _make_tty(monkeypatch, reply):
    """Present stdin as a tty and feed `input()` a fixed reply."""
    import sys

    monkeypatch.setattr(sys.stdin, "isatty", lambda: True, raising=False)
    monkeypatch.setattr("builtins.input", lambda prompt="": reply)


def test_revert_confirm_applies_on_yes(tmp_path, capsys, monkeypatch):
    repo = corpus.CORPUS["linear_history"].build(tmp_path / "repo")
    get(repo)
    feat = _revertable_feature(repo)
    assert feat is not None
    _make_tty(monkeypatch, "y")

    before = current_ideal(repo).op_ids
    rc = _in(repo, ["revert", feat])
    assert rc == 0
    out = capsys.readouterr().out

# `sgt log` overview: legible hierarchy, listed checkpoints, `f-`-free handles + fast revert

## Context

The two-tier `sgt log` and the feedforward revert confirm-gate shipped. Using them on a real repo
(153 features · 224 commits · 3881 ops · 35 subsystems) surfaced four problems the screenshot makes
plain:

1. **`sgt revert f-00aa` hangs ~2 minutes, then errors with a "did you mean".** Root cause: `f-00aa`
   is a valid *unambiguous prefix* of `f-00aa2097…`, but the revert path's `resolve_feature`
   (`sgt/lens/verbs.py:474`) only accepts an **exact** node-id. So the prefix falls through every
   deterministic rung to the **LLM** NL rung (`_resolve_via_intent`, `sgt/cli/ideal_edit.py:277`) —
   that LLM call is the 2-minute cost (the "did you mean" rationale was LLM-written).
   Meanwhile `sgt log --focus f-00aa` resolves the same prefix *instantly* (`_resolve_focus`,
   `sgt/tui/graph.py:404`). The two paths disagree.
2. **`f-` on every handle is noise.** The user wants bare hex (`004f48b6`, not `f-004f48b6`).
3. **`✦6` is opaque — 6 *what*?** The user wants the checkpoints listed by name, not counted.
4. **The flat 153-line wall is cluttered.** The user wants clearer hierarchy via whitespace.

**Layout chosen (confirmed):** *Compact chips* — one line per feature, `✦N` replaced by the actual
checkpoint slugs (`bootstrap · store-init · +1`), a blank line between subsystems, `f-` dropped.

**Collision found while planning:** feature ids are `f-<founding op id>` (`sgt/lens/reconcile.py:219`).
So bare `004f48b6` **is** the founding op's id, and `plan_revert` tries op-ids *before* features
(`ideal_edit.py:229`). Dropping `f-` from the copyable token therefore can't be purely cosmetic:
`sgt revert 004f48b6` would revert the single founding op instead of the whole feature. The fix must
make handle-shaped targets resolve as **features first**.

## Changes

### 1. Fast, prefix-aware feature resolution — `sgt/lens/verbs.py`, `sgt/intent/segment.py`

- **`resolve_feature` (`verbs.py:474`)**: after the existing exact-id / alias / exact-label misses,
  add a **unique-prefix** match over *leaf* node ids, accepting both `f-`-prefixed and bare-hex
  input (normalize: a leaf `nid` matches when `nid == ref`, `nid.startswith(ref)`, or
  `nid.startswith("f-" + ref)`). Exactly one hit → resolve it; zero or ≥2 → `None` (unchanged
  fallthrough). Mirrors `_resolve_focus` (`graph.py:409`) so the revert path and `--focus` agree.
- **`resolve_checkpoint` (`segment.py:329`)**: the feature-part prefix match (`segment.py:365`)
  gains the same `or nid.startswith("f-" + feat_part)` clause, so `004f48b6@2` / `004f48b6:slug`
  resolve now that the advertised handle is bare hex.

### 2. Handle-shaped targets resolve as features first + no LLM for handles — `sgt/cli/ideal_edit.py`

In `_kernel_edit_verb` (`ideal_edit.py:189`):
- Define handle-shaped = `re.fullmatch(r"(f-)?[0-9a-f]{3,}", target)` and not containing `::`/`@`/`:`.
- For a handle-shaped target, try `resolve_feature` **before** the single-op `plan_single`
  (`ideal_edit.py:229`) — the feature scope wins over the founding op it shadows. Symbols
  (`a.py::foo`) and `@n`/`:slug` checkpoints are untouched (they aren't handle-shaped / are handled
  earlier), so single-op-by-symbol behaviour is unchanged.
- **LLM guard:** only fall to `_resolve_via_intent` when the target is *not* handle-shaped. A
  handle-shaped target that resolves to no unique feature prints a fast, deterministic
  "no feature matches prefix `X` — did you mean: …" (near-prefix leaves, or "run `sgt log`"),
  exit 2 — never the 2-minute LLM call. Natural-language targets ("the oauth work") still reach
  the LLM as before.

### 3. Drop `f-`, keep bright-prefix, in every rendered handle — `sgt/tui/graph.py`

- `brighten_prefix` (`graph.py:593`): display the **bare hex body** — `disp = fid[2:10]` when
  `fid` starts with `f-` — and shift the bright cut by 2 (`k_disp = prefix_len[fid] - 2`). The
  copyable token is now `fid[2:10]` (bare hex). `_min_unique_prefixes` is unchanged (still computed
  over full ids; the `f-` is shared, so `k-2` is exactly the min-unique among hex bodies) — its
  existing test stays valid.
- Focus branch (`graph.py:704`): `handle = focus[2:10]`; operate-hint tokens become bare hex.
- All hint/legend strings that show `<f-XXXX>` (`graph.py:790-794`, `992`) → `<XXXX>`, and
  "bright handle chars = the minimal prefix to type" stays accurate.

### 4. Compact-chips overview — `sgt/tui/graph.py` `render_graph_lines` (default tier only)

- **Whitespace / hierarchy:** emit a blank line *before* each subsystem header (except the first),
  and indent feature rows two spaces under their header so the header→feature nesting reads. Only
  the default (`timeline=False`) path changes; `--timeline` and `--focus` untouched.
- **Checkpoint chips replace `✦N`:** build the trailing chip list from the lane's `l["cars"]` via
  `checkpoint_slug(car["label"])` (already imported, `graph.py:573`): first ~3 slugs joined by
  ` · `, then `· +K` for the remainder (`✦0` → nothing). Drop the `ckpt = ✦{n}` token
  (`graph.py:758`). Trim `title_width` to make room; keep it one line, no wrapping.

## Target overview shape

```
153 features · 224 commits · 3881 ops · 35 subsystems

▾ Core Architecture Documentation           6 feat · 902 op

  ● 004f48b6  Project Bootstrap    ▁▃▂│▅█▂  168  bootstrap · store-init · +1
  ● m1999a0e  Semantic Git Arch…   ▂▅█▃│▆▂  677  span-log · contract-dag · +4

▾ Revision Analysis & Orchestration         9 feat · 159 op

  ● 08b6c6a0  Oracle Backend Cfg   ▃▂│▄█     22  oracle-cfg · backend · +2
```
(bright hex prefix = the minimal handle to type; `│` = a rewind boundary; chips = the checkpoints)

## Tests + golden

- `tests/tui/test_graph.py`: bare-hex handle (no `f-`, bright prefix present); overview row shows
  checkpoint slug chips not `✦N`; blank line between subsystem groups. (`_min_unique_prefixes` and
  segmented-sparkline tests unchanged.)
- `tests/cli/test_revert.py` (or `tests/lens/…`): `resolve_feature` accepts a `f-`-prefix and a
  bare-hex prefix; ambiguous prefix → `None`; `sgt revert <bare-hex feature handle>` reverts the
  **feature** (not the founding op) and never invokes the LLM (feature-sized removal, fast);
  handle-shaped miss exits 2 deterministically.
- Regenerate `tests/golden/test_cli_golden.py` — the `sgt log` overview surface changes (new
  layout, bare handles, chips). Revert/restore surfaces use `c.py::qux` (a symbol, not handle-shaped)
  so their resolution path is unchanged; only handle rendering in any embedded graph shifts.
  `SGT_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/golden/test_cli_golden.py -q`, then review.

## Non-goals / notes

- **Op-level revert by raw op-id is not an advertised path** (hints only ever showed
  `<f-XXXX>` / `:slug` / `@n` / `file::name`). Preferring the feature for a handle-shaped bare-hex
  token is the intended new contract; single-op revert stays reachable via `file::name`.
- `sgt intent list`/`show` also print `f-`-prefixed ids. Out of scope for this pass (not in the
  screenshot); the resolver changes already accept bare hex there, so a later cosmetic sweep is
  additive. Flag, don't do it now.
- No change to how `@n`/`:slug` or checkpoint op-sets resolve beyond the bare-hex feature-part.

## Verification (end to end)

1. `sgt revert 00aa` (or `f-00aa`) → resolves **instantly** to the feature, draws the feedforward,
   prompts `[y/N]`; removes the feature's op-set (not one op). `time` it — well under a second.
2. `sgt revert <handle-shaped miss>` → immediate deterministic "no feature matches", exit 2, no LLM.
3. `sgt revert "the oauth work"` (NL) → still reaches the LLM rung (unchanged).
4. `sgt log` → blank line between subsystems, features indented; handles are bare hex with a bright
   minimal prefix; each row ends in checkpoint slug chips (`slug · slug · +K`), no `✦N`, no `f-`.
5. `sgt log --focus 00aa` and `--timeline` still work; `sgt revert 00aa:<slug>` / `00aa@<n>` resolve.
6. Focused suites green: `tests/tui/test_graph.py`, `tests/cli/test_revert.py`,
   `tests/intent/test_segment.py` + regenerated `tests/golden/test_cli_golden.py`.

def _no_feature_match(repo: str, cmd: str, target: str, as_json: bool) -> int:
    """A handle-shaped target (`f-`/bare-hex) that resolved to no *unique* feature -- a typo, a stale
    id, or a too-short (ambiguous) prefix. Answer deterministically and instantly (no LLM): list the
    leaf features whose handle the prefix matches, or point at `sgt log` when none do. Always exit 2."""
    from sgt.lens.tree import load as load_tree

    nodes = (load_tree(repo) or {}).get("nodes", {})
    bare = target[2:] if target.startswith("f-") else target

    def body(nid: str) -> str:
        return nid[2:] if nid.startswith("f-") else nid

    hits = sorted(
        (nid for nid, nd in nodes.items() if not nd["children"] and body(nid).startswith(bare)),
        key=lambda nid: nodes[nid].get("label", nid),
    )
    if as_json:
        import json

        cands = [{"ref": body(nid)[:8], "label": nodes[nid].get("label", nid)} for nid in hits]
        print(json.dumps({"ok": False, "verb": cmd, "target": target, "candidates": cands}, indent=2))
        return 2
    if not hits:
        print(f"? [{cmd}] no feature matches handle {target!r} -- run `sgt log` to see the handles.")
        return 2
    print(f"? [{cmd}] {target!r} is an ambiguous handle; did you mean:")
    for nid in hits[:8]:
        print(f"  sgt {cmd} {body(nid)[:8]}   {nodes[nid].get('label', nid)}")
    return 2

# LiveHub × sgt — Active Journal

Two intertwined goals:
1. **Build** LiveHub: a fully CRDT-based collaborative code repository (rooms/sockets, not async
   pull/push). Reify actions → CRDT transactions → program-analysis conflict detection where a
   dependency conflict becomes a *recognized valid state* resolved later.
2. **Debug/maintain** it *entirely through sgt* (plan/save/sync/log/revert/restore/undo/…), and at
   every step ask "does sgt's output actually make sense here?" — fix sgt architecturally when it
   doesn't. No string-match/if-else edge patches; no prompt-cheating.

---

## Design (LiveHub)

Python package `livehub/`. Layered so each layer is a distinct sgt feature (good clustering fodder):

| # | module | responsibility |
|---|--------|----------------|
| 1 | `op.py` | reify edits: `Op` (id, actor, lamport, kind, target, payload); op kinds |
| 2 | `crdt.py` | RGA sequence CRDT — insert/delete by unique position id, deterministic merge |
| 3 | `document.py` | code `Document` over the CRDT; materialize → text |
| 4 | `bus.py` | in-process pub/sub message bus (simulates rooms/sockets) |
| 5 | `room.py` | `Room`: documents + actors; apply/broadcast ops |
| 6 | `analysis.py` | program analysis: symbol dependency graph from source; dangling-ref detection |
| 7 | `conflict.py` | `SemanticConflict` type; detect over converged state; store as valid state |
| 8 | `resolve.py` | deferred resolution of recorded semantic conflicts |
| 9 | `server.py`/`client.py` | real websocket transport (later) |

Invariant that makes this *not* plain CRDT: merge always converges (CRDT), but the converged
state may carry `SemanticConflict` annotations — code-dependency problems are data, not merge
failures.

"""LiveHub — a fully CRDT-based collaborative code repository.

Unlike a pull/push VCS, LiveHub is built around live rooms: multiple actors (users or agents)
edit the same codebase concurrently. Every edit is a reified :class:`~livehub.op.Op`, edits
merge through a sequence CRDT so replicas always converge, and a program-analysis layer records
code-dependency problems as first-class :class:`SemanticConflict` state rather than blocking the
merge.
"""

__all__ = ["op"]

"""Reified collaborative edit actions.

Every change to a LiveHub document is an :class:`Op`: a first-class, content-addressed record of
an edit action. Reifying edits this way is what makes the rest of LiveHub possible — ops are the
unit transmitted between actors in a room, the unit the CRDT merges, and the unit the
program-analysis layer reasons about.

Identity has two parts that must not be confused:

* ``(actor, lamport)`` is the *causal* identity — globally unique because each actor advances its
  own :class:`LamportClock` monotonically, and it carries happens-before information.
* ``id`` is a *content* hash over the whole op — deterministic, so two replicas that independently
  receive the same op agree on its id, which is what lets a set-union merge deduplicate.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum
from typing import Any


class OpKind(str, Enum):
    """The kinds of edit an op can reify. Deliberately minimal: a sequence CRDT only needs to add
    and tombstone elements; higher-level edits (replace, move) are expressed as compositions."""

    INSERT = "insert"
    DELETE = "delete"


class LamportClock:
    """A per-actor logical clock. ``tick`` advances it for a locally issued op; ``observe`` folds
    in a timestamp seen on a remote op so this actor's next op causally follows it (the standard
    Lamport rule: on receive, ``value = max(local, remote) + 1``)."""

    def __init__(self, value: int = 0) -> None:
        self.value = value

    def tick(self) -> int:
        self.value += 1
        return self.value

    def observe(self, remote: int) -> int:
        self.value = max(self.value, remote) + 1
        return self.value


def _content_id(actor: str, lamport: int, kind: OpKind, target: str, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    """A stable content hash. Canonical JSON (sorted keys) so any replica hashing the same op
    reaches the same id regardless of dict insertion order."""
    canonical = json.dumps(
        {"actor": actor, "lamport": lamport, "kind": kind.value, "target": target, "payload": payload},
        sort_keys=True,
        separators=(",", ":"),
    )
    return hashlib.sha256(canonical.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Op:
    """One reified edit. Frozen so an op is an immutable fact once minted — replicas may hold and
    forward it but never mutate it."""

    actor: str
    lamport: int
    kind: OpKind
    target: str
    payload: dict[str, Any]
    id: str = field(default="")

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not self.id:
            object.__setattr__(self, "id", _content_id(self.actor, self.lamport, self.kind, self.target, self.payload))


def mint(actor: str, clock: LamportClock, kind: OpKind, target: str, payload: dict[str, Any]) -> Op:
    """Mint a fresh op for ``actor``, advancing their clock. The single supported way to create a
    locally issued op, so a Lamport tick can never be forgotten."""
    return Op(actor=actor, lamport=clock.tick(), kind=kind, target=target, payload=payload)

import random

from livehub.crdt import RGA, elem_id
from livehub.op import LamportClock, Op, OpKind, mint


def ins(actor, clock, value, left):
    return mint(actor, clock, OpKind.INSERT, "doc", {"value": value, "left": left})


def dele(actor, clock, target):
    return mint(actor, clock, OpKind.DELETE, "doc", {"elem_id": target})


def replay(ops):
    rga = RGA()
    for op in ops:
        rga.apply(op)
    return rga


def test_sequential_typing():
    c = LamportClock()
    ops, left = [], None
    for ch in "hello":
        op = ins("alice", c, ch, left)
        ops.append(op)
        left = elem_id(op)
    assert replay(ops).value() == "hello"


def test_concurrent_inserts_converge_under_reordering():
    # Alice and Bob both insert one char at the head, concurrently.
    a = ins("alice", LamportClock(), "A", None)
    b = ins("bob", LamportClock(), "B", None)
    orders = [[a, b], [b, a]]
    results = {replay(o).value() for o in orders}
    assert len(results) == 1  # converges regardless of order
    # deterministic tiebreak: equal lamport (1) -> higher actor id first ("bob" > "alice")
    assert results.pop() == "BA"


def test_idempotent_reapply():

def _jaccard(a: frozenset, b: frozenset) -> float:
    union = a | b
    return len(a & b) / len(union) if union else 0.0


def _entity_name(sym: str) -> str | None:
    """The user-facing entity name a footprint symbol is about, or ``None`` for a fold-ordering
    artifact that names nothing (``__residue__``/``__anchor__``). Mirrors
    ``sgt.lens.label._clean_symbol_name`` (kept inline so this hot, offline matcher never imports
    the LLM-labeling module) — the two must agree on the kernel's symbol vocabulary."""
    if "::" not in sym:
        return sym.rsplit("/", 1)[-1] or None  # bare whole-file member -> its basename
    _, _, rest = sym.partition("::")
    if "__residue__" in rest or "__anchor__" in rest:
        return None
    name = rest.split("::")[-1].replace("\x00", "").strip("_")
    return name or None


def _norm_syms(footprint) -> frozenset[str]:
    """Path-robust behavioral match keys for footprint overlap: ``basename(file)::entity`` for each
    real symbol. Dropping the *directory* prefix is what lets a plan step's best-guess
    ``op.py::OpKind`` match the mined ``livehub/op.py::OpKind`` — a plan can't reliably predict the
    package path a symbol lands under (and the very first plan, intook before any tree exists, has
    nothing to ground the prefix on at all). The *filename* is deliberately kept: a real divergence
    like planned ``rga.py::RGA`` vs built ``crdt.py::RGA`` then correctly stays unmatched drift
    rather than being papered over. ``__plan__::`` sentinels and marker artifacts drop out."""
    keys = set()
    for sym in footprint:
        if sym.startswith("__plan__::"):
            continue
        name = _entity_name(sym)
        if name is None:
            continue
        base = sym.split("::", 1)[0].rsplit("/", 1)[-1]
        keys.add(f"{base}::{name}")
    return frozenset(keys)

_MARKERS = ("__anchor__", "__residue__")


def _entity_name(sym: str) -> str | None:
    """The behavioral entity a footprint symbol is about — the join key the plan predicts against.

    Unlike ``sgt.lens.label._clean_symbol_name`` (which drops ``__anchor__``/``__residue__``
    symbols entirely, because a *label* shouldn't list a fold-ordering artifact as a member), the
    matcher keeps the entity *named by* the marker: ``crdt.py::__anchor__::RGA`` is precisely "the
    op that placed entity RGA", the per-entity granularity a plan step is written at. Dropping it
    would leave only the fat whole-file aggregate op, whose 20-symbol footprint dilutes any
    single-symbol step's Jaccard below ``THRESHOLD``. So we strip the marker *segment* and return
    the qualname it decorates."""
    if "::" not in sym:
        return sym.rsplit("/", 1)[-1] or None  # bare whole-file member -> its basename
    _, _, rest = sym.partition("::")
    for marker in _MARKERS:  # drop a leading fold-ordering segment, keep the entity it names
        if rest.startswith(marker + "::"):
            rest = rest[len(marker) + 2:]
    name = rest.split("::")[-1].replace("\x00", "").strip("_")
    return name or None

flagged **27** ops as drift — i.e. the graph said "nothing you planned happened" when in fact I'd
built exactly the RGA/Element the plan named. This is the mandate's core question ("is the graph
showing the *real* drift from plan to implementation?") and the answer was flatly no. Traced to
`sgt/loop/match.py`, three distinct architectural faults in how footprints are compared:

1. **Matched on raw footprint strings incl. the guessed directory + file.** Plan predicted
   `op.py::OpKind`; mining produced `livehub/op.py::OpKind` → Jaccard 0 purely on the `livehub/`
   prefix. **Root reframe:** the *file* a symbol lands in is the planner's guess, not the user's
   stated intent (it drifts freely — planned `rga.py::RGA` vs built `crdt.py::RGA`), and the
   codebase's own identity scheme already demotes `file::qualname` to a surface lookup. So the join
   key must be the **entity qualname**, file dropped. (Method qualnames stay qualified —
   `RGA.apply`, never bare `apply` — so cross-class collisions can't happen.)
2. **Per-entity signal was being discarded.** Mining emits the real per-entity granularity as
   `__anchor__::RGA` ops; the initial normalization (mirroring `label._clean_symbol_name`) stripped
   those to nothing, leaving only one **coarse whole-file content op** (20 symbols) whose Jaccard
   against any 1-symbol step is ~0.05. **Fix:** keep the entity an anchor *names* (it's the finest
   "entity touched here" marker), but exclude `__residue__::X` — that's the positional gap *after*
   X, named for a neighbour; matching "build RGA" to it attributes work to the wrong entity. This
   is exactly why the kernel's own `is_behavioral` excludes residue.
3. **Drift counted bookkeeping as work.** 14 residue + anchor ordering ops were reported as
   "drift", inflating 1 real content op into "27 unplanned changes". **Fix:** an op is drift only
   if it normalizes to ≥1 named entity; pure positional/ordering ops are invisible to the plan
   layer (neither match nor drift).

"""A collaborative code file, modelled as a sequence CRDT.

:class:`Document` is the thin typed layer a room hands to actors: it owns one :class:`~livehub.crdt.RGA`
and turns high-level edits (type this text after that anchor, delete that element) into reified
:class:`~livehub.op.Op` s that it both applies locally and returns for broadcast. Because every edit
is an op and the RGA merges ops order-independently, two actors editing the same document in a live
room converge without locking — the property the whole system is built to preserve.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from livehub.crdt import RGA, elem_id
from livehub.op import LamportClock, Op, OpKind, mint


class Document:
    """One collaborative file. ``apply`` folds a (local or remote) op into the CRDT; ``insert`` and
    ``delete`` mint fresh ops for a local edit, apply them, and return them so the caller can
    broadcast the exact ops that were applied — never a re-derived diff."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._rga = RGA()

    def apply(self, op: Op) -> None:
        """Fold one op into the document. Idempotent and order-independent (the RGA guarantees
        both), so a room may deliver the same remote op twice or out of causal order safely."""
        self._rga.apply(op)

    def insert(self, actor: str, clock: LamportClock, text: str, after: str | None = None) -> list[Op]:
        """Type ``text`` as a run beginning after element ``after`` (or at the head when None).

        One op per character, each anchored on the element the previous op created, so the run lands
        contiguously and every character is an independently-addressable CRDT element (a later
        concurrent edit can split the run at any point). Returns the minted ops in order for
        broadcast."""
        ops: list[Op] = []
        left = after
        for ch in text:
            op = mint(actor, clock, OpKind.INSERT, "doc", {"value": ch, "left": left})
            self._rga.apply(op)
            left = elem_id(op)
            ops.append(op)
        return ops

    def delete(self, actor: str, clock: LamportClock, element_id: str) -> Op:
        """Tombstone the element ``element_id``. Returns the minted delete op for broadcast. The
        element is retained in the CRDT (tombstoned, not removed) so concurrent inserts anchored on
        it still resolve."""
        op = mint(actor, clock, OpKind.DELETE, "doc", {"elem_id": element_id})
        self._rga.apply(op)
        return op

    def text(self) -> str:
        """The current visible source — the materialized, non-tombstoned sequence."""
        return self._rga.value()

def _overlap(a: frozenset, b: frozenset) -> float:
    """The overlap coefficient (Szymkiewicz–Simpson): ``|a ∩ b| / min(|a|, |b|)``.

    Deliberately *not* Jaccard. Whether an op fulfilled a plan step must not depend on how much
    *other* work that op also did -- a coarse "add a whole file" op carries every entity in the
    file, and Jaccard's ``|a ∪ b|`` denominator would let that unrelated bulk dilute the score of
    every step the op genuinely fulfills, below ``THRESHOLD`` (a fully-built plan then reads as
    100% drift -- the exact bug this replaced). The overlap coefficient divides by the smaller
    footprint instead, so "does the op cover the step's entities (or vice-versa)" is answered on
    its own terms; the op's extra entities are accounted for separately -- as other steps' matches,
    or as drift."""
    if not a or not b:
        return 0.0
    return len(a & b) / min(len(a), len(b))

def _is_ordering_only(footprint) -> bool:
    """True iff every symbol is pure ordering/positioning metadata -- an ``anchor`` that places an
    entity or ``residue`` gap-bytes -- with no content the plan is written in.

    Such an op is the *companion* of whatever save placed the entity (the miner emits a per-entity
    anchor beside the coarse content op that carries the bytes); it is never behavioral work done
    *outside* a plan, so it is invisible to the drift layer -- exactly as pure residue already was.
    Anchors still contribute *matching* edges (``_norm_syms`` keeps them: the finest per-entity
    signal when a batch save folds every entity's bytes into one whole-file content op), so this
    predicate governs only *drift*, where a standalone anchor would otherwise masquerade as
    unplanned work and report a fully-planned build as mostly-drift.

    (``Document.insert`` with no top-level ``Document`` symbol) is real content-drift we must keep,
    so ``nested`` stays; only the two positional-artifact kinds are stripped."""
    return all(_symbol_kind(sym) in ("anchor", "residue") for sym in footprint)

"""In-process publish/subscribe — the rooms and sockets of a session, without a network.

A live collaborative session is a set of *rooms* (channels), each with several *actors* connected
over their own *socket*. :class:`Bus` is that substrate collapsed into one process: named channels
an actor subscribes a handler to, and a :meth:`Bus.publish` that fans a message out to every other
subscriber. It carries opaque messages (LiveHub sends :class:`~livehub.op.Op` s through it, but the
bus never inspects them) so it stays a pure transport layer — the same seam a real websocket server
slots into later.

Delivery is synchronous and deterministic: ``publish`` invokes each handler inline, in subscription
order, before returning. No threads, no queue — a message is fully delivered the moment it is sent,
so a test can assert the post-delivery state directly and replicas that exchange the same ops
converge without timing races.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Callable

Handler = Callable[[Any], None]


class Bus:
    """A set of named channels, each mapping subscriber ids to their handler. One :class:`Bus` per
    process stands in for the whole room/socket fabric; a real transport replaces it without any
    caller change, because callers only ever ``subscribe``/``publish``."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._channels: dict[str, dict[str, Handler]] = {}

    def subscribe(self, channel: str, subscriber_id: str, handler: Handler) -> None:
        """Register ``handler`` for ``channel`` under ``subscriber_id``. Keyed by id (not by the
        handler object) so a re-subscribe replaces the actor's handler rather than doubling its
        deliveries, and so ``publish`` can skip the sender by id."""
        self._channels.setdefault(channel, {})[subscriber_id] = handler

    def unsubscribe(self, channel: str, subscriber_id: str) -> None:
        """Drop ``subscriber_id``'s handler from ``channel``. A no-op if it was never subscribed, so
        an actor leaving a room it never joined is harmless."""
        subscribers = self._channels.get(channel)
        if subscribers is not None:
            subscribers.pop(subscriber_id, None)

    def publish(self, channel: str, message: Any, sender: str | None = None) -> int:
        """Deliver ``message`` to every subscriber of ``channel`` except ``sender``, synchronously
        and in subscription order. Returns the number of handlers invoked.

        Skipping the sender is what keeps an actor from re-applying its own op as if it were remote.
        We iterate a snapshot of the subscribers so a handler that (un)subscribes mid-delivery can't
        mutate the dict we're walking."""
        subscribers = self._channels.get(channel, {})
        delivered = 0
        for subscriber_id, handler in list(subscribers.items()):
            if subscriber_id == sender:
                continue
            handler(message)
            delivered += 1
        return delivered

from livehub.bus import Bus


def test_publish_delivers_to_all_subscribers():
    bus = Bus()
    seen_a, seen_b = [], []
    bus.subscribe("room1", "a", seen_a.append)
    bus.subscribe("room1", "b", seen_b.append)

    delivered = bus.publish("room1", "hello")

    assert delivered == 2
    assert seen_a == ["hello"] and seen_b == ["hello"]

    assert delivered == 1
    assert seen_a == [] and seen_b == ["from a"]

"""A live collaborative session — where op, document and bus compose.

This is the layer the whole stack was built toward. An :class:`Actor` is one *replica*: its own
:class:`~livehub.document.Document` and :class:`~livehub.op.LamportClock`, editing under an actor
id. A :class:`Room` is the shared space — a :class:`~livehub.bus.Bus` channel plus the actors
connected to it. A local edit is applied to the actor's own document *and* broadcast on the channel;
every other actor's :meth:`Actor.receive` applies it to their replica. Because each replica applies
the same set of ops and the underlying CRDT merges them order-independently, all actors in a room
converge on the same source without any locking — the invariant LiveHub exists to preserve.

No catch-up for late joiners yet: an actor is expected to join before editing begins (a real
server would replay the op log to a latecomer). Kept out until there's a transport that needs it.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from livehub.bus import Bus
from livehub.document import Document
from livehub.op import LamportClock, Op


class Actor:
    """One replica in a room: an actor id, its own document, and its own logical clock. Edits go
    through :meth:`insert`/:meth:`delete` (apply locally, then broadcast); remote ops arrive through
    :meth:`receive`."""

    def __init__(self, actor_id: str, room: "Room") -> None:
        self.id = actor_id
        self.doc = Document()
        self.clock = LamportClock()
        self._room = room

    def insert(self, text: str, after: str | None = None) -> list[Op]:
        """Type ``text`` into this replica and broadcast the exact ops applied, so peers apply the
        same ops rather than re-deriving a diff."""
        ops = self.doc.insert(self.id, self.clock, text, after)
        self._room.broadcast(ops, sender=self.id)
        return ops

    def delete(self, element_id: str) -> Op:
        """Tombstone ``element_id`` on this replica and broadcast the delete op."""
        op = self.doc.delete(self.id, self.clock, element_id)
        self._room.broadcast([op], sender=self.id)
        return op

    def receive(self, op: Op) -> None:
        """Apply a remote op. Observe its Lamport timestamp *first* so this replica's next locally
        minted op causally follows what it has already seen (the standard Lamport receive rule)."""
        self.clock.observe(op.lamport)
        self.doc.apply(op)

    def text(self) -> str:
        """This replica's current materialized source."""
        return self.doc.text()


class Room:
    """A shared session over one :class:`~livehub.bus.Bus` channel. Owns the actors that have
    joined and fans each actor's ops out to the others."""

    def __init__(self, bus: Bus, channel: str = "doc") -> None:
        self._bus = bus
        self._channel = channel
        self._actors: dict[str, Actor] = {}

    def join(self, actor_id: str) -> Actor:
        """Create an actor, register it, and subscribe its :meth:`Actor.receive` to the channel so
        it receives every other actor's broadcasts."""
        actor = Actor(actor_id, self)
        self._actors[actor_id] = actor
        self._bus.subscribe(self._channel, actor_id, actor.receive)
        return actor

    def broadcast(self, ops: list[Op], sender: str) -> None:
        """Publish each of ``sender``'s ops on the channel, skipping the sender so an actor never
        re-applies its own edit as if it were remote."""
        for op in ops:
            self._bus.publish(self._channel, op, sender=sender)

`sgt log --refresh` showed 4 of 6 features named after a bare *test* filename (`tests/test_crdt.py`,
`tests/test_bus.py`, `tests/test_room.py`, `tests/test_document.py`) instead of a semantic label,
while the two op.py features (built on the genesis save) kept good LLM labels ("Operation Types",
"Operation Stamping"). The slugs were always semantic — only the bold LLM label was a filename. The
mandate's "do clustering/ops-chunks/labels align?" — answered: no.

**Root cause — two mechanisms collide.** (1) When `sgt save` adds a symbol in a brand-new module,
`ledger.assign_at_save`'s *new-lane fallback* (nothing structurally adjacent to attach to — the norm
when each feature is its own new file) minted an `af-` authored feature and seeded its label with
`symbol.split("::",1)[0]` — the **file path** — as a provisional display name. (2) But an authored
feature's label is treated as *user-authoritative* and **overrides** the clustered/LLM label in
**three** projections (`tree.label_tree`, `api.map_view`, `api._grid_labels`, all `KTD4`). So the
provisional file-path guess permanently shadowed the LLM label a rebuild computed. (The winning lane
was the *test* file purely by `af-`id sort order in `_authored_leaf_claims`, which is why it was
`tests/test_*` and not `livehub/*`.) Empirically the whole ledger was polluted: **65 of 65** authored
features carried a file-path label, **0** a deliberate rename.

**Fix (architectural, not a string-patch).** The authored label register is the LWW name a
deliberate `sgt rename` sets; a save-time guess does not belong in it. So: the new-lane cascade now
creates the authored feature with an **empty** label register (`ledger.py`), keeping the file path
only as the tree *node's* provisional display label for the pre-rebuild grid window; and all three
override sites gained the same guard — **override only when the authored label is non-empty**
(`tree.py`, `api.py` ×2). An empty register means "claimed but unnamed" → the clustered/LLM label
stands until a real rename; a genuine rename (non-empty) still wins, unchanged. Repaired livehub's
already-stored data in place (cleared the 65 file-path labels to empty, matching each only where the
label equalled a member's own file prefix, so a real rename could never be clobbered).

**Result (verified end-to-end):** `sgt log` now shows **"Replicated Growth Array"** ·
add-rga-sequence-crdt, **"Event Bus"** · add-in-process-pub-sub, **"Collaborative Room"** ·
add-room-actor-live, **"CRDT Text Document"** · collaborative-edit — the bold LLM label and the plan
slug agree for every feature. 3 regression tests pin all three arms (cascade seeds empty + provisional
node label; empty-label claim defers to the clustered label; a deliberate non-empty rename still
overrides). `test_tree` + `test_ledger` (49), `test_api` (47), and the authored-touching suites
(convergence/select/reconcile/feature_verbs) all green.

Symptom: `sgt log` labels incrementally-added features (a new module per save) with their bare **file path** (often the *test* file), while genesis-save features keep good LLM labels.

Root cause (2026-07-23, fixed): two mechanisms collide.
1. `ledger.assign_at_save`'s **new-lane fallback** (fires whenever a new symbol has nothing structurally adjacent to attach to — the norm when each feature is its own new file) minted an `af-` authored feature seeded with `symbol.split("::",1)[0]` (the file path) as a *provisional* label.

That override lives in **THREE** projection sites — `sgt/lens/tree.py::label_tree`, `sgt/api.py::map_view`, `sgt/api.py::_grid_labels` (all KTD4). A guess in the register shadows the LLM label permanently.
The winning lane is the test file purely by `af-`id sort order in `_authored_leaf_claims`.

Fix pattern: the authored label register is the LWW name a deliberate `sgt rename` sets — a save-time guess must not enter it. New-lane cascade now seeds an **empty** label register (file path stays only as the tree *node's* provisional display label); all three override sites guard `if claim.label:` (empty = "claimed but unnamed" → clustered label stands; a real rename still wins). Detection for repairing polluted data: a label equal to one of the feature's own members' file prefix is cascade-minted, never a rename.

Key lesson: any "authored/authoritative" register that also accepts an auto-derived provisional value will leak that provisional into permanence unless the override checks for a deliberate (non-empty) value — and the override may be duplicated across several read projections. from livehub.analysis import DanglingReference, defined_symbols, dependency_graph, dangling_references


def test_defined_symbols_are_the_top_level_defs_and_classes():

Symptom: `sgt checkpoint` matches **0/N** steps even though the code was built exactly as the plan
described, while a sibling plan matched fine.

Root cause (2026-07-24, F10): the LLM decomposition in `sgt/loop/plan.py::_llm_decompose` emitted
**whole-file** footprints (bare `livehub/document.py`, no `::symbol`) instead of per-entity
`file::Symbol` — even for steps whose title names the symbol. The F5 matcher (`match.py::_norm_syms`)
**strips the file path** before computing overlap, so a *wrong* file is harmless
(`document.py::defined_symbols` still matches `analysis.py::defined_symbols`); the **only** breaker is
a missing `::symbol` — a bare file normalizes to `{basename}`, real ops normalize to entity qualnames
→ overlap 0. Trigger: the plan text named no file and said "over a converged document," which anchored
the model onto an existing file *and* let it drop to whole-file granularity.

Fix: make the granularity rule explicit and general in the footprint prompt (no example — not a
string-match hack): "when the step centers on a named function/class/method, include it at symbol
granularity as `file::Symbol`; reserve a bare `file` for genuine whole-file work like a module
skeleton; [] only when you truly cannot name a file." Re-intake → 0/7 → 4/7, every code step at
overlap 1.00; the model even self-corrected the file (per-symbol reasoning dissolved the wrong-file
anchor).

Accepted limitation (do NOT hack): **test steps** stay unmatched because the planner predicts test
*function* names that cannot be known before the test is written (`test_dangling_on_delete` vs actual
`test_dangling_reference_when_a_called_symbol_is_missing`). The design (F5/F8) deliberately refuses
file-path fallback — that refusal is why entity-qualname is the join key. A bare-file prediction would
not rescue them either (test ops carry per-test qualnames, no whole-file token).

Lesson: for the plan→checkpoint loop, footprint *granularity* is the join-quality lever, not the file
guess. When diagnosing a low match count, dump `store.get_hollow(step.hollow_id).footprint` and check

"""Semantic conflicts as first-class converged state — the heart of LiveHub's thesis.

A sequence CRDT guarantees every replica converges on the same source text (see :mod:`livehub.crdt`,
:mod:`livehub.document`). :mod:`livehub.analysis` then observes that the converged text can still be
*semantically* broken — a :class:`~livehub.analysis.DanglingReference` where one actor's call outlives
another actor's deleted definition. A pull/push VCS would reject that merge. LiveHub does not: the
merge already happened and converged. Instead this module lifts each defect into a
:class:`SemanticConflict` — a piece of data the converged codebase *carries* until someone resolves it
(deferred resolution lives in :mod:`livehub.resolve`).

The one idea that makes a conflict *state* rather than a throwaway report is **stable identity**. A
conflict is keyed by the ``(source, target)`` pair — the referrer and the missing name — not by line
number, which drifts every time the surrounding text is edited. That stability is what lets a
resolution decision (``resolved=True``) survive subsequent edits: :func:`reconcile` re-detects against
fresh text and carries the flag forward for any conflict whose defect still exists.

Scope of v1, kept honest:
  * A conflict's payload is exactly one dangling reference. Higher-order defects (cycles, type
    mismatches) are out of scope — this layer reports what :mod:`analysis` can see.
  * ``resolved`` is a plain flag; the *actions* that set it, and the room wiring that holds conflicts
    live, are :mod:`livehub.resolve`'s job. Here it exists only so :func:`reconcile` can preserve it.
  * :func:`reconcile`'s rule for a defect that disappears and later returns: the return is a *fresh*
    open conflict, not the old resolved one. A clean intermediate state means the earlier resolution
    no longer applies — re-earning ``resolved`` is the safe default when the report drives real fixes.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass

from livehub.analysis import dangling_references


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SemanticConflict:
    """A recognized code-dependency defect the converged codebase carries until it is resolved.

    ``source`` calls ``target``, which resolves to no definition available in the document. ``line``
    is the 1-based line where the call currently sits — informational only. ``resolved`` records
    whether the conflict has been deliberately accepted/deferred (set by :mod:`livehub.resolve`)."""

    source: str
    target: str
    line: int
    resolved: bool = False

    @property
    def key(self) -> tuple[str, str]:
        """Stable identity: the ``(source, target)`` pair. Line is excluded on purpose — it drifts as
        the surrounding text is edited, and a conflict is "the same defect" across those edits."""
        return (self.source, self.target)


def detect(source: str) -> list[SemanticConflict]:
    """Every dangling reference in ``source``, lifted to an *open* :class:`SemanticConflict`. This is
    the state a room holds right after a merge converges: the code is agreed-upon, the conflicts are
    data layered on top. Order follows :func:`~livehub.analysis.dangling_references` (deterministic)."""
    return [SemanticConflict(source=d.source, target=d.target, line=d.line)
            for d in dangling_references(source)]


def reconcile(known: list[SemanticConflict], source: str) -> list[SemanticConflict]:
    """Re-detect conflicts in ``source`` and merge with the ``known`` set, preserving resolution:

    * a conflict whose defect still exists **and** was previously ``resolved`` stays resolved;
    * a conflict whose defect is gone (target now defined, or caller removed) is **dropped**;
    * a conflict that is newly present, or reappeared after a clean interval, is **open**.

    The result is exactly the current defects (identity by ``key``), so the returned set always
    matches the converged text — resolution is the only thing carried across, never a stale defect."""
    resolved_keys = {c.key for c in known if c.resolved}
    return [conflict if conflict.key not in resolved_keys
            else SemanticConflict(conflict.source, conflict.target, conflict.line, resolved=True)
            for conflict in detect(source)]

from livehub.conflict import SemanticConflict, detect, reconcile


def test_detect_lifts_dangling_references_into_open_conflicts():
    # foo() calls bar, which is not defined anywhere -> one open conflict.
    src = "def foo():\n    return bar()\n"
    conflicts = detect(src)
    assert conflicts == [SemanticConflict(source="foo", target="bar", line=2, resolved=False)]
    assert conflicts[0].key == ("foo", "bar")


def test_detect_is_empty_when_the_code_is_semantically_whole():
    src = "def bar():\n    return 1\n\n\ndef foo():\n    return bar()\n"
    assert detect(src) == []


def test_reconcile_carries_resolved_status_forward_while_the_defect_persists():
    src = "def foo():\n    return bar()\n"
    # A prior pass resolved the foo->bar conflict; the defect is still in the text.
    known = [SemanticConflict(source="foo", target="bar", line=2, resolved=True)]
    reconciled = reconcile(known, src)
    assert reconciled == [SemanticConflict(source="foo", target="bar", line=2, resolved=True)]


def test_reconcile_ignores_line_drift_when_matching_identity():
    # The resolved conflict was recorded at line 2; the defect now sits at a different line.
    src = "# a new leading comment\n\n\ndef foo():\n    return bar()\n"
    known = [SemanticConflict(source="foo", target="bar", line=2, resolved=True)]
    reconciled = reconcile(known, src)
    # identity is (source, target), so resolution carries despite the line moving to 5.
    assert reconciled == [SemanticConflict(source="foo", target="bar", line=5, resolved=True)]


def test_reconcile_drops_a_defect_that_no_longer_exists():
    # bar got defined, so foo->bar is no longer dangling -- the (resolved) conflict is gone entirely.
    src = "def bar():\n    return 1\n\n\ndef foo():\n    return bar()\n"
    known = [SemanticConflict(source="foo", target="bar", line=2, resolved=True)]
    assert reconcile(known, src) == []


def test_reconcile_reopens_a_conflict_that_reappears_after_a_clean_interval():
    # The old conflict was resolved, then the code went clean; a *new* call to a missing name is a
    # fresh open conflict -- the stale resolution does not apply to a defect re-earned from scratch.
    src = "def foo():\n    return baz()\n"
    known = [SemanticConflict(source="foo", target="bar", line=2, resolved=True)]  # a different target
    reconciled = reconcile(known, src)
    assert reconciled == [SemanticConflict(source="foo", target="baz", line=2, resolved=False)]

"""Deferred resolution — the actions a collaborative room takes on the conflicts it carries.

:mod:`livehub.conflict` turns each code-dependency defect into a :class:`~livehub.conflict.SemanticConflict`
the converged codebase *holds* rather than blocking the merge over. This module is the other half of that
bargain: the decisions a room makes about that held state. :func:`resolve` marks a conflict deliberately
accepted — the team has seen the dangling reference and chosen to keep editing around it — and
:func:`reopen` reverses that decision. :func:`~livehub.conflict.reconcile` carries the ``resolved`` flag
across edits; the functions here are what set it in the first place.

The whole point is *deferral*. Resolving a conflict touches no code (the CRDT already converged) and does
not make the defect go away — it records a decision. :func:`open_conflicts` is then the room's live
worklist (defects nobody has accepted yet) and :func:`resolved_conflicts` is the accepted-and-deferred
set. When a later edit actually fixes the underlying code, :func:`~livehub.conflict.reconcile` drops the
conflict regardless of its flag, so a resolution only ever suppresses a defect from the worklist — it
never masks a genuine fix.

Every function is pure and returns a new list. A :class:`~livehub.conflict.SemanticConflict` is frozen and
a room replaces its conflict set wholesale on each edit (reconcile) or decision (resolve/reopen), so there
is no in-place mutation to reason about. Targeting is by ``(source, target)`` key: acting on a conflict
that is not present is a harmless no-op, because the live set may have shifted under a concurrent edit and
a stale decision must not raise.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from livehub.conflict import SemanticConflict


def resolve(conflicts: list[SemanticConflict], source: str, target: str) -> list[SemanticConflict]:
    """Mark the ``(source, target)`` conflict as deliberately accepted, returning a new list. A no-op if
    no such conflict is present (a stale decision against a defect a concurrent edit already cleared).
    Idempotent: resolving an already-resolved conflict leaves it resolved."""
    return _set_resolved(conflicts, source, target, True)


def reopen(conflicts: list[SemanticConflict], source: str, target: str) -> list[SemanticConflict]:
    """Reverse a prior :func:`resolve`: the ``(source, target)`` conflict returns to the open worklist.
    A no-op if absent; idempotent on an already-open conflict."""
    return _set_resolved(conflicts, source, target, False)


def _set_resolved(conflicts: list[SemanticConflict], source: str, target: str,
                  value: bool) -> list[SemanticConflict]:
    """Rebuild the list with the ``(source, target)`` conflict's ``resolved`` flag set to ``value``,
    every other conflict left as-is. The shared body of :func:`resolve`/:func:`reopen`."""
    key = (source, target)
    return [SemanticConflict(c.source, c.target, c.line, resolved=value) if c.key == key else c
            for c in conflicts]

def open_conflicts(conflicts: list[SemanticConflict]) -> list[SemanticConflict]:
    """The room's live worklist: the defects nobody has accepted yet. Preserves input order."""
    return [c for c in conflicts if not c.resolved]


def resolved_conflicts(conflicts: list[SemanticConflict]) -> list[SemanticConflict]:
    """The accepted-and-deferred set: defects the team chose to keep editing around. Preserves order."""
    return [c for c in conflicts if c.resolved]

## F13 — **[sgt BUG, fixed]** `sgt log --refresh` crashes (KeyError) when an orphan af-lane's pinned members scatter (2026-07-24)

**Symptom.** Right after building feature 8, `sgt log --refresh` crashed with
`KeyError: 'af-f85c2792970743d094188eaf7eeae7b3'` deep in `sgt.lens.tree._dedup` (tree.py:884, the
`nodes[c]["depth"]` read while rebuilding a merged leaf). The plain `sgt log` (splice, no re-name)
rendered fine; only the `--refresh` re-name path tripped it.

**Root cause (a false invariant, not a bad input).** `_dedup` isn't the culprit — it was fed a
malformed tree: node `N` had the *same* child id `af-f85c…` listed **twice**. Traced the aliasing to
`_apply_assign_pins` (tree.py:767). Its docstring asserted *"must-link contraction already guarantees
one leaf per assign target, so this is a plain rename."* That guarantee holds only for a target the
recluster actually contracted. But an **orphan af-lane** — a provisional feature minted by
`assign_at_save` for a structurally-disconnected symbol — is spliced **verbatim** by the default
`force_rebuild=False` path and never reclustered, so its pinned members can land in **several current
leaves**. `af-f85c…` had 6 pinned members scattered across 2 leaves (3 resolve.py code + 3 test). The
old code built `amap = {leaf: fid}` per member, so **both** leaves mapped to the one fid →
`_apply_id_map` renamed both → duplicate children → `_dedup`'s `del nodes[dupes[1:]]` deleted the very
survivor it then tried to read. A non-injective id-map, introduced solely here (confirmed
`match_identities` is injective).

**Fix (architectural — resolve to plurality, don't alias).** Made `_apply_assign_pins` mirror the
already-correct `_authored_leaf_claims` (tree.py:785): group pinned members by fid, resolve each fid to
the **single leaf holding the plurality of its members** (tie → smallest leaf id), and let each leaf be
claimed by at most the strongest pin. The id-map is now injective in both directions by construction,
so no two leaves can ever collapse onto one node. This repairs the false invariant at its source rather
than defending `_dedup` against duplicates (CLAUDE.md §7 — root cause, not a null-check).

**Verification.** Wrote a failing-first unit test
(`test_assign_pin_with_scattered_members_resolves_to_one_leaf`) that hand-builds the scatter (one fid,
members split 2/1 across two leaves) and asserts unique children + plurality-leaf attribution +
`op_leaf` remap. Reproduced the `['af-x','af-x']` aliasing, applied the fix, test passes; full
`tests/lens/test_tree.py` green; `sgt log --refresh` in livehub now renders all 10 features. Fix
**uncommitted** per mandate.

**Adjacent observation (not this bug — F9 territory, noted).** The refreshed log shows **two**
`livehub/resolve.py` leaves (`af-f85c…`, `af-b1f33…`) still labeled with the *file path* instead of a
semantic name — the F9 file-path-fallback symptom recurring for freshly-authored/orphan af-lanes that
the labeler couldn't (or didn't) name. Distinct from F13's crash; flagged for the labels-align pass.

## F14 — **[sgt BUG, fixed]** doubled `af-af-<uuid>` authored lanes: the ownership CRDT diverges from the assign pin (2026-07-24)

**How it surfaced.** Chasing F13's incoherent "resolve.py" leaves, I dumped the authored-feature store
(`.sgt/authored/features.json`) and found exactly two lanes with a literal **doubled** prefix —
`af-af-b1f33996a…` (7 member_adds) and `af-af-f85c2792…` (6 member_adds). They are the *only* lanes
with more than one member; every legitimately-minted lane owns exactly one symbol. Meanwhile the assign
pins (`.sgt/pins/pins.json`) reference the **single-prefix** ids `af-b1f33…`/`af-f85c…`. So for those
symbols the two stores disagree: the pin says the symbol lives in `af-f85c…`, but the membership CRDT
recorded it under `af-af-f85c…`.

**Root cause (a contract violated by a new caller).** `sgt.lens.verbs._authored_id_for(feature_id)`
returned `f"af-{feature_id}"` unconditionally. Its contract (per its own docstring) is to turn a
*cluster* feature id (`N42`) into a deterministic authored handle (`af-N42`) so a reorg verb updates one
feature idempotently. But `ledger.assign_at_save` (ledger.py:229) calls it with the **lane a new symbol
attaches to**, and that lane can *already* be an `af-<uuid>` authored lane minted by a prior save. Feed
an `af-` id to a function that blindly prepends `af-` and you get `af-af-<uuid>` — a phantom lane no pin
and no tree node ever names. The symbol's assign pin was written to the real `af-<uuid>` (ledger.py:227,
`assign[symbol] = lane`), but its member was added under the doubled id (ledger.py:230–235). This is
why resolve.py's later-saved symbols (`open_conflicts`, `resolved_conflicts`, the tests) accreted onto
`af-af-…`: each was a new symbol that attached to the existing `af-…` lane.

**Why it matters (beyond dead data).** The authored feature is *"the CRDT that carries the assignment
across sync"* (ledger.py:172–174). Storing those member_adds under an id the pin never uses means a
`sync`/`reconcile` would merge ownership under `af-af-…` and never reconcile it against the `af-…` the
rest of the system keys on — a genuine convergence bug for the ownership ledger (the very thing this
branch, `feat/ownership-ledger-grid`, exists to get right), not merely cosmetic. It also hits any reorg
verb (`rename`/`merge`/`move`) invoked *on an authored feature directly* — `sgt rename af-b1f33 …` would
have written to `af-af-b1f33`.

**Fix (make the handle idempotent — the contract, stated).** `_authored_id_for` now returns the id
unchanged when it already starts with `af-`; a cluster id still gets the handle. The authored id *for
something already authored is itself*. This is the root contract, not an edge-case guard: an `af-` id is
already an authored id, so wrapping it is never correct for any caller (ledger or reorg verb).
Failing-first unit test `test_authored_id_for_is_idempotent_on_an_already_authored_id`
(reproduced `af-af-b1f33…`, now `af-b1f33…`); full `test_feature_verbs`/`test_ledger`/`test_authored`/
`test_reconcile`/`test_sync` suites green. Fix **uncommitted** per mandate.

**Residual in this workspace (pre-fix dead data).** livehub's authored store still holds the two
`af-af-…` phantom lanes minted *before* the fix. They are harmless here — no pin/tree references them
and this repo is never synced — and a fresh recluster won't reintroduce them. Left as-is (rewriting a
committed metadata artifact to scrub two dead keys isn't worth it in a single-clone test repo); the fix
guarantees no *new* save creates them.

                # `tree.label_tree` lets any non-empty authored label permanently override the
                # rebuild's own label. Seeding it here would freeze the lane's name at this snapshot
                # (and, for a provisional lane, shadow it with a file path). Only a deliberate
                # `sgt rename` fills the register; until then the rebuild owns the name.
                af[aid] = replace(
                    authored.create(node["members"], "", witness=head), id=aid,
                )

"""The network hub — bus.py's publish/subscribe fan-out, but across connections.

:class:`~livehub.bus.Bus` is this same fabric collapsed into one process; a real deployment needs the
fan-out to cross the wire between separately-running replicas. :class:`Server` is that hub. A client
connects over a :class:`Connection` — a duplex text-frame channel (a websocket in production, an
in-memory :func:`loopback` pair in tests) — subscribes to channels, and publishes ops the server
fans out to every *other* connection subscribed to that channel.

The wire is JSON frames and the server never inspects an op's payload, exactly as :class:`Bus`
doesn't: it routes frames by channel. Convergence is still the clients' sequence CRDT merging the
same set of ops — the server only moves those ops between replicas, so the invariant LiveHub
preserves in one process holds unchanged across the network.

Routing rule (mirrors :meth:`Bus.publish` skipping the sender): a published op is delivered to every
connection on the channel *except the one it arrived on*. That origin connection's own actors have
already applied the op locally (see :class:`~livehub.client.RemoteBus`), so echoing it back would
only lean on the CRDT's idempotency guard for no reason.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from typing import Any, Callable, Protocol

from livehub.op import Op, OpKind


class Connection(Protocol):
    """A duplex text-frame channel between one client and the server. A real transport (a websocket)
    and the in-memory :func:`loopback` pair below both satisfy it: send a frame, and register one
    handler that fires for each inbound frame."""

    def send(self, frame: str) -> None: ...

    def on_receive(self, handler: Callable[[str], None]) -> None: ...


def encode_op(op: Op) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """An op as a JSON-safe dict. ``kind`` flattens to its string value; ``id`` rides along so the
    receiver reuses the sender's content hash rather than recomputing it — both replicas must agree
    on the id for the CRDT's set-union merge to dedupe."""
    return {
        "actor": op.actor, "lamport": op.lamport, "kind": op.kind.value,
        "target": op.target, "payload": op.payload, "id": op.id,
    }


def decode_op(d: dict[str, Any]) -> Op:
    """Rebuild an op from :func:`encode_op`'s dict, carrying the original id through so replicas
    agree on it rather than re-deriving (which they would anyway, from the same fields)."""
    return Op(
        actor=d["actor"], lamport=d["lamport"], kind=OpKind(d["kind"]),
        target=d["target"], payload=d["payload"], id=d["id"],
    )


class Server:
    """The fan-out hub. Tracks, per channel, the connections subscribed to it, and forwards each
    published frame to the others. Keyed by the connection's identity, so one connection hosting
    several actors on a channel still counts once for routing (the client multiplexes its own
    actors; the server only cares which connection to reach)."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._channels: dict[str, dict[int, Connection]] = {}

    def connect(self, conn: Connection) -> None:
        """Attach a client connection: route each frame it sends through this server's dispatch."""
        conn.on_receive(lambda frame: self._dispatch(conn, frame))

    def _dispatch(self, conn: Connection, frame: str) -> None:
        msg = json.loads(frame)
        t = msg["t"]
        if t == "sub":
            self._channels.setdefault(msg["ch"], {})[id(conn)] = conn
        elif t == "unsub":
            subscribers = self._channels.get(msg["ch"])
            if subscribers is not None:
                subscribers.pop(id(conn), None)
        elif t == "pub":
            self._fanout(msg["ch"], frame, origin=conn)

    def _fanout(self, channel: str, frame: str, origin: Connection) -> None:
        """Forward ``frame`` verbatim to every connection on ``channel`` except ``origin``. We
        iterate a snapshot so a handler that (un)subscribes mid-delivery can't mutate the dict we
        walk (same guard as :meth:`Bus.publish`)."""
        subscribers = self._channels.get(channel, {})
        for key, conn in list(subscribers.items()):
            if key == id(origin):
                continue
            conn.send(frame)


class _Endpoint:
    """One side of an in-memory :func:`loopback` pair. Sending invokes the peer's receive handler
    inline — synchronous, in-order delivery, the same determinism as :class:`Bus` (no threads, no
    queue), so a test can assert converged state directly without timing races."""

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._peer: _Endpoint | None = None
        self._handler: Callable[[str], None] | None = None

    def on_receive(self, handler: Callable[[str], None]) -> None:
        self._handler = handler

    def send(self, frame: str) -> None:
        peer = self._peer
        if peer is not None and peer._handler is not None:
            peer._handler(frame)


def loopback() -> tuple[_Endpoint, _Endpoint]:
    """A connected pair of in-memory endpoints — a synchronous stand-in for a websocket pair, so
    server/client convergence is testable without a network. Whatever one endpoint sends, the other
    receives inline. A networked deployment swaps these for two ends of a real websocket, which
    satisfy the same :class:`Connection` protocol."""
    a, b = _Endpoint(), _Endpoint()
    a._peer, b._peer = b, a
    return a, b

"""Client-side transport — a drop-in :class:`~livehub.bus.Bus` that fans out over a server connection.

:class:`~livehub.room.Room` and :class:`~livehub.room.Actor` were written against
:meth:`Bus.subscribe`/:meth:`Bus.publish` and nothing else, precisely so the in-process bus could be
swapped for a network one without touching them. :class:`RemoteBus` is that swap: the same two-method
surface, but a publish also crosses the wire to a :class:`~livehub.server.Server`, and frames arriving
from the server are dispatched to the local actors. Build a ``Room(RemoteBus(conn), channel)`` and its
actors converge with actors on any other connection to the same server — the CRDT does the merging,
the transport just moves the ops.

Local vs. remote delivery (the one subtlety worth stating): a :meth:`publish` delivers to this bus's
*own* subscribers directly, skipping the sender exactly like :class:`Bus`, *and* sends the op to the
server, which fans it out to the *other* connections. An inbound frame from the server is delivered to
*every* local subscriber — a remote op has no local sender to skip. So an op reaches each actor once by
routing, and the CRDT's idempotency guard covers any redelivery besides.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
from typing import Any, Callable

from livehub.op import Op
from livehub.server import Connection, Server, decode_op, encode_op, loopback

Handler = Callable[[Any], None]


class RemoteBus:
    """A :class:`Bus`-compatible fan-out over a :class:`Connection` to a server. Holds its own local
    subscribers (so co-located actors see each other without a wire round-trip) and forwards every
    publish across the connection for the other replicas."""

    def __init__(self, conn: Connection) -> None:
        self._conn = conn
        self._subscribers: dict[str, dict[str, Handler]] = {}
        conn.on_receive(self._dispatch)

    def subscribe(self, channel: str, subscriber_id: str, handler: Handler) -> None:
        """Register ``handler`` locally and tell the server this connection is on ``channel`` (so the
        server routes other replicas' ops here). Keyed by id, like :class:`Bus`, so a re-subscribe
        replaces rather than doubles."""
        self._subscribers.setdefault(channel, {})[subscriber_id] = handler
        self._conn.send(json.dumps({"t": "sub", "ch": channel, "id": subscriber_id}))

    def unsubscribe(self, channel: str, subscriber_id: str) -> None:
        """Drop a local subscriber and, if it was this connection's last on the channel, the server
        could stop routing here — we always send the unsub; the server no-ops a redundant one."""
        subscribers = self._subscribers.get(channel)
        if subscribers is not None:
            subscribers.pop(subscriber_id, None)
        self._conn.send(json.dumps({"t": "unsub", "ch": channel, "id": subscriber_id}))

    def publish(self, channel: str, message: Op, sender: str | None = None) -> int:
        """Deliver locally (skipping ``sender``, like :class:`Bus`) then send across the wire for the
        other connections. Returns the local delivery count. LiveHub only ever publishes an
        :class:`~livehub.op.Op` here, so the message is wire-encoded as one."""
        delivered = self._deliver_local(channel, message, skip=sender)
        self._conn.send(json.dumps({"t": "pub", "ch": channel, "op": encode_op(message)}))
        return delivered

    def _deliver_local(self, channel: str, op: Op, skip: str | None) -> int:
        delivered = 0
        for subscriber_id, handler in list(self._subscribers.get(channel, {}).items()):
            if subscriber_id == skip:
                continue
            handler(op)
            delivered += 1
        return delivered

    def _dispatch(self, frame: str) -> None:
        """Handle a frame from the server. Only ``pub`` frames carry work for a client: apply the op
        to every local subscriber (a remote op has no local sender to skip)."""
        msg = json.loads(frame)
        if msg["t"] == "pub":
            self._deliver_local(msg["ch"], decode_op(msg["op"]), skip=None)


def connect(server: Server) -> RemoteBus:
    """Wire a fresh :class:`RemoteBus` to ``server`` over an in-memory :func:`loopback` pair — the
    one-call setup for an in-process client (tests, single-process demos). A networked client builds a
    :class:`RemoteBus` on a real websocket :class:`Connection` instead; nothing else changes."""
    client_end, server_end = loopback()
    server.connect(server_end)
    return RemoteBus(client_end)

def _file_of(sym: str) -> str:
    """The file a footprint symbol lives in -- everything left of the first ``::`` (a bare
    whole-file symbol IS its own file). This is the scope a *file-granularity* plan prediction
    joins on (see ``_step_keys``)."""
    return sym.split("::", 1)[0]


def _op_keys(footprint) -> frozenset[str]:
    """A real op's match keys, indexed at BOTH granularities so a step predicted at either finds
    it: the entity *qualname* of each symbol (``ent:`` keys) AND the *file* each touches (``file:``
    keys). The two namespaces are prefix-disjoint, so a file path can never collide with a qualname.

    An op is *reality* -- it always knows both its entities and their file -- so it is indexed every
    way a prediction might name it. Whether the file actually gates a match is decided entirely on
    the plan side (``_step_keys``): a symbol-level prediction contributes no ``file:`` key, so an
    op's ``file:`` keys sit inert against it and file drift stays free.

    ``__plan__::`` sentinels drop out. So does ``residue`` (positional gap-bytes named after the
    *preceding* entity -- ``__residue__::RGA`` is the gap that follows RGA, not RGA itself, so
    matching a "build RGA" step to it would attribute the work to a neighbour; the kernel's
    ``is_behavioral`` excludes residue for the same reason). An ``anchor`` is kept: it is the
    genuine per-entity creation marker, and the finest-grained "this entity was touched here"
    signal when a batch save folds the actual bytes into one coarse whole-file content op."""
    keys = set()
    for sym in footprint:
        if sym.startswith("__plan__::") or _symbol_kind(sym) == "residue":
            continue
        name = _entity_name(sym)
        if name is not None:
            keys.add("ent:" + name)
        keys.add("file:" + _file_of(sym))
    return frozenset(keys)


def _step_keys(footprint) -> frozenset[str]:
    """A plan step's match keys, at the granularity the planner *stated* -- the crux of the
    two-level join.

    A ``file::qualname`` step entry keeps only its qualname (``ent:`` key). The entities are the
    stated intent (``RGA``, ``Element``, ``Op.__post_init__``); the *file* they land in is the
    planner's guess -- it drifts freely (planned ``rga.py::RGA`` vs built ``crdt.py::RGA``) and
    gating on it would report a fulfilled-but-moved entity as drift, the opposite of the truth. So
    identity is the qualname, matching the codebase's own scheme (``file::qualname`` is a surface
    lookup, not the join key). Qualnames stay *qualified* (``RGA.apply``, never bare ``apply``), so
    two methods of different classes never collide; only two top-level entities sharing a name
    across files could, and a checkpoint match is preview-only -- never written without an explicit
    ``confirm``.

    A *bare-file* entry (no ``::``) is a genuine file-granularity predicate: the file IS the stated
    intent (the LLM decomposer's usual output -- "work in ``livehub/server.py``"), so it becomes a
    ``file:`` key that matches any op touching that file. Without this, a file-level prediction --
    which carries no qualname -- could never join the symbol-level ops (``server.py::Server``) that
    implement it, and a faithfully-built file-level plan read as 100% drift.

    ``__plan__::`` sentinels and ``residue`` drop out, as in ``_op_keys``."""
    keys = set()
    for sym in footprint:
        if sym.startswith("__plan__::") or _symbol_kind(sym) == "residue":
            continue
        if "::" in sym:  # entity-level prediction: the qualname is identity, the file is dropped
            name = _entity_name(sym)
            if name is not None:
                keys.add("ent:" + name)
        else:  # bare file: a file-granularity predicate joins on file scope
            keys.add("file:" + sym)
    return frozenset(keys)

def active_sessions(repo: str | Path) -> dict:
    """Every *active* session, keyed by id -- the review surface's read side (mirrors
    `sgt.core.rewrite.pending_drafts`). A `completed` (every step matched, or explicitly
    `mark_done`) or already-abandoned plan is history, not review surface, so it drops out here:
    that is what stops the workbench and status bar from rendering a growing pile of finished
    plans. The full table -- including completed history -- is still readable via `_load_sessions`
    for provenance."""
    return {sid: rec for sid, rec in _load_sessions(Path(repo)).items() if rec["status"] == "active"}

def mark_done(repo: str | Path, session_id: str) -> bool:
    """Explicitly close a session an agent (or human) has finished with. Unlike `abandon` (which
    deletes the record), the record is kept as `completed` history -- so `sgt revert --session` and
    the trust queue can still attribute its landed work -- while its still-pending hollows are
    cleaned up and it leaves the active review surface. `False` if `session_id` is unknown.

    A fully-matched session already reaches `completed` on its own (see
    `sgt.loop.match.confirm_match`); this is the manual close for a plan whose remaining steps were
    done differently than predicted and will never match."""
    repo = Path(repo)
    table = _load_sessions(repo)
    record = table.get(session_id)
    if record is None:
        return False
    store = Store(repo)
    for step in record["steps"]:
        if step["status"] == "pending":
            (store.hollow_dir / step["hollow_id"]).unlink(missing_ok=True)
    record["status"] = "completed"
    record["last_activity_ts"] = time.time()
    _save_sessions(repo, table)
    return True
