\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Programming by request}

The unit of work in studies of programming with a language model has grown, and
it grew fast. Barke et al.\ watched 20 programmers and found them using the model
in two ways, finishing a line they had already planned, or asking for a starting
point in code they did not yet know how to write~\cite{barke2023}. Vaithilingam
et al.\ found that 24 participants using Copilot did not complete tasks faster
and still preferred to keep it on, because it gave them something to start
from~\cite{vaithilingam2022}. In both studies the thing the developer accepted
was a line or a block. Four years later the benchmark that organises the field
gives a model a natural language issue report from a real repository and scores
it on whether the repository's own tests pass afterwards~\cite{jimenez2024}, and
the systems built to score well on it edit several files in a
loop~\cite{yang2024}. The unit a developer hands over has gone from a line to a
paragraph of English, and the code that comes back is correspondingly larger.

What this literature studies is the moment of acceptance. It asks whether the
code is correct~\cite{perry2023}, whether the developer can tell that it is
correct~\cite{vasconcelos2025}, and whether they trust
it~\cite{liang2024,nguyen2024}. It stops there. A week later the same developer
wants to remove the rate limiting they asked for on Tuesday and keep the caching
they asked for on Wednesday, and that is a version control operation. We know of
no study of what happens to agent-written code after it is committed, and the
tools it is committed with were designed for a workflow in which the person
committing wrote the lines.

\subsection{What a version control system agrees to record}

Git records a version as a snapshot of the whole working tree, and each commit
names its parents plus a tree of file contents addressed by hash~\cite{git2026}.
Two properties follow directly, and both are worth the design. Verifying that a
history has not been altered is a matter of rehashing, and a merge is computed on
demand from a common ancestor, so no operation in git has to reason about how two
edits interact. Pérez De Rosso and Jackson analysed git's concepts against the
purposes users bring to them and found several places where a concept serves a
purpose users do not have, the staging area and detached \cmd{HEAD} among them.
Their redesign, Gitless, removes
both~\cite{perezderosso2013,perezderosso2016}. The concept our argument turns on
survives their redesign untouched, because it is not a misfit. A commit is the
smallest thing git can name, so any operation over less than a commit works by
having the developer point at lines, which is what \cmd{git add -p} and
\cmd{git rebase -i} are for. Under git's original constraints this is the
cheapest correct design available. The person running \cmd{git add -p} in 2005
had typed the lines minutes earlier, so the decomposition was already in their
head, and recording it in the repository would have meant maintaining a second
structure that could disagree with the first. Asking the developer at commit time
is free when the developer knows.

Darcs takes the other option and records a version as a patch that adds and
removes lines in a stated context~\cite{roundy2009}. Patches that do not depend
on each other commute, so a user can pull the third patch in a series without the
first two, and the theory behind this has been formalised more than
once~\cite{jacobson2009,mimram2013}. Pijul reimplements it on a data structure
designed to make the operations fast~\cite{pijul2024}. What that buys is an
honest cherry-pick. In git, moving a commit to another branch reapplies a diff in
a context it was not written against and produces a second commit with a second
hash, so the same work has two identities and a later rebase has to be told which
one you meant. In Darcs the patch that moves is the patch that was recorded, and
the dependencies it names travel with it. The place this design runs out is where
the dependency is not textual. When an agent adds a \sym{Retry} class in a new
file and edits \sym{api.py::handle} to call it, the two patches share no line, so
nothing in the record says that pulling the second without the first yields a
file referring to a name that does not exist. Darcs is explicit about this and
offers a way to declare a dependency by hand. We would have made the same call in
2003. Computing a dependency between two functions requires parsing the language,
and a version control system that parses is a version control system that works
for some languages and not others. That is a price Darcs declined to pay and one
we do pay, in the form of a system that reads Python, TypeScript and TSX and
treats a Go file as an opaque blob.

Jujutsu and Mercurial both add a record of history's own history. Jujutsu gives
each change an identifier separate from its commit hash, so rewriting a commit
produces a new commit id while ``the change ID generally remains the
same''~\cite{jjglossary2026}, and a change with more than one visible commit is
called divergent. Conflicts are recorded in commits so that no command fails
because of them, and rewriting a commit automatically rebases its
descendants~\cite{jujutsu2026}. Mercurial's changeset evolution records
obsolescence markers, stored apart from changeset data, that say which changeset
superseded which, and the wiki describes the result as ``a history of changeset
modifications that is orthogonal to the repository history of file
modifications''~\cite{mercurial2026}. Both designs let a developer say ``the
change I was working on yesterday'' after five rebases and be understood, and
both let two people rewrite the same region of history and have the disagreement
recorded rather than resolved by whoever pushed second. \sgt{}'s treatment of two
competing versions of one function is the same construction, and we take
Jujutsu's divergent change and Mercurial's content-divergent changeset as
evidence that recording the disagreement is the right response to it. The scope
is where we part company. The thing given a durable identity is a commit, so it
is exactly as coarse as the commit was, and after a developer squashes a two-hour
agent session into one commit, one change id covers all three requests and
nothing smaller has a name. The same reasoning appears outside version control.
Peritext gives formatting marks in collaborative rich text their own
representation, because a record whose unit is the character gets the boundary of
a bold span wrong when two people edit it at once~\cite{litt2022,kleppmann2019}.
Choosing a unit of record is choosing which questions the record can answer.

\subsection{Recovering a decomposition after the fact}

A commit that serves several purposes at once is a known problem with a measured
cost. Herzig and Zeller examined the histories of five open source Java projects
and found that a substantial share of changes address more than one concern, and
that separating them changes the conclusions of the defect prediction studies
built on those histories~\cite{herzig2013,herzig2016}. A line of tools follows
from that finding. They partition a diff using definition and use relationships
between the changed statements~\cite{barnett2015}, use the fine-grained edit
events an IDE can record~\cite{dias2015}, build a dependency graph across the
versions a commit spans~\cite{partachi2020}, or present a partition to the
developer for correction~\cite{shen2021,tao2015}, and they are evaluated on
whether they reproduce a grouping that a human labelled. Every one of them is
solving a harder problem than \sgt{} solves, because they run after the
information is gone. The developer who typed three sentences into an agent stated
the boundary out loud before any of the code existed, and the only reason it is
absent from the repository is that nothing wrote it down. Our contribution here is
no better inference algorithm. It is the observation that the constraint these
tools were designed around has loosened.

\sgt{} does depend on two results from this literature. Keeping a function's
identity when it is renamed or moved is the problem that refactoring detection
and tree differencing address~\cite{tsantalis2018,falleri2014,fluri2007}, and it
is the weakest link in our implementation, since a rename we fail to detect
appears as one function removed and another added. Grouping edits into features
is a clustering over which functions change together and which call each other,
which is the signal the co-change mining literature
established~\cite{zimmermann2004,ying2004,kim2005,godfrey2005}, resolved with a
community detection algorithm~\cite{traag2019,traag2011}. Both are inferences,
and Section~\ref{sec:design} states what a developer does when they are wrong.

\subsection{Histories the editor keeps}

A second tradition puts the record in the editor and asks nothing of the
developer. Azurite stores a programmer's editing operations at a finer grain than
any commit and lets them undo one past edit while keeping the edits made after
it~\cite{yoon2015,yoon2013}, which is worth building because backtracking is a
routine part of programming and not an exceptional one~\cite{yoon2014}. Variolite
lets a data scientist wrap a region of code as a variant and switch between
variants in place, and Kery et al.\ built it after finding that people doing
exploratory work avoid version control for exactly that
work~\cite{kery2017}. Related systems keep alternative program versions side by
side~\cite{hartmann2008,terry2004}, replay a document's editing
history~\cite{grossman2010}, version at the grain of a single
experiment~\cite{mikami2017}, and help a person clean up a notebook after the
fact~\cite{kery2018,head2019}. \sgt{} shares the central commitment of all of
these, which is that the record is a byproduct of working and the developer is
never asked to prepare it. Where these systems stop is at the boundary of the
machine. The history is in the editor's own store, so a collaborator, a build,
and a code review do not see it, and the unit is an edit event, which means a set
of related edits still has no name a person can use. \sgt{} pays for crossing
that boundary by writing its record into the git repository as files committed
with the code, and Section~\ref{sec:design} describes what that costs when a
colleague who has not installed \sgt{} commits to the same branch.

\subsection{Layers over git built for the way people work now}

The tools developers reach for today accept git's storage and add a layer above
it. GitButler keeps several branches applied to one working directory at once,
draws each as a vertical lane with its own staging area, and lets the developer
drag a change into the lane it belongs to~\cite{gitbutler2026}. Its premise is
one we agree with completely, that a developer should not have to decide which
branch a piece of work belongs to before starting it, because that decision is
easiest once the work exists. The unit assigned to a lane is an individual file
change, so the case it does not cover is the one at the centre of
Figure~\ref{fig:two-records}, where two requests both edited
\sym{api.py::handle} and no assignment of \sym{api.py} to a lane is correct.
Graphite and GitHub's stacked pull requests take the ordered series as their
unit. A stack is a sequence of changes in which each one targets the layer below
it, and the tooling keeps the chain consistent, rebasing and retargeting the
higher layers when a lower one merges and landing every unmerged layer beneath
the topmost ready one in a single
operation~\cite{graphite2026,githubstacked2026}. This is the right answer to a
real problem, which is that a large change is unreviewable and a series of small
ones is reviewable. It also states its own precondition plainly. Graphite's guide
says that developers must understand how to break down their work into small,
incremental changes, and every command it offers operates on a decomposition the
developer has already performed. The agent session is the case where that
decomposition exists in the developer's request history and nowhere in the code.

The closest system to ours is sem, which parses about 32 languages with
tree-sitter and reports which functions, methods and classes a commit changed,
resolving an entity's identity across versions in three passes, by exact
identifier, by a structural hash that ignores whitespace and comments, and by
token overlap above 80\%~\cite{sem2026}. Its commands answer questions about
entities. \cmd{sem impact} lists an entity's dependencies, dependents and tests,
\cmd{sem log} surfaces which entities change most often and which change
together, and \cmd{sem context} assembles a bundle about an entity for a model
within a token budget. The design decision we want to draw attention to is where
sem keeps all of this, in a derived SQLite cache outside the repository, under
the operating system's cache directory. That makes sem safe to adopt and safe to
abandon, gives entity-level answers about a history recorded years before sem
existed, and requires agreement from nobody else on the team. It also fixes what
sem can offer. A record that any teammate's ordinary commit can silently
invalidate cannot be the thing an operation acts on, because there is nowhere to
record the outcome, so every sem command reports and none of them changes state.
A developer learns from \cmd{sem diff} that \sym{get\_cached} changed and then
removes it with a line-level tool. \sgt{} commits its record to the repository in
order to act on it, and the bill for that arrives in two places. A colleague
without \sgt{} installed can merge code and leave the record describing a state
that no longer exists, and a record that operations depend on has to be repaired
when it is wrong. Sections~\ref{sec:design} and~\ref{sec:walkthrough} are largely
about how a developer notices that gap and closes it.

\section{Five Things a Developer Cannot Ask For}
\label{sec:scenarios}

The five scenarios below come from our own use of \sgt{} while building it and
from watching colleagues work with coding agents on repositories we maintain.
Each one is an operation a developer tried to perform, stated in the words they
used, and none of the five is available in git for the same underlying reason.
The thing the developer named is a set of edits identified by the purpose they
served, and the smallest thing the record can name is a line inside a commit
(Figure~\ref{fig:granularity}). Every scenario has a workaround, all the
workarounds work, and what they cost is the argument.

\subsection{``Commit this when it is done, and I do not know yet when that is''}

Three requests went into one sitting, and the third changed code the first had
produced. Committing after each request puts a version of \sym{api.py::handle}
into the permanent record that existed for twenty-nine minutes and that nobody
ever ran the test suite against, and it files the 15:01 rework of the cache under
the retry commit, because that is when it happened. A single commit at the end
holds all three requests and the rename, which is the state
Figure~\ref{fig:two-records} shows. Staging hunk by hunk produces three clean
commits and requires the developer to decide, for each of fifteen hunks, which of
four purposes it serves. Green and Petre named these costs premature commitment,
where a notation forces a decision before the information needed to make it is
available, and viscosity, the resistance a notation puts up when that decision
turns out to be wrong~\cite{green1996,blackwell2003}. Git asks for the
decomposition at the moment of writing. In a session driven by requests the
boundary does exist at that moment, the agent is the only party holding it, and
the developer's cost of recovering it grows with every later request that touches
the same functions.
\emph{The operation.} Record the boundary the developer already stated, without
asking them to state it a second time in a different notation.

\subsection{``Change the rate limiter I built yesterday''}

The rate limiting from 14:02 used a fixed one-minute window, and a week later it
needs a sliding one. The work lands in three of the four functions the original
request produced, and the developer's first question is what the rate limiting
looked like before they touched it. Git answers a version of this question.
\cmd{git log -L :handle:api.py} follows one function through the history by
matching a name pattern, and \cmd{git log -S} finds the commits where a given
string appeared or disappeared. Both take one function or one string at a time,
so the developer runs the first command four times, once per function they
believe was involved, and assembles the four answers themselves. The set has no
name, so nothing checks whether four was the right number. Codoban et al.\ asked
developers why they examine history and found the most common reason to be
understanding the rationale behind a piece of code~\cite{codoban2015}, and LaToza
and Myers found questions about why code is the way it is to be among those
developers report as hardest to answer~\cite{latoza2010}. The rationale in this
case was three sentences of English, typed a week ago into a window that is now
closed.
\emph{The operation.} Name the work one request produced, see its current state
and its previous state, and change it as a unit.

\subsection{``Take the caching back out and leave the rest alone''}

The caching turned out to serve a stale price for up to sixty seconds, and it has
to go. Its six edits are spread over three files and two commits, mixed with
eleven hunks belonging to three other purposes, and one of the six is a parameter
added to \sym{db.py::query} that the rename touched afterwards.
\cmd{git revert} takes back a whole commit, so reverting either of these two
removes work the developer is keeping. The path that works is to check out both
commits, select the six hunks by hand, reverse them, and then confirm that no
function still calls \sym{get\_cached} and that removing the parameter did not
break the two callers the rename had already rewritten. That confirmation is
where the time goes, because the record contains no statement that the
\sym{db.py::query} signature and the \sym{handle} call site were changed for the
same reason. Brindescu et al.\ found that the difficulty of resolving a conflict
is predictable from properties of the change, and that how far the change reaches
is one of the properties that predicts trouble~\cite{brindescu2020}. A
hand-assembled reverse patch across two commits has exactly the shape their model
warns about.
\emph{The operation.} Remove a named set of edits together with everything
recorded as depending on it, and leave every other edit to the same files
untouched.

\subsection{``Send just the export work to the release branch''}

An export bug fix has to ship today, and it was written on a branch that also
carries two unfinished features. \cmd{git cherry-pick} moves a commit, and the
export work is four functions inside three commits that also contain the
unfinished work. The usual answer is a temporary branch and an interactive rebase
that splits those three commits, and the conflict the developer meets during it
is in the one function all three purposes touched. Darcs solves the part of this
problem that is about lines, because a Darcs patch carries the dependencies it
was recorded with and moving it involves no reapplication
(Section~\ref{sec:related}). The dependency that decides this case is that the
export code calls a helper introduced by one of the unfinished features, no
line-level record states that, and the developer finds out when the release
branch fails to import.
\emph{The operation.} Carry a named set of edits and its dependencies to another
branch, and be told before the operation which dependencies would come along.

\subsection{``Let someone review the rate limiter while I keep building on it''}

Reviewers want small, focused changes, which is what code review research has
converged on and the reason stacked pull requests
exist~\cite{bacchelli2013,rigby2013}. The rate limiter was finished at 14:30 and
the caching that followed calls \sym{ratelimit.py::\_bucket}, so the two form a
stack of two layers with the rate limiter underneath. Submitting them that way
required the rate limiter to be on its own branch at 14:30, which required
knowing at 14:30 that the caching would build on it. Graphite and GitHub's
stacked pull requests automate every step after that decision, including
rebasing the upper layer when a reviewer asks for a change to the lower one
(Section~\ref{sec:related}). The decision itself belongs to the developer, it is
made before the work exists, and an agent session is the case where the layering
becomes visible only once both layers are written. Church et al.\ call this a
hidden dependency, a relationship the system relies on that the notation does not
show, and they make the point about version control
specifically~\cite{church2014}.
\emph{The operation.} Discover the layering after the work exists, and submit one
layer while continuing to work on the layer above it.

\subsection{What the five have in common}

Every one of these operations takes a set of edits as its argument, and the set
is identified by the purpose those edits served. Git expresses a set of lines, a
set of files, and a set of commits, and a developer can build all five operations
out of those three by hand. The cost of building them is the cost of recovering a
decomposition that nobody recorded, which the untangling literature has been
measuring for a decade and which used to be affordable for one specific reason.
The person doing the recovery had written the code.
Section~\ref{sec:design} describes what we changed so that the argument these
five operations want is a thing a developer can type.

\section{What \sgt{} Commits To}
\label{sec:design}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \input{figures/fig3-model}
  \Description{\FigThreeDescription}
  \caption{\FigThreeCaption}
  \label{fig:model}
\end{figure*}

\sgt{} makes one decision about what a save writes down, and the other three
commitments in this section are what that decision drags along with it. We state
each one as the developer meets it, with the price attached, because all four
prices arrive in the first hour of use. Figure~\ref{fig:model} shows the first
two at work on the sitting from Figure~\ref{fig:two-records}.

\subsection{One edit to one function, filed under the request}
\label{sec:grain}

A save reads the working files, compares them against the last recorded state,
and writes one record per changed function. Each record names the function, the
version of it the edit started from, the version it produced, and the other
functions the new code refers to. The developer supplies one sentence,
\cmd{sgt save -m "retry the upstream call when it returns a 5xx"}, and \sgt{}
reads everything else out of the files, so a record can be no more wrong than the
code it was read from.

We chose the function as the unit because both neighbouring choices fail on the
same case, and the case is ordinary. The price cache in Figure~\ref{fig:model}
added a parameter to \sym{db.py::query} and passed a matching argument from
\sym{api.py::handle}. Those two changes share no line and no file. A record whose
smallest addressable thing is a line has nowhere to write down that they were
made for one reason, which is why the developer who removes the cache six weeks
later learns about the second one when the import fails. The other direction is a
commit, which holds whatever was pending when the developer typed the command. In
Figure~\ref{fig:two-records} that is three requests and a rename the agent did on
its own initiative, divided across two commits by the clock. A function is the
smallest thing that both the developer and the agent name out loud while the work
is happening, and it is the unit the feature location literature settled on for a
related reason, that a concern is a set of functions and almost never a set of
lines~\cite{biggerstaff1993,dit2013}.

The grain has a price in two directions and the developer meets both. \sgt{}
finds functions in Python, TypeScript, and TSX with tree-sitter~\cite{treesitter}
and records every other file as its whole content, at the grain git already
offers, so a repository whose interesting logic is in Go gets one record per file
and none of the operations below become sharper than the ones it has now. Within
the three parsed languages, a function can be smaller than a purpose. The rename
in Figure~\ref{fig:two-records} moved \sym{db.py::fetch} to \sym{fetch\_row} and
updated four call sites, and \sgt{} writes five records for what the developer
thinks of as one action. Those five records are one named group, so the mismatch
shows up only when a developer reads the edit list underneath the name. A
function can also be larger than a purpose in the way that matters most, which is
two requests changing opposite ends of one fifty line function, and
Section~\ref{sec:fork} is what \sgt{} does then.

\subsection{A version is a set of edits, and the files are rebuilt from it}
\label{sec:sets}

Two rules decide which sets are versions. No edit is included without the edits
it was built on, and each function has one included version. \sgt{} rebuilds each
file by writing out the included version of every function it contains and
keeping the text between functions exactly as it was, which produces the bytes
that are checked out. The middle panel of Figure~\ref{fig:model} is one such set
before and after a revert, and the right panel is the file each set produces.

What this buys is that \cmd{revert}, \cmd{restore}, \cmd{diff}, and \cmd{switch}
all take a set and return a set. Two properties follow that a developer can check
on their own repository. Reverting the price cache and then restoring it produces
a file byte-identical to one nobody ever touched, because both operations are set
arithmetic over the same records and neither reapplies a patch. And every one of
the four can be shown in full before it happens, because working out the
resulting files takes no more than rebuilding them from the proposed set.
\cmd{sgt revert "price cache"} prints the twelve edits that would remain, the
functions whose text would change, the resulting diff, and then
\cmd{not applied — this was the preview}.

The interesting case is the function three requests wrote. \sym{api.py::handle}
in Figure~\ref{fig:model} carries an edit from the rate limiter, one from the
cache, and one from the retry policy, in that order. Removing the cache's edit
under the first rule alone means removing everything recorded above it in that
function, and the retry policy is above it. We shipped that behaviour first. On a
history where features interleave inside a shared function it removed a later
feature in order to remove an earlier one, with a preview that counted edits and
therefore looked reasonable, and we changed the default in August 2026 after it
emptied a test repository we were using for exactly this measurement. The default
now keeps the later edits and subtracts the reverted feature's lines from the
current text of the shared function with a three-way merge, the same operation
git performs when it merges a text file. Three of the twelve remaining edits in
Figure~\ref{fig:model} are spliced this way and they are marked. The old
behaviour is still available as \cmd{revert --take-dependents}, and its help text
says what it removes.

That splice is the one place \sgt{} changes text that no person wrote, so it is
also where we are most careful about what it declines to do. When the subtraction
overlaps a line a later edit changed, \sgt{} leaves the function exactly as it is
and prints \cmd{kept unchanged (the removal overlaps later edits — needs your
edit)} with the function named. When a function \sgt{} is keeping still calls
something the revert removed, it prints \cmd{still references removed code (fix
or revert separately)}. Both of these are reports and neither stops the
operation, which is the stance \sgt{} takes throughout. Running
\cmd{sgt log --summary} in our own repository today prints \cmd{279 file(s) on
disk differ from the recorded state — `sgt save` absorbs them}, and every command
still works while that is true. The honest cost of the default is that after a
splice the shared function is text the developer has not read, and their test
suite is what decides whether the revert was correct. We think that is the right
place for the decision, and printing the diff and the warning is as far as we are
willing to go on the developer's behalf.

\subsection{Two versions of one function, and a person decides}
\label{sec:fork}

When two edits change the same function from the same starting version, \sgt{}
records both, includes neither, and asks the developer. This is the commitment
that costs the most goodwill in the first week, so we want to be precise about
whose behaviour we are departing from and why theirs is right.

Git merges text and knows nothing about what a function is, which is the correct
choice for a system that has to work on every text file in every language anyone
will ever write, and it is why \cmd{git merge} is useful on a Makefile. The
consequence shows up on a function two agent sessions edited. One session added a
cache lookup in the first three lines of \sym{api.py::handle} and the other
wrapped the outbound call at the end of it in a retry, forty lines away, with no
line in common. Git merges the two without comment and produces a function that
consults a cache and then retries, and no test run anywhere covered that function
in that state. \sgt{} sees one function with two versions from one parent, names
it, and stops. \cmd{sgt resolve api.py::handle} drafts a single version, runs the
project's test command against it, and includes it when the command passes. A
developer who disagrees with the test result passes \cmd{--override pass} with a
\cmd{--reason}, and the reason and their name are recorded beside the resolution,
so the next person to read that function finds out why it looks the way it does.

The price is being stopped in cases where the merge would have been fine, and we
know a shape where \sgt{} stops for nothing at all. Deleting a function and adding
it back with byte-identical content in two places produces two versions from one
parent, and \sgt{} treats it as a disagreement. Our position is that the cost of
being asked is bounded and visible at the moment it is paid, and the cost of a
silent textual merge inside one function is a failure that surfaces later
somewhere else. We hold that loosely. A developer who merges thirty branches a
day would reasonably weigh the two the other way, and for them the current design
is worse.

\subsection{The names are inferred, and correcting one moves labels only}
\label{sec:names}

The rails in every figure in this paper carry names, and the names are the part
of \sgt{} that guesses. Functions that changed in the same saves and that refer to
one another are grouped together, using the change coupling signal established by
Zimmermann et al.\ and Ying et al.~\cite{zimmermann2004,ying2004} and a community
detection method over the resulting graph~\cite{traag2019}. A language model then
reads the saves in a group and writes the label. Membership is computed from the
code and the label is written from the words, and those two steps fail in
different ways, so we treat them separately.

We considered asking the developer to confirm the grouping at save time and
decided against it, because that request is commit hygiene in different clothes.
A developer who could reliably answer it could also have staged the hunks. The
design question we care about is what a wrong guess costs, and the answer is that
a correction moves labels and touches no recorded edit.
\cmd{sgt feature rename f-001f73c2 "price cache"} renames a group whose
identifier stays what it was, \cmd{sgt feature regroup} moves functions between
groups, and \cmd{sgt save --as "price cache"} files a new save into a group that
already exists. Because identifiers survive all three, a revert written down in a
code review comment last month still removes the same edits after somebody
renames the group today.

Two failures are worth naming because a reader will hit them. A function that
everything calls, an argument parser or a logging helper, changes in nearly every
save and pulls otherwise unrelated work into one group, and the fix is a regroup
the developer has to notice they need. A save with no message gives the language
model less to read, and \sgt{} says so at the time, printing \cmd{· no words
captured} under the save it just wrote. The label on a group summarises what the
developer said about the work, so a developer who says nothing gets a name derived
from the code alone.

\subsection{What \sgt{} will not do}

\sgt{} writes no code of its own. Every byte in the working files came from the
developer or their agent, apart from the three-way merge splice in
Section~\ref{sec:sets}, which reports every case it cannot perform cleanly. We
have been asked more than once during this work why \sgt{} does not hand the
shared function to a language model and have it redrafted after a revert, and our
answer is that a version control system whose output nobody wrote is a version
control system nobody can audit.

\sgt{} also does not stand between a developer and git. The records are files
under \cmd{.sgt/} committed alongside the code, \cmd{sgt git <args>} passes
through to git untouched, and a colleague who has never installed \sgt{} clones an
ordinary repository with an ordinary history. There is no server and no
background process. Two commands refuse to run, \cmd{switch} when there are
unsaved edits because \sgt{} has nowhere to put them, and \cmd{restore} into a
function that currently has two competing versions, and each of the two prints the
command that clears the way. Everything else \sgt{} finds wrong it reports, and
then it proceeds.

\subsection{The five operations, and what a developer types}

\begin{figure*}[t]
  \centering
  \input{figures/fig4-operations}
  \Description{\FigFourDescription}
  \caption{\FigFourCaption}
  \label{fig:operations}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:operations} lists every operation \sgt{} offers with its cost
beside it. The five operations Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} ended on map onto them
directly. Recording a boundary without declaring it is \cmd{sgt save -m}, run
whenever the developer feels like running it, since the grouping is recovered
afterwards from the code. Changing the work one request produced is
\cmd{sgt show "rate limiting"} for its current state and
\cmd{sgt show "rate limiting"@1} for the state it was in before the most recent
stretch of work on it. Removing a named set is \cmd{sgt revert "price cache"},
which prints its consequences first. Carrying a named set to another branch is
\cmd{sgt propose land --subset "export"}, which declines a subset that omits a
group another chosen group depends on and names the group that is missing.
Discovering the layering is reading the recorded dependencies, since the cache
edits record that they were built on \sym{api.py::\_bucket} and therefore on the
rate limiter, which is the fact the developer needed at 14:30 and did not have.
Section~\ref{sec:walkthrough} runs these in order on one repository.

\section{One Repository, Five Sittings}
\label{sec:walkthrough}

The repository here is a five thousand line Python service that answers price
quotes for a trading dashboard, and the first sitting is the hour
Figure~\ref{fig:two-records} draws. We assembled the sequence from sessions we ran
while building \sgt{} so that one repository contains the five operations
Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} asked for, in that order, followed by the one case
where \sgt{} stops and asks. Every command and every block of output is what
\sgt{} does today. Output lines too wide for this column are wrapped onto a second
line and are otherwise unchanged. What to watch is which decisions the developer
is asked to make, and when.

\subsection{Monday, 14:02 to 15:20: two saves and four names}

Three requests went to the agent in that hour, and the agent renamed a function on
its own initiative. At 14:33, with the rate limiting finished and the price cache
first drafted, the developer saved.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt save -m "rate limiting and a price cache on quotes"\\
\ttok{} save c39ab2f "rate limiting and a price cache on quotes"\\
~~├─ \ttnew{} new feature (4a1c9e02) \ttdash{} unnamed; name it:\\
~~│~~~~sgt feature rename 4a1c9e02 "<label>"\\
~~│~~~~api.py::\_bucket, api.py::\_key, api.py::\_window +1 more\\
~~├─ \ttnew{} new feature (001f73c2) \ttdash{} unnamed; name it: \dots\\
~~│~~~~cache.py::get\_cached, cache.py::\_ttl, db.py::query +1 more\\
~~└─ \ttnew{} new feature (9d20b18a) \ttdash{} unnamed; name it: \dots\\
~~~~~~~db.py::fetch\_row, api.py::export\_row, util.py::load\_row +1 more\\
~~\ttwarn{} one save touched 3 features \ttdash{} deliberate? `sgt log --map'\\
~~~~~shows them; `sgt feature regroup move' re-files work\\
~~\ttundo{} reverse this save:~~sgt undo
\end{out}

\noindent
The developer typed one sentence and \sgt{} wrote twelve records. The three groups
have no names yet, because \sgt{} writes records when the developer saves and works
out names when the developer next reads, and a name costs a language model call
that has no business running while somebody is mid-session. The warning is the one
line here that resembles what git asks for, and it is a statement rather than a
request. The developer read it, agreed the sitting had been mixed, and carried on,
which is the case Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} opened with.

The second save at 15:20 covered the retry policy and the 15:01 rework of the
cache. By then the first save's groups had names, so its echo read
\cmd{● Price Cache (001f73c2)} for the group that already existed and
\cmd{\ttnew{} new feature (7c02b4d1)} for the retry work.
\cmd{sgt log --tree} afterwards printed the four groups the hour produced.

\begin{out}
Rate Limiting (4a1c9e02) \ttdot{} 4 symbol(s)\\
Price Cache (001f73c2) \ttdot{} 4 symbol(s)\\
Retry Policy (7c02b4d1) \ttdot{} 3 symbol(s)\\
Row Accessor Rename (9d20b18a) \ttdot{} 5 symbol(s)
\end{out}

\noindent
Three of the four names are what the developer would have written. The fourth is
the agent's unrequested rename, named from the code because the developer never
said anything about that part of the work, which is the failure
Section~\ref{sec:names} predicts. It is also the only one of the four whose name
nobody needs, so nobody corrected it.

\subsection{Thursday: changing the rate limiter}

The fixed one minute window has to become a sliding one, and the developer starts
from what the rate limiting is now.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt show "Rate Limiting"\\
feature 4a1c9e02~~"Rate Limiting"\\
~~4 edits \ttdot{} 4 symbols in 1 file \ttdot{} last touched 3d ago\\
~~symbols~~~~~~api.py::\_bucket, api.py::\_key, api.py::\_window,\\
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~api.py::handle\\
~~saves~~~~~~~~c39ab2f~~rate limiting and a price cache on quotes\\
~~reverting this removes 11 edits \ttdash{} 7 of them work built on top
\end{out}

\noindent
The four functions are the answer to the question that took four runs of
\cmd{git log -L} in Section~\ref{sec:scenarios}, and nothing here required the
developer to guess that four was the right number. The last line is the one they
did not ask for and read anyway. Seven later edits are recorded as built on this
rate limiting, so a sliding window is a change under other people's work, and the
developer knows that before opening the file.

The new logic goes into \sym{api.py::\_window} and \sym{api.py::\_bucket}.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt save --as "Rate Limiting" -m "sliding window, 60s of buckets"\\
\ttok{} save 1f0aee3 "sliding window, 60s of buckets"\\
~~└─ ● Rate Limiting (4a1c9e02)~~api.py::\_bucket, api.py::\_window\\
~~\ttok{} named "Rate Limiting"
\end{out}

\noindent
\cmd{--as} is the one place a developer states a grouping by hand, and it changed
nothing here, because both functions were already in that group and the edits would
have been filed there without it. They typed it because they knew the answer and
had no reason to let \sgt{} work it out. The rate limiting now has two stretches of
work on it, and \cmd{sgt log --focus 4a1c9e02} names both.

\begin{out}
● Rate Limiting~~4a1c9e02~~\ttdot{}~~2 checkpoint(s)\\[0.35ex]
~~~[0\ttfull\ttfull\ttfull]~~4a1c9e02@0~~:rate-limiting~~Rate Limiting\\
~~~(1\ttfull\ttfull\ttempty)~~4a1c9e02@1~~:sliding-window~~Sliding Window\\[0.35ex]
~operate:~~sgt revert 4a1c9e02:sliding-window~~(one checkpoint, by\\
~~~~name)~~\ttdot{}~~sgt revert 4a1c9e02~~(whole feature)
\end{out}

\noindent
Nobody asked for these two stretches. \sgt{} cut them where the developer's words
changed, which in this repository is where one request ended and the next began,
and \cmd{sgt show "Rate Limiting@0"} is now the state before Thursday. The last two
lines exist because we watched people in our own team learn that a thing had a
name and then stop, having no idea which command took it.

\subsection{The following Monday: taking the cache out}

The cache serves a stale price for up to sixty seconds and has to go.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt revert "Price Cache"\\
~~~~[the log region redrawn, with the 6 removed edits marked]\\
~~subtracted from shared code (later work kept): api.py::handle,\\
~~~~~util.py::load\_row, util.py::save\_row\\
~~removed going forward: cache.py::get\_cached, cache.py::\_ttl\\
~~\ttwarn{} still references removed code (fix or revert separately):\\
~~~~~api.py::export\_row\\[0.35ex]
apply this revert? [y/N]
\end{out}

\noindent
Three of these lines carry the argument of this paper. The cache contributed lines
to three functions that later work also edited, and those three keep their later
work and lose the cache's contribution, so removing a two week old feature does not
remove a change made yesterday. Two functions existed only for the cache and go
away with it, which empties \sym{cache.py} and removes the file. One function the
developer is keeping still calls \sym{get\_cached}, and \sgt{} names it and
proceeds, because whether the repair is deleting that call or reverting the export
work as well is not a question about the recorded edits.

The developer answered \cmd{y} and ran the test suite. \sym{util.py::load\_row} was
correct after the subtraction and \sym{api.py::export\_row} was not, which is what
the warning said, and the repair was four lines. Then they checked the property we
think is the strongest practical argument for keeping all of this as set
arithmetic.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt restore "Price Cache"\\
~~\ttok{} restore applied \ttdash{} 0 edit(s) removed, 6 added.\\
~~~~(`sgt undo' reverses this.)
\end{out}

\noindent
Putting the cache back produced the same bytes that were in the files before the
revert, and it kept the four line repair the developer had made in between, because
both directions are set arithmetic over the same records and neither one reapplies
a patch. They then reverted it again, which is what they had wanted, and the
second run printed the same three lines as the first.

\subsection{Wednesday: shipping the export fix alone}

The export bug fix has to ship today, and the branch it sits on also carries two
unfinished features. The developer proposes the branch and lands one group out of
it.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt propose create --base release\\
\ttok{} proposal 3f9a2c81b04d~~4 feature(s) in \textnormal{$\Delta$}\\
\$ sgt propose land 3f9a2c81b04d --subset "CSV Export"\\
\textnormal{$\times$} 'CSV Export' requires Rate Limiting -- include it in\\
~~--subset too
\end{out}

\noindent
That refusal is the fifth operation from Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} arriving
without being asked for. The export code calls \sym{api.py::\_bucket}, which the
rate limiting introduced, and the record of that call was written at the moment the
export code was saved. Git would have taken the cherry-pick and the release branch
would have failed to import. Nobody decided on the Monday that the export work
would depend on the rate limiter, and nobody had to.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt propose land 3f9a2c81b04d --subset "Rate Limiting" "CSV Export"\\
\ttok{} propose land release: 8b21c0d4e7fa (+9 op(s))
\end{out}

\noindent
Two layers went to the release branch in the order the records put them in, and the
two unfinished features stayed behind. This is the stack from
Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} without the branch that had to exist before the work
did.

\subsection{Thursday: two versions of one function}

The colleague on this repository had also been editing \sym{api.py::handle}, adding
a request identifier to every outbound log line. The developer syncs.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt sync\\
\ttwarn{} sync origin/main: merged 4f2a1c8b93de\\
~~~~+7 op(s)\\
~~~~\ttwarn{} 1 OPEN FORK(S) \ttdash{} forked symbol(s) sit at the common\\
~~~~~~ancestor until resolved:\\
~~~~~~api.py::handle: sgt merge-op 3c91ab02 8ee14d77
\end{out}

\noindent
The last line names the low-level command rather than the one a person should run,
which is a wart we have not cleaned up; \cmd{sgt log} prints
\cmd{api.py::handle \ttarrow{} sgt resolve api.py::handle} in the same situation.
The colleague's edit is inside the logging block at the end of the function, the
developer's is at the top where the rate limit check runs, and no line is common
to both. Git merges these two. \sgt{} prints them beside each other and asks.

\begin{out}
\ttrule{} fork on api.py::handle \ttrule{}~~(\ttleft{} left = tip A~~\ttright{} right = tip B)\\
~~~~[the two versions of the function, side by side]\\
pick [l]eft / [r]ight / [e]dit / [q]uit:
\end{out}

\noindent
The developer picked \cmd{e}, merged the two by hand in about thirty seconds, and
\sgt{} ran the project's test command before including the result. We are not going
to claim the automatic merge would have been wrong. It would most likely have been
right, and \sgt{} charged thirty seconds and one interruption to establish that.
The case we designed for is the one where it is wrong, where one edit adds an early
return and the other edit's code sits below it, and the test run that would have
caught it happens on a branch nobody has pushed. A developer who merges often and
reads carefully is paying us for a certainty they already had.

\subsection{What this cost}

Across five sittings and one fork the developer made three decisions \sgt{} could
not make for them. They decided the export fix should ship without the cache, they
decided how the two versions of \sym{api.py::handle} should read, and they decided
that \sym{api.py::export\_row} needed a four line repair once the cache was gone.
All three are decisions about the code, which is where we wanted them.

They paid in three places. One group carries a name derived from the code, because
nobody said anything about that part of the work. The revert left a shared function
whose current text nobody had read, and the test suite was the thing that decided
the revert had worked. The fork stopped them on a merge that was probably fine.
The second and third are direct consequences of Section~\ref{sec:sets} and
Section~\ref{sec:fork}, and on this repository we would choose both again. On a
repository where twenty people edit the same functions each day, the fork rule is
the first thing we would expect to have to change.

\cmd{\ttnew{} new feature (7c02b4d1)} for the retry work.
\cmd{sgt log --tree} afterwards printed the four groups the hour produced.

\begin{out}
Rate Limiting (4a1c9e02) \ttdot{} 4 symbol(s)\\
Price Cache (001f73c2) \ttdot{} 4 symbol(s)\\
Retry Policy (7c02b4d1) \ttdot{} 3 symbol(s)\\
Row Accessor Rename (9d20b18a) \ttdot{} 5 symbol(s)
\end{out}

\noindent
Three of the four names are what the developer would have written. The fourth is
the agent's unrequested rename, named from the code because the developer never
said anything about that part of the work, which is the failure
Section~\ref{sec:names} predicts. It is also the only one of the four whose name
nobody needs, so nobody corrected it.

\subsection{Thursday: changing the rate limiter}

The fixed one minute window has to become a sliding one, and the developer starts
from what the rate limiting is now.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt show "Rate Limiting"\\
feature 4a1c9e02~~"Rate Limiting"\\
~~4 edits \ttdot{} 4 symbols in 1 file \ttdot{} last touched 3d ago\\
~~symbols~~~~~~api.py::\_bucket, api.py::\_key, api.py::\_window,\\
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~api.py::handle\\
~~saves~~~~~~~~c39ab2f~~rate limiting and a price cache on quotes\\
~~reverting this removes 11 edits \ttdash{} 7 of them work built on top
\end{out}

\noindent
The four functions are the answer to the question that took four runs of
\cmd{git log -L} in Section~\ref{sec:scenarios}, and nothing here required the
developer to guess that four was the right number of places to look. The last line
is the one they did not ask for and read anyway. Seven later edits are recorded as
built on this rate limiting, so a sliding window is a change underneath other
people's work, and the developer knows that before opening the file.

The new logic goes into \sym{api.py::\_window} and \sym{api.py::\_bucket}.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt save --as "Rate Limiting" -m "sliding window, 60s of buckets"\\
\ttok{} save 1f0aee3 "sliding window, 60s of buckets"\\
~~\ttlast{}\ttdisc{} Rate Limiting (4a1c9e02)~~api.py::\_bucket, api.py::\_window\\
~~\ttok{} named "Rate Limiting"
\end{out}

\noindent
\cmd{--as} is the one place a developer states a grouping by hand, and it changed
nothing here, because both functions were already in that group and the edits would
have been filed there without it. They typed it because they knew the answer and
had no reason to let \sgt{} work it out. The rate limiting now has two stretches of
work on it, and \cmd{sgt log --focus 4a1c9e02} names both.

\begin{out}
\ttdisc{} Rate Limiting~~4a1c9e02~~\ttdot{}~~2 checkpoint(s)\\[0.35ex]
~~~[0\ttfull\ttfull\ttfull]~~4a1c9e02@0~~:rate-limiting~~Rate Limiting\\
~~~(1\ttfull\ttfull\ttempty)~~4a1c9e02@1~~:sliding-window~~Sliding Window\\[0.35ex]
~operate:~~sgt revert 4a1c9e02:sliding-window~~(one checkpoint, by\\
~~~~name)~~\ttdot{}~~sgt revert 4a1c9e02~~(whole feature)
\end{out}

\noindent
Nobody asked for these two stretches. \sgt{} cut them where the developer's words
changed, which in this repository is where one request ended and the next began,
and either half is now addressable on its own:
\cmd{sgt revert "Rate Limiting:sliding-window"} takes Thursday's work off and
leaves Monday's four edits in place. The last two lines exist because we watched
people in our own team learn that a thing had a name and then stop, having no idea
which command took it.

\subsection{The following Monday: taking the cache out}

The cache serves a stale price for up to sixty seconds and has to go.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt revert "Price Cache"\\
~~~~[the log region redrawn, with the 6 removed edits marked]\\
~~subtracted from shared code (later work kept): api.py::handle,\\
~~~~~util.py::load\_row, util.py::save\_row\\
~~removed going forward: cache.py::get\_cached, cache.py::\_ttl\\
~~\ttwarn{} still references removed code (fix or revert separately):\\
~~~~~api.py::export\_row\\[0.35ex]
apply this revert? [y/N]
\end{out}

\noindent
Three of these lines carry the argument of this paper. The cache contributed lines
to three functions that later work also edited, and those three keep their later
work and lose the cache's contribution, so removing a two week old feature does not
remove a change made yesterday. Two functions existed only for the cache and go
away with it, which empties \sym{cache.py} and removes the file. One function the
developer is keeping still calls \sym{get\_cached}, and \sgt{} names it and
proceeds, because whether the repair is deleting that call or reverting the export
work as well is not a question about the recorded edits.

The developer answered \cmd{y} and ran the test suite. \sym{util.py::load\_row} was
correct after the subtraction and \sym{api.py::export\_row} was not, which is what
the warning said, and the repair was four lines. Then they checked the property we
think is the strongest practical argument for keeping all of this as set
arithmetic.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt restore "Price Cache"\\
~~\ttok{} restore applied \ttdash{} 0 edit(s) removed, 6 added.\\
~~~~(`sgt undo' reverses this.)
\end{out}

\noindent
Putting the cache back produced the same bytes that were in the files before the
revert, and it kept the four line repair the developer had made in between, because
both directions are set arithmetic over the same records and neither one reapplies
a patch. They then reverted it a second time, which is what they had wanted, and
that run printed the same three consequence lines as the first.

\subsection{Wednesday: shipping the export fix alone}

A bulk export endpoint has to ship to the release branch today, and the branch it
sits on also carries the retry policy, which is half finished. The export code goes
into a new \sym{export.py} and applies the rate limit before streaming, so
\sym{export.py::write\_csv} calls \sym{api.py::\_bucket}. Nobody thought about that
call as a dependency while writing it.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt propose create --base release\\
\ttok{} proposal 3f9a2c81b04d (base release, +17 op(s), 4 feature(s))\\
\$ sgt propose land 3f9a2c81b04d --subset "Quote Export"\\
\textnormal{$\times$} 'Quote Export' requires Rate Limiting -- include it in\\
~~--subset too
\end{out}

\noindent
That refusal is the fifth operation from Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} arriving
without being asked for. The record of the call to \sym{api.py::\_bucket} was
written at the moment the export code was saved, and \sgt{} reads it now to answer
a question nobody was thinking about then. Git would have taken the cherry-pick and
the release branch would have failed to import.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt propose land 3f9a2c81b04d --subset "Rate Limiting" "Quote Export"\\
\ttok{} propose land release: 8b21c0d4e7fa (+8 op(s))
\end{out}

\noindent
Two groups went to the release branch in the order the records put them in, and the
half finished retry policy and the accessor rename stayed behind. This is the stack
from Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} without the branch that had to exist before the
work did.

\subsection{Thursday: two versions of one function}

The colleague on this repository had also been editing \sym{api.py::handle}, adding
a request identifier to every outbound log line. The developer syncs.

\begin{out}
\$ sgt sync\\
\ttwarn{} sync origin/main: merged 4f2a1c8b93de\\
~~~~+7 op(s)\\
~~~~\ttwarn{} 1 OPEN FORK(S) \ttdash{} forked symbol(s) sit at the common\\
~~~~~~ancestor until resolved:\\
~~~~~~api.py::handle: sgt merge-op 3c91ab02 8ee14d77
\end{out}

\noindent
The last line names the low-level command rather than the one a person should run,
and \cmd{sgt log} in the same state prints
\cmd{api.py::handle \ttarrow{} sgt resolve api.py::handle}. Two commands disagreeing
about which one the developer should type is a wart we have not cleaned up. The
colleague's edit is inside the logging block at the end of the function, the
developer's is at the top where the rate limit check runs, and no line is common to
both. Git merges these two without comment. \sgt{} prints them beside each other
and asks.

\begin{out}
\ttrule{} fork on api.py::handle \ttrule{}~~(\ttleft{} left = tip A~~\ttright{} right = tip B)\\
~~~~[the two versions of the function, side by side]\\
pick [l]eft / [r]ight / [e]dit / [q]uit:
\end{out}

\noindent
The developer picked \cmd{e}, merged the two by hand in about thirty seconds, and
\sgt{} ran the project's test command before including the result. We are not going
to claim the textual merge would have been wrong here. It would most likely have
been right, and \sgt{} charged thirty seconds and one interruption to establish
that. The case we designed for is the one where the merge is wrong, where one edit
adds an early return and the other edit's new code sits below it, and the test run
that would have caught it happens on a branch nobody has pushed yet. A developer
who merges often and reads carefully is paying us for a certainty they already had.

\subsection{What this cost}

Across five sittings and one fork the developer made three decisions \sgt{} could
not make for them. They decided the export endpoint should ship without the retry
policy, they decided how the two versions of \sym{api.py::handle} should read, and
they decided that \sym{api.py::export\_row} needed a four line repair once the cache
was gone. All three are decisions about the code, which is where we wanted them.

They paid in three places. One group of five edits carries a name derived from the
code, because nobody said anything about that part of the work. The revert left
three shared functions whose current text nobody had read, and the test suite was
the thing that decided the revert had worked. The fork stopped them on a merge that
was probably fine. The second and third of those are direct consequences of
Section~\ref{sec:sets} and Section~\ref{sec:fork}, and on a repository this size we
would choose both again. On a repository where twenty people edit the same
functions each day, the fork rule is the first thing we would expect to have to
change.

\section{Where the Design Breaks}
\label{sec:discussion}

Every number in this section comes from running \sgt{} on the repository that
contains \sgt{}, today, with the command a user would run. We have been the
heaviest users of this system for eight months, and the six things below are what
we would want to know before adopting it.

\subsection{Most of a repository is not functions}

\cmd{sgt log --summary} prints \cmd{371 file(s), 6781 symbol(s), 154 feature(s),
27\% entity coverage}. That last figure is the fraction of recorded files with any
function-level record at all, so roughly three quarters of this repository is
recorded as whole files, at the grain git already offers. The files in that three
quarters are Markdown, JSON, HTML, and lock files. Every operation in
Section~\ref{sec:design} runs on them and none of them gets sharper than
\cmd{git revert} would be.

Adding languages does not fix this, and we want to be clear about which part of it
they do fix. A tree-sitter grammar plus a decision about which node kinds count as
a function is a day of work per language, and we would take Go and Rust that way
tomorrow. The case that remains after that is a repository whose interesting change
is four lines of a deployment configuration, where the thing a developer names has
no function to be filed under, and git's grain is the correct grain for it. We say
this plainly because calling the design language-independent would be false, and a
reader deciding whether to adopt \sgt{} should start by counting how much of their
repository is code.

\subsection{Where a function loses its history}

Section~\ref{sec:grain} claims a record survives a rename, and that claim rests on
a matcher with a threshold in it. \sgt{} links a function across a commit first by
its name, then by identical bytes, then by identical structure with formatting and
comments ignored, and last by token overlap above 0.80, with a guard that rejects
any pair whose token counts differ by more than a factor of two. The 0.80 comes
from sem, which uses the same figure for the same job~\cite{sem2026}. A rename that
also rewrites about a fifth of the function falls below it and is recorded as one
function removed and a different function added.

What the developer sees then is a function whose recorded history begins at that
commit, with its earlier edits still filed under a group the function is no longer
part of. The case that produces it is an agent asked to clean up a module, which
renames six functions and rewrites their bodies in one sitting. Origin analysis is
a well studied problem, and the accurate detectors work from a full syntax tree
comparison~\cite{godfrey2005,kim2005,falleri2014,tsantalis2018}. \sgt{} uses the
token count because it runs on every save and has to finish while the developer is
waiting. Lowering the threshold would link functions that merely resemble each
other, and a wrong link is the worse failure, because it files one function's edits
under another function's name and gives the developer no reason to doubt the
answer. \cmd{sgt identity join} states a link by hand, and it requires the
developer to notice that a history restarted, which is one of the things they were
using \sgt{} in order to stop having to notice.

\subsection{Fifty-six files the record cannot rebuild}

The same command reports 56 files whose bytes on disk no valid set of records can
produce. \sgt{} keeps every one of them, prints the count, names the first five,
and points at \cmd{sgt advanced fsck --tree}. Nothing was deleted and nothing was
quietly wrong, which is the stance in Section~\ref{sec:sets} doing its job. What
the developer loses is the record for those files. A revert of a group that touched
one of them leaves the file as it is, and \cmd{sgt show} on a function inside it
answers from an incomplete chain.

We have not tracked down what put all 56 in that state. This repository has been
mined by five successive versions of our miner, and some of these files are the
residue of our own format changes. A developer adopting \sgt{} on a repository with
two years of history should expect a number of this kind on the first run, and
should read it as work the design has not finished.

\subsection{The gate we lean on is switched off here}

Section~\ref{sec:fork} says a resolved fork has to pass the project's test command
before \sgt{} will include it. The summary above also prints
\cmd{oracle: unconfigured}. In the repository we use every day, resolving a fork
means the developer picks a version and \sgt{} takes their word for it, because
nobody ever pointed \sgt{} at our test runner.

This is the most uncomfortable line in this section, and we have kept it here
because it says something general. A safety property a developer has to configure is
a safety property most repositories will not have, so the set of repositories where
our strongest claim about forks holds is the set where somebody did the setup, and
on the evidence of our own it is smaller than we assumed. The fix needs no
research. \sgt{} should find the test command the project already uses and offer it
during \cmd{sgt init}, and making the developer ask for it was the wrong default.

\subsection{Who should turn the fork rule off}

We designed the fork rule for a repository with three contributors, where a merge
nobody reviewed turns into a bug three days later and the person who finds it is
the person who wrote both sides of it. On a repository where twenty people edit the
same functions every day, the same rule produces a queue of decisions nobody has
time to work through, and the honest prediction is that they would switch it off and
take the textual merge. We also know one shape where \sgt{} asks about nothing at
all. Deleting a function and adding it back with byte-identical content on two
branches produces two versions from one parent, and \sgt{} reports a disagreement
that does not exist.

The setting we would build merges when the two edits changed no overlapping lines
and asks when they did, which is git's rule applied at the grain of a function.
Guimarães and Silva argue for telling a developer about a divergence while both
sides are still being written~\cite{guimaraes2012}, and that setting would let
\sgt{} do it without stopping anybody. We have not built it, because we cannot yet
tell a reader which of the two should be the default. Our answer comes from
repositories with three contributors and a shared understanding of the code, and it
is the part of this design that a study of larger teams would most usefully
overturn.

\subsection{The record the agent already had}

The grouping \sgt{} recovers by clustering existed before any of the code did. The
agent held it while it worked, and every agent we have used discards it when the
session ends. A record written by the agent, one entry per request naming the
functions it changed, would make the inference in Section~\ref{sec:names}
unnecessary, and it would fix the case in Section~\ref{sec:walkthrough} where a
rename nobody asked for got a name derived from the code.

We did not build that, and the reason is a commitment about what \sgt{} is allowed
to depend on. Reading the working files works with any agent, any editor, and a
developer typing by hand, and it keeps working when a vendor changes an output
format. A record the agent writes works while that agent is the one being used, and
a developer who switched agents mid-project would find their history split into a
part with stated groupings and a part with inferred ones. We would take both
sources, with the files as the one \sgt{} trusts and the agent's account as a hint
that improves a label. Which of the two should be authoritative is the design
question we would put to a reader of this paper first.

\section{Introduction}

A developer working with a coding agent describes the change they want in a
sentence or two of English, and the agent writes the code. When a developer on
one of our projects asked for a price lookup to be cached because it had become
slow, the agent added a cache module, gave the database query a parameter for how
long a cached price stays good, changed the request handler to consult the cache
before the database, and chose the names of the three new functions. Over the
following hour that developer made two more requests, and while carrying out the
third the agent revised two of the functions it had written for the second.
Barke et al.\ describe programmers in this mode reading what comes back for the
shape they expected rather than line by line~\cite{barke2023}, and among 410
developers surveyed by Liang et al., understanding and trusting generated code
was one of the most frequently reported difficulties~\cite{liang2024}. The three
sentences the developer typed stayed in the chat window, and what entered the
repository was eighteen changes to fourteen functions in five files.

A week later the developer wants the caching gone, and to ask for that they have
to state it in the terms their version control system understands, all of which
are lines and commits. Git records a version as a snapshot of the whole working
tree~\cite{git2026}, Darcs and Pijul record it as a patch that adds and removes
lines in a stated context~\cite{roundy2009,pijul2024}, and under either design
the smallest thing a history can name is a line in a file. \cmd{git revert} takes
back one commit, \cmd{git cherry-pick} moves one commit, and a branch points at
one commit. The caching the developer asked for is six changes to four functions
in three files, spread across the two commits that hour produced, and neither
commit holds only those six. Herzig and Zeller found changes serving several
unrelated purposes throughout the histories of five open source Java
projects~\cite{herzig2013,hattori2008}, and a decade of work on separating such
changes after the fact follows from that
observation~\cite{barnett2015,tao2015,dias2015,partachi2020,shen2021}.

Separating them by hand means deciding, for each of the fifteen hunks in those
two commits, whether it belongs to the caching, to the rate limiting the
developer asked for half an hour before the caching, to the retry policy they
asked for half an hour after it, or to a rename the agent performed without being
asked. Six of the fifteen turn out to be the caching, and the developer then
splits both commits so those six stand alone, reverses them, and checks that no
function they kept calls a function they just deleted. Recovering which functions
implement a named concern is what Biggerstaff et al.\ called the concept
assignment problem~\cite{biggerstaff1993}, and the feature location literature
exists because reading code to answer it is expensive~\cite{dit2013}. Xia et al.\
instrumented professional developers and found that roughly 58\% of their working
time went to understanding code~\cite{xia2018}.

For as long as developers wrote the lines themselves this work was cheap, because
the person doing it remembered writing the code, so the history only had to
remind them of a decomposition they already held in their
head~\cite{ko2006,sillito2008}. An agent leaves the developer nothing to
remember. What the developer does hold is the sentence they typed, which stated
the boundary of the change exactly, in their own words, before any of the code
existed, and which no version control system records. What a developer decides
and what their repository records are no longer the same size.

The answer a careful maintainer will give to all of this is discipline at commit
time. Commit small, commit often, stage hunk by hunk with \cmd{git add -p}, and
each request ends up with a commit of its own. We have asked contributors on our
own projects for exactly this and have held ourselves to it, and it works. It
asks the developer for one thing, which is to know at the moment of committing
which lines serve which purpose, and an agent session is the case where the
developer does not know. When fourteen changed functions come back and the
developer's own contribution was three sentences of English, staging hunk by hunk
means reading the whole diff to reconstruct a boundary the agent held and never
wrote down. Thimbleby argued that a system should let a person defer a decision
until they hold the information the decision needs~\cite{thimbleby1988}. Commit
hygiene asks for the decision first, and that was affordable for twenty years
because the person deciding had just typed the lines.

We present \sgt{}, a version control system that records a change as one edit to
one function and files each edit under the request it was made for. The developer
keeps the editor and the agent they already use, and \sgt{} reads what those two
leave in the files, so nothing about how the developer works has to change. A
save turns the pending changes into one record per changed function, and each
record names the function it changed, the version it started from, the version it
produced, and the other functions it was built on. \sgt{} writes those records
into the repository and commits them with the code, so a colleague who has not
installed \sgt{} pulls an ordinary git history.
Figure~\ref{fig:two-records} shows the hour described above under both records.

Recording at that grain turns the operations the developer already wanted into
things they can type. \cmd{sgt revert "price cache"} removes the six edits filed
under the price cache and names every function where later work had built on
them, and the rate limiting in the same file is byte for byte what it was.
\cmd{sgt show cache.py::get\_cached} reports which request that function came
from, which save reworked it, and how many edits would come out along with it.
When the developer decides a week later that the cache was needed after all,
\cmd{sgt restore} puts the same six edits back, and a database index a colleague
added in the meantime is still there, because it was never in the set that came
out. None of these commands asks the developer to look at a hunk.

Three consequences of this design cost the developer something, and we would
rather state them here than in a limitations section at the end. Two edits to the
same function made from the same starting point are recorded as two competing
versions and a person has to decide which one survives, including the case of two
edits at opposite ends of a fifty line function that touch no common line and
that git would merge without comment. The grouping of edits into named requests
is inferred from which functions change together and which call each other, so it
is a guess and it will sometimes be wrong, and the property we designed for is
the cost of correcting it, which is a rename, a merge, or a split that moves
labels and leaves every recorded edit alone. \sgt{} reads Python, TypeScript, and
TSX with tree-sitter~\cite{treesitter} and versions every other file whole, at
the grain git already uses, so a repository whose interesting logic is written in
Go gets nothing from \sgt{} today.

This paper contributes the following. We characterise the mismatch between the
unit a developer using an agent decides in and the unit a version control system
records, one attempted operation at a time
(Section~\ref{sec:scenarios}), following the style of conceptual analysis Pérez
De Rosso and Jackson applied to git
itself~\cite{perezderosso2013,perezderosso2016}. We describe \sgt{}'s design as
four commitments and say what each one buys and what it costs

\begin{abstract}
A developer asks a coding agent for three things in one hour, and fourteen
functions in five files come back changed. The developer stated each request as
one thing they wanted, and the two commits that arrive hold all three requests
interleaved with a rename the agent made on its own initiative. Git addresses a
history by lines and by commits, so a developer who wants one of those three
requests out of it has to name the lines that request produced, and after an
agent wrote the code the developer cannot name them. The unit of record and the
unit of thought have come apart.

We present \sgt{}, a version control system that records a change as one edit to
one function, files each edit under the request it was made for, and keeps the
whole record inside an ordinary git repository. A developer names a request to
remove it, put it back, compare two attempts at it, or carry it to another
branch, and the code that other requests contributed to the same files stays
where it is. Every byte of code in the working files came from the developer or
their agent, and \sgt{} reads that code rather than writing any of it.

The design costs the developer three things and we state them at the front. Two
edits to the same function from the same starting point are recorded as
competing versions that a person decides between, including the pair at opposite
ends of a fifty line function that git would have merged without comment. The
grouping of edits into named features is inferred from which functions change
together, so a person corrects it. Code in a language \sgt{} does not parse is
versioned whole, at the grain git already uses.
\end{abstract}
