\section{Introduction}

When a developer works through a coding agent, the change they want and the code
that implements it become two separate descriptions, and the developer authors
only the first one. A developer on one of our projects asked for a price lookup to
be cached because it had become slow, and the agent added a cache module, gave the
database query a parameter for how long a cached price stays good, changed the
request handler to consult the cache before the database, and chose the names of
the three new functions. Over the following hour that developer made two more
requests, and while carrying out the third the agent revised two of the functions
it had written for the second. Barke et al.\ describe programmers in this mode
reading what comes back for the shape they expected rather than line by
line~\cite{barke2023}, and among 410 developers surveyed by Liang et al.,
understanding and trusting generated code was one of the most frequently reported
difficulties~\cite{liang2024}. The three sentences the developer typed stayed in
the chat window, and what entered the repository was eighteen changes to fourteen
functions in five files.

A week later that developer wants the caching gone, and the request has to be
restated in whatever terms their version control system understands. Those terms
are lines and commits, in every system in wide use. Git records a version as a
snapshot of the whole working tree~\cite{git2026}, Darcs and Pijul record it as a
patch that adds and removes lines in a stated context~\cite{roundy2009,pijul2024},
and under either design the smallest thing a history can name is a line in a file,
so \cmd{git revert} takes back one commit, \cmd{git cherry-pick} moves one commit,
and a branch points at one commit. The caching is six changes to four functions in
three files, spread across the two commits that hour produced, and neither commit
holds only those six. Commits that carry work for more than one purpose are
ordinary. Herzig and Zeller found them throughout the histories of five open
source Java projects~\cite{herzig2013,hattori2008}, and the tools built since to
separate them are scored on whether they recover a grouping a person supplied by
hand~\cite{barnett2015,tao2015,dias2015,partachi2020,shen2021}.

Separating the caching out by hand means deciding, for each of the fifteen hunks
in those two commits, whether it belongs to the caching, to the rate limiting the
developer asked for half an hour before the caching, to the retry policy they
asked for half an hour after it, or to a rename the agent performed without being
asked. Six of the fifteen turn out to be the caching, and the developer then
splits both commits so those six stand alone, reverses them, and checks that no
function they kept calls a function they just deleted. Biggerstaff et al.\ called
the task of recovering which functions implement a named concern the concept
assignment problem~\cite{biggerstaff1993}, and the feature location literature
that followed measures how much of a program a developer has to read before they
can answer one such question~\cite{dit2013}. Xia et al.\ instrumented professional
developers and found that roughly 58\% of their working time went to understanding
code~\cite{xia2018}.

For as long as developers wrote the lines themselves this recovery was cheap. The
person doing it remembered writing the code, so the history had only to remind
them of a decomposition they already held~\cite{ko2006,sillito2008}. An agent
leaves nothing to remember. The developer holds instead the sentence they typed,
which stated the boundary of the change exactly, in their own words, before any of
the code existed, and which no version control system records. The unit a
developer decides in and the unit their repository records have come apart.

A careful maintainer will answer all of this with commit hygiene: commit small,
commit often, stage hunk by hunk with \cmd{git add -p}, and each request ends up
with a commit of its own. We have asked contributors on our own projects for
exactly this and have held ourselves to it, and it works whenever the developer
knows at the moment of committing which lines serve which purpose. An agent
session is the case where they do not. When fourteen changed functions come back
and the developer's own contribution was three sentences of English, staging hunk
by hunk means reading the whole diff to reconstruct a boundary the agent held and
never wrote down. Thimbleby argued that a notation should let a person defer a
decision until they hold the information the decision
needs~\cite{thimbleby1988}, and commit hygiene asks for the decision first, which
stayed affordable for twenty years because the person deciding had just typed the
lines.

We present \sgt{}, a version control system that records a change as one edit to
one function and files each edit under the request it was made for. The developer
keeps the editor and the agent they already use, and \sgt{} reads what those two
leave in the files, so nothing about how the developer works has to change. A
save turns the pending changes into one record per changed function, and each
record names the function it changed, the version it started from, the version it
produced, and the other functions it was built on. \sgt{} writes those records
into the repository and commits them with the code, so a colleague who has not
installed \sgt{} pulls an ordinary git history.
Figure~\ref{fig:two-records} shows the hour described above under both records.

Recording at that grain gives each of the operations the developer already wanted
a command whose argument is a name. \cmd{sgt revert "price cache"} removes the six
edits filed under the price cache and names every function where later work had
built on them, and the rate limiting in the same file is byte for byte what it
was. \cmd{sgt show cache.py::get\_cached} reports which request that function came
from, which save reworked it, and how many edits would come out along with it.
When the developer decides a week later that the cache was needed after all,
\cmd{sgt restore} puts the same six edits back, and a database index a colleague
added in the meantime is still there, because it was never in the set that came
out. None of these commands asks the developer to look at a hunk.

This design costs the developer three things, and we would
state them here rather than in a limitations section at the end. Two edits to the
same function made from the same starting point are recorded as two competing
versions and a person has to decide which one survives, including the case of two
edits at opposite ends of a fifty line function that touch no common line and
that git would merge without comment. The grouping of edits into named requests
is inferred from which functions change together and which call each other, so it
is a guess and it will sometimes be wrong, and correcting it costs the developer a
rename, a merge, or a split, all three of which move labels and leave every
recorded edit alone. \sgt{} reads Python, TypeScript, and
TSX with tree-sitter~\cite{treesitter} and versions every other file whole, at
the grain git already uses, so a repository whose interesting logic is written in
Go gets nothing from \sgt{} today.

This paper makes four contributions. We characterise the mismatch between the
unit a developer using an agent decides in and the unit a version control system
records, one attempted operation at a time
(Section~\ref{sec:scenarios}), following the style of conceptual analysis Pérez
De Rosso and Jackson applied to git
itself~\cite{perezderosso2013,perezderosso2016}. We describe \sgt{}'s design as
four commitments and say what each one buys and what it costs
(Section~\ref{sec:design}). We run the whole set of operations on one repository
and give the reasoning behind each command (Section~\ref{sec:walkthrough}). We
report what we have learned from \sgt{} tracking its own development, and where
the design breaks down (Sections~\ref{sec:study} and~\ref{sec:discussion}).

\section{What Would Show This Is Wrong}
\label{sec:study}

Three claims in this paper fail independently of one another, and each one fails
in a way that a different kind of evidence catches. The record either reproduces
the bytes the developer's editor and agent left in the files or it does not, and
that is a question about a program, settled by running it over histories that
already exist. The grouping either lines up with the requests a developer made or
it does not, and that is a question about an inference, settled by comparing it
against sessions where somebody happened to write the requests down. A developer
either gets more of these operations right with \sgt{} than without it, or does
not, and that is a question about people. The first is finished, the second is
under way on a corpus we are still assembling, and the third is designed and not
yet run.

\smallskip\noindent\emph{We state the design of the third before we have its
results, and every number it would produce is absent from this section.} We wrote
the design out in this form because the measure that decides the argument is not
the one a reader would expect, and committing to it before the data exists is the
only way to be believed about which measure that is.

\subsection{The rebuild has to be exact}
\label{sec:eval-exact}

If \sgt{} reassembles a file into bytes that differ from what the developer left
there, then every operation in Section~\ref{sec:design} is set arithmetic over a
fiction, and nothing else in this paper is worth reading. This is the one
measurement whose failure would end the work rather than qualify it, so it goes
first and it is the only one we insist on before adoption.

The procedure follows the shape of the claim. We walk a repository's history one
commit at a time, mine each commit into records, rebuild every file from the set
of records that commit's state implies, and compare the result against the blob
git holds, byte for byte. A repository passes at a commit only if every file
matches; a single differing byte in a single file is a failure at that commit, and
we report the fraction of files that rebuild rather than an average over
repositories, because a developer cares whether their file comes back and not
whether most files do. We run this over open source Python and TypeScript
repositories chosen for length of history rather than for anything else, and over
our own, which is the hardest case available to us because five successive
versions of our miner have written into it.

Section~\ref{sec:discussion} reports the residue we have today: fifty-six files in
our own repository that no valid set of records reproduces, out of three hundred
and seventy-one recorded. That number is the honest form of this measurement, and
we would rather print it than an average that hides it. What we do not yet know is
whether fifty-six is the cost of our own format changes or the cost of the design,
and the corpus run above is how we intend to find out, since a repository \sgt{}
has never touched before cannot have our migrations in it.

\subsection{Whether the grouping matches what was asked for}

The names in every figure in this paper are inferred, and a developer who types
\cmd{sgt revert "price cache"} is trusting that inference with the contents of
their files. The question is not whether the clustering scores well against a
partition somebody drew, which is how the untangling literature is evaluated for
the good reason that its authors had nothing better to compare against
(Section~\ref{sec:related}). The question is whether the set that comes back when
a developer names one request is the set of edits that request produced.

That question needs a corpus where the requests were recorded, which agent
sessions now supply as a matter of course, since the transcript of a session names
each request and the files the agent touched while carrying it out. We mine each
repository without reading any transcript, derive a reference grouping from the
transcripts alone, and then ask two things of every request in the session. How
much of what that request produced comes back when the developer names it, and how
much else comes with it. Those two quantities are what a developer feels: the first
is the edit the revert missed and left behind in the file, and the second is the
edit belonging to a different request that the revert took out. They fail
asymmetrically, and the second is worse, because a developer who is handed too
little notices when the code still runs the way it did and a developer who is
handed too much has already lost work they meant to keep.

We expect the shared helper to be where this measurement goes wrong, because
Section~\ref{sec:names} predicts it and eight months of use have not stopped it
happening. An argument parser or a logging function that changes in nearly every
save is coupled to everything by the signal the clustering reads, and it draws
otherwise unrelated requests into one group. If most of the disagreement between
our grouping and the transcripts turns out to sit on functions of that kind, then
the fix is to weight a function's coupling down as the number of things it couples
to grows, and that is a change to one term rather than to the design. If the
disagreement is spread evenly across ordinary functions instead, then the coupling
signal is not carrying the grouping and the developer should be asked at save
time, which is the design we argued against in Section~\ref{sec:names} and would
have to argue for.

\subsection{Three requests, a transcript, and code nobody in the room wrote}

\label{sec:eval-study}
The study puts a developer in the position the paper is about, which means giving
them a repository whose code they did not write and the three sentences that
caused it. Each participant receives a five thousand line Python service, a
transcript of the session that produced its most recent hour of work, and a
request to take one of the three things in that transcript back out. This is the
state of the developer in Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} a week later, and it is also
the state of the developer who picks up a colleague's branch on a Monday, and it
is the only arrangement we found that holds the interesting variable still.
Participants who direct the agent themselves each remember a different amount of
what came back, and that remembering is the thing whose absence we are claiming
matters.

We recruit developers who use a coding agent as part of their ordinary work,
because the difficulty we describe belongs to them and to nobody else, and we ask
each of them to work through two repositories, one with git and one with \sgt{},
in a counterbalanced order. In the git condition they use whatever they normally
use, including a graphical client, since the argument is about what git's record
can express and not about anybody's command line fluency. Each repository holds
three requests whose edits interleave inside shared functions, and each has a
different set of three so that a participant who has learned the shape of the
first task cannot apply it to the second. The tasks are the three operations from
Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} with a checkable outcome: take one named request out
and leave the other two working, carry one request to a release branch on its own,
and find the earlier state of a request in order to change it. We leave the other
two scenarios out of the study because their outcome is a judgement about when to
commit and how to stack, and we would be scoring participants against our
preference rather than against a result.

A submission is correct when a script says so, and the script asks three
questions. The tests belonging to the removed request fail, the tests belonging to
the two kept requests pass, and no function outside the intended set differs from
the reference repository. That third question is the one that catches the failure
this paper is about, because a participant who removes the caching and quietly
takes half the retry policy with it has produced a repository that passes its own
tests.

Table~\ref{tab:measures} lists what we measure and what each measure would have to
show for the design to be wrong. The first row is the one that matters, and it is
worth saying plainly why. A developer who spends an extra twenty minutes
untangling a commit by hand has lost twenty minutes, and a developer who
submits a repository they believe is clean and that still calls a function they
deleted has lost something they will not find until the release branch fails to
import. Hand untangling fails silently, and a design whose whole argument is that
the developer no longer holds the decomposition has to be measured against silent
failure rather than against the clock. We collect time because a reader would
want it and because a tool that is correct and unbearably slow is not adopted, and
we would not publish a time difference as the finding.

The last two rows of Table~\ref{tab:measures} measure the prices we stated in
Section~\ref{sec:design} rather than the benefits, and they are there because a
study that measures only what a design buys is a study that cannot be wrong. Two
of the four commitments cost the developer something at a moment we can observe.
A fork stops them and they either resolve it or judge it pointless, and a wrong
label makes them type a rename or a regroup. Both are countable in the session,
and both have a threshold past which we would change the design rather than defend
it.

\subsection{Eight months on one repository}

The fourth strand is what \sgt{} has recorded of its own construction, which is
the only evidence any of this holds up past an afternoon. The system has been the
version control for its own repository since it first ran, so every commitment in
Section~\ref{sec:design} has been paid for by us daily, and two of the design
decisions in this paper exist because a default we shipped removed work we wanted
to keep. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} reports that evidence, including a safety
gate nobody in our own team configured and a coverage figure of twenty-seven
percent, and it is the one part of the evaluation whose numbers are real today. We
put it there rather than here because everything it has to say is a limit.

\subsection{What none of this would tell us}

Each of the four strands has a boundary, and three of the four cannot be pushed
past it by running more of the same.

A recorded request is not an intention. A developer who types
\emph{make the price lookup faster} holds a view of what should change that the
sentence does not contain, and the agent's response is a guess at the remainder.
The alignment we measure in the second strand is therefore alignment with what was
said, and the transcript sets a ceiling on it that no better clustering can pass.
We think this is the right measurement anyway, on the ground that what was said is
what the developer will type when they come back to remove it, but a reader who
believes intention and utterance come apart more often than we do should read that
number as an upper bound on something smaller.

Two hours with a transcript is not a week of forgetting. The cost we describe in
Section~\ref{sec:scenarios} grows as a developer's memory of the session fades,
and our design substitutes reading somebody else's transcript for that fading.
A participant who has just read three sentences knows more about the session than
the developer who typed them a week ago, so the git condition in our study is
easier than the situation it stands for, and the difference we measure understates
the one that matters. We prefer the understatement to a study nobody can run.

Our own repository has three contributors who wrote the system. The fork rule was
designed for that repository and Section~\ref{sec:discussion} says which team we
expect to switch it off, and no amount of use by us will settle that, because the
property that decides it is how many people edit one function in a day. This is
the single result we would most like a reader with a larger repository to
establish, and we have said so in the plainest terms we can find.

Finally, every task in the study has an answer a script can check, and we chose
those three tasks for that reason. The operations a developer wants most may be
the ones with no checkable answer, and deciding whether a stack of two reviews
was the right shape is one of them. We can say what \sgt{} makes possible there
and we cannot measure it, and Section~\ref{sec:discussion} keeps that distinction.

edits.new:
For as long as developers wrote the lines themselves this recovery was cheap. The
person doing it remembered writing the code, so the history had only to remind
them of a decomposition they already held~\cite{ko2006,sillito2008}. Naur argued
that a program text and its documentation are insufficient carriers of the theory
a programmer builds while writing it, and that the continued modification of a
large program therefore depends on a group of programmers in close and continuous
contact with it~\cite{naur1985}. A developer who directs an agent stands outside
that group from the first minute. They did not write the lines, they remember
nothing about them, and the theory Naur describes was held, for as long as it was
held at all, by something that discards it when the session ends.

What that developer does hold is the sentence they typed, which stated the
boundary of the change exactly, in their own words, before any of the code
existed, and which no version control system records. A history, we think, should
be regarded as a record of what its author asked for, with the text those requests
produced as the secondary product. Every system in wide use takes the opposite
view, treating the text as the record and the reasons behind it as something a
later reader reconstructs, and that view was correct for as long as the reader had
been the writer. Getting this unit wrong does not put an operation out of a
developer's reach. It makes them pay for the operation in reading, every time they
want it, and it teaches them to call ordinary difficulty what is a property of
their notation. The unit a developer decides in and the unit their repository
records have come apart.

decided against it, because answering that question takes the same knowledge
commit hygiene takes, and a developer who could reliably answer it could also have
staged the hunks. Shipman and Marshall collected the reasons people abandon
systems that ask them to formalise their own work, premature structure among them,
and the design they arrived at has the system propose a structure that its user may
accept, modify, reject, or leave alone, in place of a system that demands one
before the work is understood~\cite{shipman1999}. That is the arrangement here, and
we are applying it under easier conditions than the ones they wrote about. The
structure their systems tried to elicit was tacit, so a user asked to state it had
first to work out what they thought. The structure \sgt{} recovers was said out
loud, in a request, before any of the code existed, and the only reason it needs
recovering at all is that nothing wrote it down. What matters, then, is not whether
the guess is right but what a wrong one costs, and correcting one moves labels and
touches no recorded edit.

nobody reviewed turns into a bug three days later and the person who finds it is

This repository's history carries three git identities and one human being behind
all of them, so every merge \sgt{} has ever seen had the same person on both sides
of it. That is the condition the fork rule was designed for and the only condition
it has been tested under, and it is the condition in which the rule is most
obviously right, because the person a fork stops is the person who wrote both
versions and can therefore answer it in seconds. It is also the condition in
which the rule is cheapest, and we should not draw a conclusion about teams from
it. On a repository where twenty people edit the same functions every day, the
same rule produces a queue of decisions whose two sides were written by people who
have not spoken, and we expect that team would switch it off and take the textual
merge. Our evidence cannot tell them not to.

edits.old:
The grouping \sgt{} recovers by clustering existed before any of the code did. The
agent held it while it worked, and every agent we have used discards it when the
session ends. A record written by the agent, one entry per request naming the
functions it changed, would make the inference in Section~\ref{sec:names}
unnecessary, and it would fix the case in Section~\ref{sec:walkthrough} where a
rename nobody asked for got a name derived from the code.

We did not build that, because we are unwilling to let \sgt{} depend on any
particular agent. Reading the working files works with any agent, any editor, and a
developer typing by hand, and it keeps working when a vendor changes an output
format. A record the agent writes works only while that agent is in use, and
a developer who switched agents mid-project would find their history split into a
part with stated groupings and a part with inferred ones. We would take both
sources, with the files as the one \sgt{} trusts and the agent's account as a hint
that improves a label. We do not know which of the two should be authoritative,
and we would put that question to a reader of this paper before any other.
edits.new:
The grouping \sgt{} recovers by clustering existed before any of the code did. The
agent held it while it worked, and every agent we have used discards it when the
session ends. A record written by the agent, one entry per request naming the
functions it changed, would make the inference in Section~\ref{sec:names}
unnecessary, and it would fix the case in Section~\ref{sec:walkthrough} where a
rename nobody asked for got a name derived from the code.

Half of that record we do take, and the half we take is the half a vendor cannot
spoil. Where the developer's agent is Claude Code, \sgt{} installs a hook on
prompt submission and stores every sentence the developer typed, with its time, so
the words that named the work are on disk before any code exists and \cmd{sgt now}
answers with what was asked for rather than with a count of edits. That is twenty
lines and one vendor's hook interface, and the same twenty lines have to be
written again for the next agent, which is the price we decided we could pay,
because what they capture is the developer's own English and a change of vendor
cannot make yesterday's sentence wrong.

The half we do not take is the agent's account of which functions each request
touched, and the reason is that a record of that kind is a claim about the files
which we would have to either trust or check. Trusting it puts the correctness of
a revert inside a transcript nobody validated against the code. Checking it means
reading the files and computing the answer, at which point we did not need the
account. What the agent's account would improve is the label, which is the part of
\sgt{} that is allowed to be wrong, and improving a label is worth a hint and not
worth a dependency. So the split we have arrived at is that membership is read
from code and names are read from words, and the words come from the hook where
there is a hook and from the save message where there is not. What we do not know
is whether an agent's account of its own edits is accurate enough to move
membership too, and that is the measurement we would ask a reader of this paper to
make before any other.

\cmd{sgt log --summary} prints \cmd{371 file(s), 6781 symbol(s), 154 feature(s),
27\% entity coverage}. That last figure is the fraction of recorded files with any
function-level record at all, so roughly three quarters of this repository is
recorded as whole files, at the grain git already offers. The files in that three
quarters are Markdown, JSON, HTML, and lock files. Every operation in
Section~\ref{sec:design} runs on them and none of them gets sharper than
\cmd{git revert} would be.

How much of that three quarters is a limit of our implementation depends on the
file. Markdown, JSON, and lock files hold no functions at any grain. Go and Rust
do, and a tree-sitter grammar plus a decision about which node kinds count as a
function is a day of work per language, so we would take both tomorrow.
With every language parsed, a repository whose interesting change is four lines of
a deployment configuration still has no function for the developer's name to be
filed under, and git's grain is the correct grain for that change. We say
this plainly because calling the design language-independent would be false, and a
reader deciding whether to adopt \sgt{} should start by counting how much of their
repository is code.
edits.new:
\cmd{sgt log --summary} prints \cmd{396 file(s), 6821 symbol(s), 154 feature(s),
25\% entity coverage}. We printed that last figure for months and it is the wrong
figure, because its denominator is every file \sgt{} has a record for and its
numerator counts only the ones whose records name functions. Markdown holds no
functions at any grain, so a repository with a lot of documentation in it reads as
though \sgt{} were failing at its one job.

Counting the records themselves says something different. Of the files this
repository's store has ever recorded, 381 carry function-level records and 153 are
recorded whole. The whole-file set is 82 Markdown files, 19 JSON, 15 \LaTeX{}, 13
HTML, and a scattering of CSS, SVG, and configuration, and it contains no Python
and no TypeScript. Every file in a language \sgt{} parses has a function-level
record. The design's coverage of code is complete and its coverage of a repository
is a quarter, and those two sentences are about different things.

So the limit here is not the parser, and saying it was let us describe a property
of software repositories as though it were a defect we could fix. Go and Rust have
functions, a tree-sitter grammar plus a decision about which node kinds count as
one is a day of work per language, and we would take both tomorrow. It would not
move the quarter much. Three quarters of this repository is prose, configuration,
and generated files, that ratio is ordinary, and a change to four lines of a
deployment manifest has no function for the developer's request to be filed under
no matter how many grammars we ship. Every operation in Section~\ref{sec:design}
still runs on those files, at git's grain, and none of them gets sharper than
\cmd{git revert} would be. A reader deciding whether to adopt \sgt{} should ask how
much of the work they need to take apart happens inside functions, which is a
different question from how much of their repository is code.

developer who reads a wrong name fixes it with a rename that moves no code. An

\subsection{What a colleague sees}
\label{sec:colleague}

Because the records are files in the repository, everyone who pulls the repository
gets them whether they asked for them or not, and this section is about what that
means for the three people who did not install \sgt{}.

The one we worried about most turned out to be the easy case. A colleague who has
never heard of \sgt{} commits ordinary code, and the next \cmd{sgt sync} mines
their commits into function-level records on contact, the same way \sgt{} mined the
history that existed before it was installed. Their edits arrive at the right
grain, they group with the work they belong to, and nothing has to be repaired. What
does not arrive is the request, because there was no request to capture: their
records carry no sentence, so the name for their group is drawn from their commit
subjects, and where one subject accounts for most of a group \sgt{} uses that
subject as the name. A colleague who writes \cmd{fix tests} and \cmd{wip} gets a
group named from the code instead, which is the same failure
Section~\ref{sec:names} describes for a save with no message. So the grain
\sgt{} recovers from anybody and the request only from somebody who was running it,
and a team that half-adopts \sgt{} gets a history that is half named.

The harder case is a colleague who does install it, and runs a different version.
The identifier of an edit is computed from its content together with the version of
the miner that read it, so two versions of \sgt{} mint different identifiers for
the same edit, and a sync across that gap would quietly alias records that mean
different things. \sgt{} refuses the whole union instead and prints what to do.
That refusal is correct and it is also the cost we are least able to speak to,
because Section~\ref{sec:unreproducible} reports five miner versions inside
fifty-seven days and every one of those transitions would have stopped a
collaborator. It stopped nobody, since there was nobody to stop, and a design
decision that a solo repository charges nothing for is a decision that repository
cannot evaluate.

The third case is the reviewer, and here we have no answer at all. A pull request
that carries \sgt{} records shows them as what they are on disk, a few hundred JSON
files whose names are hashes, and no reviewer reads that. They review the code, as
they should. But it means the record that makes \cmd{revert} work is not part of
what anybody approved, so a resolution one developer reasoned through and a label
another corrected both enter the shared branch unexamined. Section~\ref{sec:fork}
argues that a fork should be settled by a person on the ground that a silent merge
inside one function surfaces later as somebody else's bug. On a team, the person who
settles it is still one person, and the review that would have caught them being
wrong reads a diff their decision does not appear in.

\subsection{Version control that already knew about functions}
\label{sec:priorfine}

Recording a version at the grain of a function has been built before, more than
once, and the reason none of it displaced the commit is the reason we think it can
now. Historage rewrites a Java repository so that every method sits in a file of
its own, at which point git's existing machinery gives each method a history of
its own~\cite{hata2011}, and FinerGit refines the file format so that git's rename
detection keeps working when a method moves~\cite{higo2020}. Stellation and Coven
made the fine-grained unit the thing the repository stores rather than a
transformation applied to it, so a developer could check out a single method and a
team could see which methods their colleagues had
open~\cite{chucarroll2002,chucarroll2000}. MolhadoRef settled the problem
Section~\ref{sec:identity} reports as our weakest link, by having the development
environment record each refactoring as the developer performed it, so a rename
entered the history as an operation instead of arriving as something a later tool
had to guess at~\cite{dig2007}. Mylyn recorded, for each task a developer worked
on, the set of program elements they touched while working on it, and used that set
to decide what the environment showed them~\cite{kersten2006}. All of this existed
at least fifteen years before the first coding agent, all of it worked, and a
working programmer today uses none of it.

We do not read that as a failure of engineering, because a finer grain buys a
developer only what they cannot already supply for themselves, and until recently
they could supply all of it. Whoever wanted the caching out of a 2010 repository
had written the caching, so a system that told them which methods it touched was
performing work they had already done, and the price of being told was a repository
their colleagues could not clone with plain git. What has changed is not the value
of the grain but the identity of the author, and a record that was redundant while
the developer wrote the lines is the only surviving copy of the decomposition once
they have stopped writing them. Mylyn's task context and \sgt{}'s named group of
edits are the same object built for two different situations, and the difference is
that Mylyn watched a developer's attention move through code that developer was
writing, whereas the attention \sgt{} reconstructs belonged to a process that has
already exited.

The merge question in this literature was approached from the end opposite to ours.
Horwitz, Prins and Reps showed that two versions of a program can be integrated
automatically when a semantic analysis proves the changes do not interfere, and
that it is the analysis which licenses the guarantee~\cite{horwitz1989}. Apel et
al.'s semistructured merge parses a file far enough to see that two edits landed in
different methods, and resolves a large share of what a line-based merge reports as
a conflict~\cite{apel2011}. Lippe and van Oosterom argued for merging the
operations rather than the states~\cite{lippe1992}, Zeller and Snelting put the
area on a formal footing by treating a version as a set with a logic over it, which
is the construction Section~\ref{sec:sets} uses~\cite{zeller1997}, and the
distributed systems literature arrived at the same shape from another direction in
the conflict-free replicated data types~\cite{shapiro2011}. \sgt{} goes the other
way from the first two deliberately. Where semistructured merge combines two edits
to one method as soon as it can see they touch different lines, \sgt{} stops and
asks a person, and Section~\ref{sec:fork} makes that argument where the rule is
stated while Section~\ref{sec:forkoff} concedes that a repository with one person
in it is the wrong place to have tested it.

edits.new:
\section{Introduction}

A version control system should record the changes made by a developer in a way
that is both revisitable and reversible. Most of them therefore record the
artefact the programmer wrote, lines of code, throughout the development life
cycle, whether by recording snapshots of the codebase~\cite{git2026} or a
sequence of changes to those lines~\cite{roundy2005,pijul2024}. This is a
reasonable design choice, because code is authored by the developer, who
possesses at least a rough idea of when, how, and why it was
changed~\cite{naur1985,ko2006}. With the practice of the last few years of
writing code through large language models, where developers specify prompts in
natural language in a much vaguer form and the model translates them into a
series of code edits~\cite{sarkar2025}, we question whether this design choice
still holds.

In practice we find three places where the design philosophy of current version
control systems misfits the new workflow. First, the codebase is highly iterated.
Models make prototyping very easy, and tools like Lovable, Bolt.new, v0, and
Replit generate an entire codebase from a single prompt, marketed on the premise
that what they produce is finished software, which is arguably only true when that
software has no bugs and is tolerably aligned with what the developer was
imagining. We do not claim that writing code will be automated away in the near
future, but this reflects how capable models are at generating large chunks of
code across files, through the features of the software, iterating over interface
components, and so on, and what matters is no longer where a line of code was but
what the version of the feature was two turns ago. Across 211 million changed
lines authored between 2020 and 2024, the share associated with refactoring,
which is to say lines being moved into a better position rather than written
afresh, fell from a quarter to under a tenth, while copied lines rose from 8.3\%
to 12.3\% and overtook moved lines for the first time~\cite{gitclear2025}, so a
line is now replaced faster than it settles into a position worth recording.

Second, prompts in natural language are underspecified and lack the detail that
code carries~\cite{sarkar2025}. This means there will always be large chunks of
code carrying logic that the model inferred during implementation and that the
developer only becomes aware of reactively. Barke et al.\ describe programmers in
this mode reading what comes back for the shape they expected rather than line by
line~\cite{barke2023}, Tang et al.\ found that developers often do not notice
which code a model wrote, and delete and rewrite it rather than repair it when
something is wrong~\cite{tang2024}, and among 410 developers surveyed by Liang et
al., understanding and trusting generated code was one of the most frequently
reported difficulties~\cite{liang2024}. Version control over code that never
existed in the developer's memory loses the purpose of version control, which is
that a programmer can trace back to the version they desired, because a history
can only be searched with the words that person already has.

Third, prompts are mostly constituted by what the programmer desires to do,
rather than, as they once were, by specifying the location of files and the target
of interest for the change. In that sense, developers are constructing their
theory about the codebase~\cite{naur1985} at the level of what a feature of the
software is, the components in the interface, the policy for retries, the stages
in the pipeline, none of which currently serves as the unit a version control
system records. This is the level the comprehension literature has always found
people working at: Biggerstaff et al.\ called recovering which functions
implement a named concern the concept assignment problem~\cite{biggerstaff1993},
and the feature location field exists because answering it by reading code is
expensive~\cite{dit2013}. The commit is the closest thing a version control
system offers and it is not the same unit, since Herzig and Zeller found changes
serving several unrelated purposes throughout the histories of five open source
Java projects~\cite{herzig2013}, and an agent session produces exactly that,
because a commit ends where the developer stopped to type a command and a request
ends somewhere else.

We thus describe a new version control system, which we designed to version
control the highly iterated codebase at the more semantic level of the feature,
where each version of the code is a set of edits filed across those features.
Instead of version controlling the line of code, we parse each file into its
functions and classes~\cite{treesitter} and record one edit per changed function,
where each edit names the function, the version it started from, the version it
produced, and the other functions the new code refers to. We then group those
functions into features from which ones changed in the same save, which ones call
one another, and where they
sit~\cite{zimmermann2004,ying2004,traag2019}, and label each group with the words
the developer and the agent used while the work was happening. A version is then
a set of these edits held to two rules, that no edit is included without the edits
it was built on and that each function has one included version, and the files on
disk are rebuilt by writing out the included version of every function and
leaving the text between them alone.

For example, a service that answers price quotes for a trading dashboard has a
handler, a database layer, and a set of row accessors. On Monday the developer
prompts \cmd{cache the price lookup, it takes 400ms and the price barely moves},
and the agent writes \sym{cache.py::get\_cached} and \sym{cache.py::\_ttl}, gives
\sym{db.py::query} a parameter for how long a cached price stays good so the cache
can pass one through, and changes \sym{api.py::handle} to consult the cache before
the database. That is six edits to four functions in three files, and the two in
\sym{cache.py} share no line with the one in \sym{api.py}, yet all six are filed
under one name. Over the next two days two further prompts change
\sym{api.py::handle} again, one adding a rate limit and one adding a retry policy,
and a colleague adds a metric for quote latency. Three weeks later the developer
finds the dashboard showing a price sixty seconds stale, so they type
\cmd{sgt revert "price cache"}. \sgt{} prints the six edits that would come out,
names \sym{api.py::handle} as the one function where later work was built on
something being removed, shows the text each change would produce, and asks before
touching anything. The rate limit and the retry policy stay, because their edits
are still included; the colleague's metric stays, because it was never in the set
coming out; and the parameter leaves both \sym{db.py::query} and
\sym{api.py::handle}, because both were in it. When the developer decides a week
later that the cache was worth keeping after all, \cmd{sgt restore} returns the
files byte for byte, because putting the six edits back is the same set arithmetic
as taking them out and nothing is replayed as a patch.
Figure~\ref{fig:two-records} draws that Monday under both records, and
Section~\ref{sec:walkthrough} follows this repository through five sittings.

Three prices are paid for this, all of them in the first hour of use rather than
in some later edge case. Two edits to the same function made from the same
starting point are recorded as competing versions that a person has to decide
between, including the pair at opposite ends of a fifty line function that touch
no common line and that git would have merged without comment. The grouping of
edits into named requests is inferred, so it is a guess and it will sometimes be
wrong, and correcting it costs the developer a rename, a merge, or a split, none
of which moves a recorded edit. \sgt{} reads Python, TypeScript, and TSX and
versions every other file whole, at the grain git already uses, so a repository
whose interesting logic is written in Go gets nothing from \sgt{} today.

The paper makes four contributions. We characterise the mismatch between the unit
a developer using an agent decides in and the unit a version control system
records, one attempted operation at a time (Section~\ref{sec:scenarios}), in the
style of conceptual analysis Pérez De Rosso and Jackson applied to git
itself~\cite{perezderosso2013,perezderosso2016}. We describe \sgt{}'s design as
four commitments, say what each one buys and what it costs, and run the whole set
of operations on one repository (Sections~\ref{sec:design}
and~\ref{sec:walkthrough}). We state which observation would show each of our
claims to be wrong, and fix the design of the study that would produce it before
we hold its results (Section~\ref{sec:study}). We report what fifty-seven days of
\sgt{} versioning its own construction has taught us about where the design
breaks down, which is the one part of this paper whose numbers are real today
(Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).

work they measure changed inside that span. Barke et al.\ watched 20 programmers
and found them using the model
in two ways, finishing a line they had already planned, or asking for a starting
point in code they did not yet know how to write~\cite{barke2023}. Vaithilingam
et al.\ found that 24 participants using Copilot did not complete tasks faster
and still preferred to keep it on, because it gave them a draft to work
from~\cite{vaithilingam2022}, and Sarkar et al.\ collected what the experience
felt like from the developer's side~\cite{sarkar2022}. In both studies the
developer accepted a line or a block of code. Four years later SWE-bench
gives a model a natural language issue report from a real repository and scores

the systems built to score well on it edit several files in a

All of this work studies the minutes around acceptance, asking whether the code
is correct~\cite{perry2023}, whether the developer can tell that it is
correct~\cite{vasconcelos2025}, whether they trust
it~\cite{liang2024,cheng2024}, and how much faster they
finish~\cite{mozannar2024,cui2025}, and it stops once the developer has said yes.
A week later that same developer wants to remove the caching they asked
for and keep the rate limiting they asked for in the same hour, and removing one
and keeping the other is a version control operation. We know of
no study of what happens to agent-written code after it is committed. Acceptance is
where this literature's outcome measures end, so none of them can say what the code
costs to own, and the cost of owning it is what a version control system is for.
